title: Ethics of care and female sacrifice in Puella Magi Madoka Magica
abstract: Puella Magi Madoka Magica (2011) is an anime television series that imagines an alternate world in which teenage girls have served as magical girls, who fight against witches and stop them from cursing and killing people, for centuries. However, these girls’ sacrifices for their local communities will eventually drive them to despair and turn them into the witches. It is only through the titular character, Madoka, that the exploitative system can be disrupted. This paper engages with the ethics of care to interrogate the ways in which the anime show offers (re-)imaginations of female sacrifice, a notion that threads through the show. Care ethicists such as Nel Noddings (2013) and Inge van Nistelrooij (2014, 2017) have suggested that it is not necessarily a patriarchal idea for female subjects to sacrifice themselves; instead, it may be proper for one to sacrifice herself when it attests her identity and preserves her value. This paper argues that Puella Magi Madoka Magica simultaneously critiques the form of sacrifice that leads to the carer’s self-erasure and recasts sacrifice as a manifestation of the carer’s relational identity, self-care, and resistance to any systems that exploit (girls’) care.

title: Normalising consent and co-ordinating intimacy in Normal People (Lenny Abrahamson; Hettie Macdonald, Ireland/UK, BBC Three/RTÉ One/Hulu 2020)
abstract: In Sex and the Series (2019), Brey points out that whilst online movements have opened up a public space to talk about scarring sexual encounters, too frequently the stories told are ones where in private women did not have the words to express how they felt. Adapting Brey’s premise towards a study of intimacy on screen, through close textual analysis of Normal People I argue that two strategies are adopted to (audio)visualise intimacy in the adaption: first, it is verbalised through key scenes in which consent is foregrounded and second it is expertly choreographed by intimacy co-ordinator Ita O’Brien.

title: Television’s scalar play: Invitations to scalar thinking across the intimate and the global
abstract: This article examines how contemporary television engages with scale, arguing that the medium routinely prompts viewers to navigate conceptually between micro and macro perspectives. Bringing television studies into dialogue with scale theory, the article demonstrates how diverse programmes – using The Last of Us (2023–present), Familier som vores [ Families Like Ours ] (2024), Eurovision Song Contest (1956–present) and UEFA Champions League (1956–present) as case studies – mobilise narrative, thematic and visual strategies of scalar play that invite the viewer to conduct scalar thinking across individual experiences, collective formations and planetary frameworks. Aerial views, long shots emphasising size differences, glocal address and repeated returns to life-sized close-ups invite audiences to consider their position within networks that extend beyond the human. While television often re-centres anthropocentric perspectives through its grammar of intimacy, these scalar dynamics still encourage meaningful shifts in perception. The article argues that television’s routine engagements with scale cultivate everyday multi-scalar awareness.

title: Cultural specificity and transnational coproduction: A case study of Irish/New Zealand crime drama, The Gone
abstract: This article offers a case study in transnational coproduction using Irish/New Zealand crime drama serial, The Gone (TVNZ/RTÉ, 2023-24), the first major coproduction between these countries. Examining The Gone ’s exemplification of what Havens’ (2018) terms ‘conspicuous localism’, the article links the cultural equality that characterised this drama’s writing and filming to the maximisation of cultural specificity in the finished show. Informed by interview insights from The Gone ’s producers and writers, the article foregrounds creative processes for high-end drama, and reveals the continuing importance of traditional coproduction pathways when SVoD investment is unavailable, for high-end TV dramas produced in small markets.

title: “Getting along with despair”: finding healing within the post-apocalypse
abstract: This paper focuses on the manga-turned-anime, Shoujo Shuumatsu Ryokou , to analyze the potential for the hybrid genre of post-apocalyptic iyashi-kei to transcend the neoliberal ideologies that tend to characterize each genre respectively. Iyashi-kei, translated to mean ‘healing’, is a category of self-care that prioritizes control over one’s ambiance to help individuals regulate the psychosomatic self. In observing how these qualities manifest in post-apocalyptic television, I argue that iyashi-kei healing leverages the post-apocalyptic genre to embrace the potentials of queer failure and aligning the self with the Other, while simultaneously rejecting repro-futurism.

title: “I don’t want to be a Hulk. I just got my own office!”: She-Hulk: Attorney at Law (2022) and representations of gendered corporate cultures
abstract: This article analyses, through a feminist media studies lens, the representations of corporate cultures portrayed within the Marvel series She-Hulk: Attorney at Law (2022) produced for Disney+. The protagonist, Jennifer Walters, in both “normal Jen” and “She-Hulk” forms, is forced to navigate numerous gendered environments and expectations as part of working within the legal profession as a defence lawyer. The show, in line with popular forms of western fourth wave feminism engages with numerous contemporary gender issues, including women’s safety, expectations of normative femininity, workplace identity, and diversity work. This article explores how the character of Jen/She-Hulk, within the parameters of the superhero comedy form, provides a site for pop culture critique of the gendered aesthetic and emotional labour women undertake within corporate workplaces, as well as the diversity work expected of women and racially minoritised people. In a post #MeToo context the series makes sophisticated use of its comedic elements to humorously examine the pressures women experience when working in male-dominated corporate environments.

title: Movie halls and cinema-theatres. A failed ‘second birth’ of film exhibition in 1910s non-urban Lombardy
abstract: This article uses the Lombardy region as a case study to examine the emergence of cinemas in non-urban Italian areas between 1905 and 1920. The main hypothesis is that the so-called ‘second birth of cinema’ (the establishment of dedicated commercial movie halls with daily screenings, which followed the initial birth of film exhibition in non-dedicated venues) was unsuccessful in rural and small-town Italy, leading to the development of cinema-theatres instead. Unlike dedicated movie halls, cinema-theatres (often under the control of associations, including mutual-aid societies) were politicised, mainly active on weekends and open to different forms of entertainment. The persistence of cinema-theatres lasted for decades and indicates a slower commercialisation and autonomisation of leisure time. The article also addresses the methodological importance of accounting for geographical differences in the spread of cinemas of different types. The historical materials consulted are varied and come from state archives, the local press, and municipal archives, the latter of which have been underused thus far.

title: Introducing and Institutionalizing the Projection Lantern into University Teaching in England and Scotland (1880-1914)*
abstract: While historians of the optical lantern in academic teaching at universities have rarely discussed the financial aspects of slide lectures, departmental funding was critical in accommodating the projected image as a teaching tool in the service of this educational project. Between 1880 and 1914, the governors and financial committees provided subsidies that were approved by administrators and departments, allowing the projection lantern to become institutionalized in some English and Scottish universities. During the 1880s, lecturers struggled to incorporate lanterns into their daily activities because the apparatus and slide making facilities were expensive and time-consuming. Between the 1890s and 1910s, funding for the sciences and photography departments resulted in the expansion and diversification of the academic lantern and slide use across multiple departments. Reading lantern practices through the analysis of financial records, manuals, and photography journals reveals that the practicalities of transitioning from benchtop demonstration to gas-lit lanterns to electrification stood in stark contrast to individual lecturer innovation and inert university infrastructure. This analysis sheds light on the development of the projection lantern as a teaching tool in England and Scotland, as well as why educational institutions like Yorkshire College, Edinburgh University, University of Glasgow, and University College Bristol were able to produce and store large quantities of lantern slides. Examining the integration of projection lanterns in academic teaching from a funding perspective uncovers the pedagogical, sociopolitical, and bureaucratic reasons that influenced their development and institutionalization in English and Scottish universities. This analysis also argues for a business and economics approach to the optical lantern as an academic innovation, seeking to identify the various factors that created a conducive environment for accommodating projected images as teaching tools in this educational initiative.

title: Animalizing the political other: Qian Binghe’s caricatures of Yuan Shikai and revolutionary propaganda in early Republican China
abstract: This article examines Chinese political caricature in the early 1910s, focusing on Qian Binghe (1879–1944) and his caricatured depictions of Yuan Shikai (1859–1916), the first president of the Republic of China. A staunch revolutionary aligned with Sun Yat-sen, Qian opposed both the Manchu dynasty and Yuan’s authoritarian rule. Despite his contributions, his political caricatures remain underexamined. This article investigates how Qian Binghe’s revolutionary engagements intersected with his deployment of animalized imagery to visually construct political otherness in early Republican China. Central to this analysis is Qian’s use of animal imagery, particularly the homophonic association between ‘ape’ (yuan) and Yuan Shikai’s surname, in his collections A Pictorial History of the Yuan Shikai Government (1913) and A Hundred Performances of Old Ape (1913). I argue that Qian’s caricatures, by animalizing Yuan Shikai and circulating this representation through revolutionary propaganda networks, constructed the president as a political other. His work reflects broader political struggles between pro-Sun revolutionaries and Yuan’s government, as well as tensions among various political and ethnic factions in early Republican China. By bestializing Yuan Shikai, Qian’s drawings offer a dissident perspective on Republican politics, particularly opposition to Yuan’s imperial ambitions. As one of the earliest political cartoon collections of the Republican era, Qian’s works provide a critical lens for understanding the entanglements between visual culture, print media, and politics in China’s transitional years.

title: Brownhills Pottery ABC plates and transmedia Crusoe
abstract: Offering the first text- and media-analytical study of the set of Robinson Crusoe ABC plates the Staffordshire Brownhills Pottery produced in the late Victorian period, this article will trace the transmedial use of transfer-printed illustrations for the literacy-formational purpose of these ceramic objects. It will discuss the plates’ uses of two previously identified illustrations that Sir John Gilbert had produced for Nelson & Sons’ 1860 edition of Robinson Crusoe and identify the sources of the designs for other plates in the set, specifically three die cuts and another illustration. The greater part of the article will examine the transmedial adaptation, including the altering, of the illustrations. It will study how the Brownhills plates generated a multi-medial version of Robinson Crusoe that, in significant ways, departed from the reading protocols of the original image material and how the meanings of the designs on the plates were shaped by their new material modality and media environment.

title: The art and science of the nineteenth-century lantern show: towards an intersectional media history of images
abstract: The late nineteenth-century lantern shows were public platforms for intermixing the arts and sciences. Their display of still images spanned various spheres of knowledge and culture, from art history to astronomy to the actualities of the day, and the events could take the form of stage art performances, media spectacles or science lectures. The aim of this article is to examine how the nineteenth-century lantern show intersected the arts and sciences and what this could imply for what I propose to call an intersectional media history of images. To that end, the study sets out to bridge the two research traditions of image studies and media history. In three example cases the article shows: 1) how lantern images of world exhibitions, which played on a double representation of extensive sites and sight as the sense of extension, were part of a set of conceptual interlinks between the media, arts and sciences of vision; 2) how a series of astronomy lectures embedded scientific photographs of celestial bodies in a staging of the sublime; 3) how lectures on a South Polar expedition intertwined art-historical image conventions with a photographic slide series documenting, among other things, cartographic findings. These examples also align Swedish materials with the recent discussions of international lantern practices. Finally, the article considers how the case of the lantern shows can inform a broader intersectional media history of images.

title: Cosmoramas, immersive viewing and the evolution of peep practice
abstract: The cosmorama was one of the most common forms of visual show between 1820 and 1860. Exhibited widely across Europe and the Americas, it has nonetheless been overshadowed by scholarship on the more large-scale formats of the panorama, diorama and magic lantern. This is partly because it is often conflated with the peepshow due to them sharing very similar features: both formats engrossed and entranced by having audiences view painted scenes through large convex lenses. Yet the cosmorama (which itself had a number of cognate names) is important as a distinct genus, part of a family of immersive lens-based viewing formats. The cosmorama demonstrates how ‘peep practice’ diversified in response in response to new audience constituencies and display opportunities in the first half of the nineteenth century. It was a vital agent in taking pictures to the people, engaging bourgeois viewers in cities across Europe. Through a detailed study of cosmorama exhibition in Britain, this article demonstrates that the cosmorama was a key part of the proliferation of popular shows beyond established and formal venues. It was in the vanguard of pop-up shows that could open in all types of city centre locations, moving between these and established fairground circuits. Finally, the cosmorama illuminates the hitherto overlooked development of transnational networks of exhibition, with a number of examples of European showpeople visiting Britain.

title: ‘Smile or weep even in the social circle’: secrecy, sharing, and the circulation of affect with Stanhope microphotographic viewers
abstract: ‘Stanhope’ viewers are optical bijoux most popular in the 1860s, when they were first mass-produced in France, although they were widely available in Britain. These small novelty items contained a microscopic photograph (microphotograph) that could only be viewed or indeed seen through a tiny cylindrical magnifying lens, which was often hidden in the design of the object. Stanhopes were developed in the context of a rich media ecology. They draw on the work of John Benjamin Dancer and René Dagron in microphotography. They join kaleidoscopes, stereoscopes, and peep eggs as domestic peep media, and they stand with cosmoramas and microscopes themselves as peep practices dependent on magnification for effect. Although Dagron marketed them with hints of luxury and mystery, they were inexpensive mementoes available to purchasers for only a shilling. Stanhopes were often sold as souvenirs, fitted with microphotographs of notable places, but they could also be customized with personal images, such as photographs of friends or family members. This essay argues that Stanhopes were a uniquely affordable, adaptable, accessible, and portable way to reanimate and circulate memory and affect. They promised both secrecy and sociality. Stanhopes offer a unique perspective on Victorian tourism and souvenirs, fashion and jewelry, religious sentiment and death culture, and even erotica. With a Stanhope in hand, Victorians could readily access a hidden photographic image and stir up or share recollected love, friendship, faith, nostalgia, or desire.

title: Multilayered enactments of A Christmas Carol in magic lantern shows
abstract: This article examines the multilayered enactments of the visual, auditory, and dramatic features of Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol (1843) through the medium of the magic lantern show in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It maps the complex processes by which the familiar story is translated into optical spectacles and reveals how they generate new interpretations. To illustrate these processes, the study analyses seven lantern versions of the story’s book illustrations, especially John Leech’s ‘Mr. Fezziwig’s Ball’. It shows how the removal of characters, shifts in perspective, and modifications to accompanying readings re-perform and transform the tale, imbuing it with authenticity and immediacy. Building on these pictorial transformations, life model slides (enabled by advances in photography) emulate the intra-iconic elements of illustrations, merge them with the extra-iconic embodied performances of models, and thereby layer these re-enactments. Artists, stage managers, photographers, and colouring assistants each contribute their own interpretations through interlocking practices, which blur the boundaries between extratextual and intratextual realms and engage audiences in immersive narrative experiences. To deliver a multimedia, multisensory experience, magic lantern performances of the fictional story were often clustered with other disparate attractions under unifying themes such as An Evening with Dickens. These optical presentations of Dickens’s biography and real-world locations, together with other pictorial, musical, and theatrical performances, reinscribe the medium’s polyvocal nature. By examining these performances, this article charts the iconic, photographic, and polyvocal enactments to demonstrate the evolution of the Christmas tale in Victorian and Edwardian lantern culture.

title: Spellbound: encounters between the spectatorial regimes of spiritualism, hypnosis, and cinema in nineteenth-century Barcelona
abstract: This article explores the continuity, kinship, and process of substitution between supernatural spectacles and cinema in Barcelona from the second half of the nineteenth century onward. More specifically, it examines the turning-tables fad and the reception of hypnotists’ shows in the city in order to understand how cinema later appealed, often in the same venues, to bodies and gazes equally eager for marvellous experiences. The filmic medium is thus approached as a late agent of the modern supernatural, although this spectatorial connection would be blurred by early popular films depicting practices of spiritism and hypnosis in a parodic or pejorative manner. Nevertheless, the entanglement between cinematic wonder and the legacies of mesmerism rested on a shared field of knowledge and practices, including parallels between scenic apparatuses and a mode of reception apparently based on contagion among spellbound audiences.

title: Itinerant cosmorama practices and exhibition networks in Northwestern Europe: Carl Georg Enslen’s travelling ‘room journeys’ (1810s–1860s)
abstract: This article explores the development and circulation of itinerant cosmoramas in Northwestern Europe between the 1810s and 1860s, relating them to the vibrant fairground culture of the period. Fairs are recognized as venues for showcasing visual and optical media, including cosmorama displays. Drawing parallels with travelling entertainment like ballad singing and peep box exhibitions, this study posits that cosmoramas quickly emerged as ambulant variants of stationary ‘room journeys’, following established fairground circuits across Northwestern Europe. Re-examining the itinerant nature of these largely forgotten attractions, which appeared under a wide variety of names, this study elaborates on the cosmorama attraction of Carl Georg Enslen (1792–1866), a renowned artist in his time who toured extensively across Europe between 1816 and 1866. The analysis of his circulation and display strategies highlights that while fairs were major public exhibition venues, they represent only part of the broader exhibition networks and practices of itinerant cosmorama attractions.

title: Cosmoramas and the emergence of bourgeois spectatorship in nineteenth-century Spain
abstract: This paper examines the emergence of cosmoramas in Spain during the 1830s as a key element in the formation of new modes of spectatorship, developing in parallel to the consolidation of the liberal society under the reign of Isabel II (1833–1868). It traces the proliferation of such spectacles through an analysis of newspaper advertisements and archival materials related to cosmorama shows held in Madrid and Barcelona. Initially, itinerant performances dominated the scene. However, by the late 1830s, permanent venues operated by local figures gained prominence, such as the Galería Topográfica in Madrid and the optical shows organized by Felipe Maglia and Francesc Dalmau in Barcelona. Central to this analysis is a material case study of the cosmorama dispositif based on the uniquely surviving example preserved in the Museu del Cinema in Girona. This new form of entertainment ensured spatial separation and order through its very dispositif. Unlike earlier optical boxes, cosmoramas invited viewers to physically move from lens to lens, simulating the act of traveling through the images themselves. The aim of this study is to investigate how cosmoramas shaped the visual landscape, redefining agents, networks, and social spaces in both major cities.

title: ‘Amputating the sick man’: metaphorical representations of Ottoman and Chinese weakness in Western political cartoons, 1876–1909
abstract: This article examines the parallel usage of the ‘Sick Man of Europe’ metaphor and its extension, the ‘Sick Man of Asia’, as monikers for the Ottoman Empire and China, respectively, in the Euro-American illustrated press between 1876 and 1909. Often referenced, this phenomenon is little analyzed. Political cartoons published in popular periodicals portrayed the Ottoman Empire and China as ‘sick men’, supplementing a prolific textual construction of parity between the Ottoman Empire and China. These directly compared the Ottoman Empire and China and utilized similar motifs of Orientalization and weakness to discuss individual states. While this metaphor illustrated the condescending attitude of Western observers towards each empire’s ‘decline’, its visual flexibility also facilitated the portrayal of ‘recovery’ following perceived political and military accomplishments. The intimate link between metaphors of sickness and metaphors for partitioning the Ottoman and Chinese states is established, and the thematic characteristics of, commonalities, and differences between British, American, and French cartoons portraying the metaphorical partitions of the Ottoman Empire and China are systematically examined in this light. Finally, it is shown that the designation of the Ottoman Empire and China as ‘sick men’ was internalized by Ottoman and Chinese constitutionalist reformers who themselves perpetuated discourses of Ottoman and Chinese weaknesses, respectively, in the domestic publication of reformist cartoons. These demonstrate an inchoate reciprocal admiration between Ottoman and Chinese reformists, the latter of which were particularly cognizant of the usage of the ‘sick man’ metaphor to describe both states.

title: The cosmorama as republican experimentation in nineteenth-century Latin America
abstract: This article examines the place of the cosmorama in public life in postrevolutionary Latin America. It argues that, as both a social practice and a recurring rhetorical figure, the cosmorama served to imagine and configure collective social actors during a time marked by what Hilda Sábato has called ‘republican experimentation’, when the new nations of the region struggled to identify and define the pueblo, or people, in order to secure legitimacy. Cosmoramas began appearing with regularity during the early 1830s, and the advertisements in local print media consistently promoted these spectacles with a cosmopolitan discourse that imagined a rapprochement between Latin America and the societies of the north Atlantic. Examining how letrados, or men of letters, such as the Chilean Mariano Egaña and the Venezuelan Simón Rodríguez incorporated references to the cosmorama in their writings indicates how they regarded its techniques of exhibition, namely the ordered, collective viewing of select landscapes, as potentially productive in the service of a republican pedagogy for (in)forming citizens. Last, an analysis of the frontispiece of the costumbrista anthology Los cubanos pintados por sí mismos, which depicts a crowd gathering around a tutilimundi, or portable peepshow box, reinforces the linkages between spectacle and literature, reading and seeing. In synthesis, the cosmorama helped shape the experience of political modernity in Latin America.

title: Imperial visions on tour: cosmoramas, neoramas, and Eurocentrism in Andorfer’s Grand Optical Gallery
abstract: This article explores the international journey of the Grand Optical Gallery (1828–1854), operated by Austrian showman Thomas Karl Andorfer, with a particular focus on the unique combination of optical attractions it offered, including cosmoramas, neoramas, dioramas, and a new solar microscope. It investigates the Eurocentric perspective embedded in Andorfer’s exhibitions and the cultural impact of these shows, especially in Brazil, his first overseas destination. Drawing on historical press records, the article traces Andorfer’s itinerary from the early fairs in Italy, where he showcased his Grand Cosmorama, through the Iberian Peninsula and Brazil, culminating on Broadway, where the Grand Optical Gallery was met with acclaim. In Brazil, Eurocentrism became especially pronounced as local audiences began to demand specific iconographic adjustments to the exhibitions. This article argues that, much like panoramas, cosmoramas were entangled with imperialist discourses from their inception, fostering an imperially oriented worldview among spectators. This mindset is starkly illustrated in Brazilian newspapers, where advertisements for cosmorama shows appeared alongside slave sale notices, revealing how such spectacles were embedded in broader colonial economies. By situating cosmoramas within this context, the article analyses how they functioned as cultural commodities that reinforced colonial identities and shaped their viewers’ cultural imagination. Finally, it considers the extent to which the cosmorama, as a global phenomenon, was influenced by and responsive to local cultural contexts.

title: Autosociobiography and social mobility: An introduction to the special issue
authors: Mike Savage; Sam Friedman; Carlos Spoerhase
abstract: This introduction explains why the autosociobiography genre offers the potential for an innovative and important way to link sociological research on social mobility with literary scholarship. It introduces and contextualises the papers included in this special issue.

title: Beyond the ‘Scholarship Boy’ paradigm: Autosociobiography and social mobility
authors: Sam Friedman; Mike Savage; Carlos Spoerhase
abstract: This article reflects on the potential of the rapidly emerging literary genre of autosociobiography to extend analyses of the personal experience and feelings associated with social mobility. We reflect on the congruence of its themes regarding the dislocating and isolating effects of upward social mobility with important recent research in qualitative sociology, which have exposed the weakness of quantitative social scientific studies for understanding the ‘social mobility malaise’. We argue that the theme of dislocation, sometimes encapsulated in the phrase that the upwardly mobile are ‘fish out of water’, can be rooted back to a paradigm of the ‘scholarship boy’, originating in the 1950s. We discuss how autosociobiography is a vital genre because it radicalises this framing and provides more critical and provocative perspectives which are more attuned to the period of intensifying economic inequalities in the early 21st century. Drawing on Jaquet’s arguments regarding ‘transclasses’, and reflecting on numerous autosociobiographical accounts, and recent sociological contributions, our article demonstrates the interdisciplinary reach of this genre.

title: ‘I’d like to thank the academy’ – Social mobility, education and literary form
abstract: This article analyses the entanglements of sociological research on social mobility and autosociobiographies (class-transition narratives) in France. This emerging and very successful genre has, since Didier Eribon’s Returning to Reims , established itself as a literary form. Drawing on recent autosociobiographies from sociologists, I discuss the critical contribution made by those that came in the wake of Eribon to the ongoing debate on upward mobility via education and ‘widening participation’ campaigns within elite French universities. The article demonstrates that central elements of the debate, such as the figure of the ‘scholarship boy/girl’ and the costs of such efforts – most notably, psychosocial uprooting – are shaped both by sociology and literature. While literature’s renewed interest in class and social inequality demonstrates the critical potential and impact of the genre, my study also interrogates the consequences and risks of the boom in autosociobiography: namely the showcasing of individual success-through-education and the danger of the genre being perceived as an academic one, since it is mainly academics (sociologists inclusive) who feel such a narrative ‘transclass’ desire.

title: Before the educated and individualised transfuge de classe : Autobiographical narratives of social advancement in the 19th and early 20th centuries
abstract: Research and public debate on social mobility is often based on a specific conception of social mobility. We typically think of long-distance intergenerational mobility of individuals, paradigmatically between the working class and the educated middle class. Autosociobiographies, although critical of optimistic assessments of social mobility, are based on the same paradigm. This article explores the historical diversity of understandings of social mobility, aiming to historicise our current concept. It presents a small number of typical examples drawn from a sample of 530 German-language autobiographies and life-story interviews with men and women born into the working or lower middle classes between 1830 and 1950. I analyse which concepts of social mobility these people use to narrate their social trajectories. I also ask whether they attribute social mobility more to individual effort and merit or to external factors, and how this shapes the personal identities crafted in these autobiographical accounts. This article argues that our current understanding is the result of a long-term shift: There is a trend towards individualised conceptions of social mobility. Abstract notions of achievement have replaced older morally charged concepts when it comes to explanations of social mobility. Education has only gradually come to the centre of popular ideas about social advancement.

title: Zombie states, adrenalised academics and spectral shadows: A transclass perspective on social mobility
abstract: The over-riding theme of autobiographical social mobility narratives is the celebration of individual success. However, the analysis in Chantel Jacquet’s book Transclasses develops a very different understanding. In this article, I draw on Jacquet’s interpretation, and Bourdieu’s concept of habitus, to weave into a common thread social mobility strands from writing from across the 20th and 21st centuries. First, I look at Education and the Working Class , written in the 1960s, followed by Pierre Bourdieu’s Sketch for a Self-Analysis . I interlace both texts with contemporary writing by Cynthia Cruz and Fran Lock, poets and essayists from US and UK working-class backgrounds, and my own autobiographical writing, in order to develop a perspective that recognises the salience of gender for social mobility journeys. Throughout, I draw on the concept of habitus developed in my own work, and that of Skeggs, to make links between individuals’ inner emotional worlds, their affective dispositions, and external social and structural processes.

title: Social mobility is a joke: Working-class women and British TV comedy on ‘the social floor’
abstract: This article examines a range of recent autosociobiographical representations of and by working-class women in the contemporary UK, focusing on Rain Dogs , Chewing Gum and Alma’s Not Normal . It argues that what unites these different representations – all of which are TV comedy-dramas, some with connecting iterations as memoir and play – is a vigorous critique and rejection of the neoliberal meritocratic dream. These representations show that the idea of a level playing field in which working hard to activate talent results in success is simply not a possibility for most working-class women: upwards social mobility is a joke. Yet crucially, this situation is not simply portrayed as a thwarted tragedy of the downtrodden, or as poverty porn in the tradition of reality TV. Instead, through life-affirming exuberant comedy, they show how the wider socio-political landscape is unjust while energetically refusing to accept its limits or internalise its stigma: they ‘reject respectability’. Unlike the majority of autosociobiographies, these representations primarily use a comedic tone. Their focus is not on ‘escape’, ‘transcendence’ or the aspiration for a middle-class life, but on the complexities of working-class lives as lived in context, and on critiquing institutional structures. They do value collective community support and crave the security of putting a ‘social floor’ on their circumstances, of not having to constantly worry about losing everything. Considering why the televisual is a useful vehicle for these narratives, the article asks: what do these women’s exuberant rejections of neoliberal meritocracy and bourgeois standards of judgement indicate about the wider cultural, social and political context, or current conjuncture?

title: ‘Words were needed . . .’ Poetics and politics of the voiceover in contemporary autosociobiographical filmmaking
abstract: The article examines autosociobiographical film practices within contemporary European experimental and essay film, and specifically focusses on their use of voiceover narration. Comparing and contrasting three recent examples of autosociobiographical filmmaking from France, Austria and Germany, the article explores both the poetics and the politics of autosociobiographical voiceover, and asks how they relate to some of the fundamental ethico-political questions and problems associated with the genre of autosociobiography.

title: Talking back: Social mobility, class and reflexivity in Darren McGarvey’s ‘Poverty Safari’
abstract: This article examines Darren McGarvey’s Poverty Safari as a meaningful yet underexplored contribution to the emerging field of autosociobiographies—a genre where authors intertwine personal narratives with critical reflections on the social and cultural structures that shape their lives. We argue that McGarvey disrupts dominant, idealised accounts of social mobility by interrogating the classed dynamics of the book market, offering a distinctive form of reflexivity within the genre. Through an analysis of his narrative strategies, we explore two key questions: How does Poverty Safari narrate social mobility in ways that foreground the conditions, constraints, and expectations shaping autosociobiographical storytelling? How does McGarvey’s mode of reflexivity (re-)configure the analytical potential of autosociobiography for studying social class and mobility? We demonstrate that McGarvey critiques the expectations placed on authors of autosociobiographies, revealing the power structures that both allow and limit their success. His self-reflexive approach acts as a form of ‘talking back’—an act of reclaiming the right to critically narrate one’s struggles. By situating McGarvey’s work within current debates on mobility narratives and class representation, this study highlights the genre’s potential to reframe discussions of class and education.

title: Can organic vegetables convert an urban and conservative Catholic movement to political ecology?
abstract: This article explores whether concrete practices—such as participation in an Association for the Maintenance of Peasant Agriculture (AMAP)—can reshape the imaginaries and lifestyles of conservative Catholics toward a more systemic and political ecology. It focuses on the Altercathos , a group of young Lyonnais Catholics, through the experience of their community café, Le Simone . The question is especially relevant given that, while Anglophone studies often highlight a negative correlation between conservative Christianity and ecological concern, the French Catholic context is more nuanced. Since the 1970s, French Catholicism has nurtured a tradition of ecological commitment. However, the Vatican has often used the “ecologization of religion” to reinforce conservative positions on gender and sexuality, particularly through the concept of “human ecology.” The Altercathos , initially active in protests against same-sex marriage, come from a conservative background but underwent a “militant disillusionment” that gradually distanced them from the Church’s reactionary stance. They embraced the notion of integral ecology from Pope Francis’s Laudato si’ , seeking to reconnect faith with civic and ecological engagement in urban life. Yet, the analysis of Le Simone ’s AMAP reveals a more complex reality. Despite aspirations toward “ecological conversion,” the initiative did not lead to a strong collective transformation or spiritualization. Participants’ motivations were diverse—ranging from practicality to social ties—reflecting a dynamic of individual engagement rather than collective commitment. This case illustrates the gap between papal discourse on ecological conversion and lived Catholic practice. Rather than a unified movement, Le Simone reflects slow, fragmented transformations and a pluralism of motivations, calling for a more nuanced understanding of faith-based ecological engagement.

title: Political representation of displacement and escape in the neoliberal city: Körfez and Arada in Turkish independent cinema
abstract: Focusing on two independent Turkish films, Körfez (2017) and Arada (2018), this article examines how displacement and escape are politically represented in the neoliberal city. It argues that neoliberal urban transformation in Turkey generates not only physical displacement but also alienation and a drive to escape. Using qualitative narrative analysis and close readings, the study shows how both films stage the erosion of belonging in urban life. Körfez portrays a suffocating, stagnant city through an introspective protagonist; Arada tracks the chaotic nocturnal journey of a young man planning to leave the country. Despite their aesthetic differences, the two films politicise displacement and urban alienation through two distinct forms of escape: Körfez figures escape as inward withdrawal, while Arada stages it as kinetic boundary-crossing. This distinction shows how these independent films make the human costs of neoliberal urban transformation legible through contrasting forms of belonging and non-belonging.

title: ‘Alexa, dinner time’: Exploring how connected devices shape domestic atmospheres, intimacy, and power
abstract: This paper explores how people use smart home technologies in home-making practices. Employing the concept of atmospheres, we examine how smart home technologies contribute to producing the feeling of home and give texture to everyday activities. The concept of atmosphere denotes shared feelings and moods in a particular space or environment that are produced and experienced among different configurations of objects, technologies, and (human and non-human) bodies. The article is based on in-depth interviews with 12 people living with smart home technologies in Norway. The analysis shows different ways people use the technology to make the home feel right through setting different moods and scenes, engaging in playful improvisations and renegotiating the felt boundaries of the home. At the same time, employing Internet-connected technologies for these tasks has gendered and privacy implications, as they are mostly controlled by one (male) household member and collect data from users and the domestic sphere in which they are situated. The paper contributes to existing literature by demonstrating how everyday processes of home-making, shaped by smart home technologies, may mask their role in reinforcing traditional domestic gender dynamics and the traditional Western image of the home as an enclosed and private space – despite this image being strongly challenged by the political economy within which smart homes are situated.

title: Memory as decoloniality
abstract: European colonialism is an epistemic project in which collective memory plays a crucial role. Memory creates linear histories and consolidates cohesive identities while erasing difficult or marginalised histories and projecting contemporary Others across history. Memory, however, is also never singular: the dominant narrative of the past constantly interacts with, and is contested by, grassroots counter-narratives. As such, counter-narratives of national memory in postcolonial nations may enact memory as decoloniality. Drawing from decolonial and postcolonial theory, queer theory, cultural studies and memory studies, I argue that memory as decoloniality plays out in three ways. First, it entails delinking from official narratives of the past as false or incomplete. Second, it involves unsanctioned acts of mourning and melancholic reiterations of the unsettled past. Third, it writes new narratives and invents new traditions, replacing monumental history with a pluriverse of fragmented memories. This paper engages with a transnational range of cases of memory as decoloniality, reflecting critically on their promises and limitations. I conclude by reflecting on the implications of memory for larger political and cultural processes of decoloniality.

title: Moving images, moved audiences? A focus group study into audience interpretations of distant suffering in The Impossible (2012)
authors: Valerie Vanhove; Stijn Joye; David Ongenaert
abstract: While distant suffering has been thoroughly explored in factual media such as news and documentaries, this article examines Western audiences’ interpretations of distant suffering and non-Western ‘Others’ in the format of fiction films. Through five focus groups ( N = 22) in Flanders, the northern Dutch-speaking part of Belgium, this explorative study examines whether the film The Impossible (2012) fosters empathy, raises awareness and encourages action towards the portrayed distant suffering. The film tells the story of a British family during the tsunami of 2004 and is largely based on true events. Findings show that the film proves effective in increasing Western viewers’ awareness of distant suffering. However, this sense of closeness mostly resulted in passivity and rarely translated into concrete action. A proper distance from the portrayed Other appears crucial for Western viewers to be motivated to show compassion and consider action. Nevertheless, the study also suggests that audiences’ emotional connection is heavily influenced by individual film consumption preferences.

title: Scrolling for sanity, performing for the algorithm: Theratainment and the governance of care on TikTok
abstract: Drawing on 42 semi-structured interviews with US-based clinicians, this study examines how licensed mental health professionals navigate TikTok’s governing infrastructures while attempting to educate and care for audiences within an algorithmically curated attention economy. It identifies three interlocking pressures: (a) engagement-optimisation systems that reward affectively charged, trend-aligned posts, making clinically nuanced communication difficult to sustain; (b) the emergence of ambient caregiving, an always-on, low-intensity form of audience support that generates emotional labour without institutional scaffolding; and (c) opaque, automated moderation practices that disproportionately suppress content addressing trauma, structural inequality and marginalised identities. Conceptually, the article develops theratainment to describe the fusion of therapeutic language with entertainment aesthetics and entrepreneurial self-branding that clinicians must negotiate under platform logics and elaborates ambient caregiving as a domain-specific extension of affective labour in short-form video. The findings reframe clinicians not only as educators but also as subjects of platform governance who continually balance visibility, credibility and ethical responsibility within engagement-first infrastructures. The article concludes with policy and design implications, including verification, trauma-informed and anti-bias moderation practices, and potential public-platform partnerships to support evidence-based care. This article forms part of the European Journal of Cultural Studies Special Issue on Digital Mental Health.

title: Cute, goofy, and wholesome: Inventing social media otherwise in virtual reality
abstract: Recently, the hype around the Metaverse has faded, with artificial intelligence taking the spotlight. Although the Big Tech vision of the Metaverse never materialized, under the radar of this mainstream discourse, thousands of users have quietly built thriving communities across various social VR platforms, forging identities, social practices, and collective imaginaries that diverge sharply from this vision. Taking the popular social VR platform, VRChat, as its case study, this article explores how these grassroots communities still experience and imagine these social VR environments from a bottom-up perspective. Drawing on over 1.5 years of digital ethnography in the platform, conducted since January 2024, this study reveals that for many—particularly queer, neurodivergent, and disabled individuals—VRChat offers a reprieve from the normative aesthetics and toxic cultures of traditional social media, fostering alternative modes of self-expression and social connection. Here, a significant number of users prefer “cute” avatars over hypersexualized appearances, embrace “goofy” and “clumsy” gestures over polished embodiments and nourish a “wholesome” environment of care over polarizing and isolating dynamics. Conceptualizing these emergent communities as a counterpublic, this article contends that these practices offer a glimpse into a social media otherwise more queer and crip in its aesthetics, rhythms, and relations.

title: Haunting data: Mental health, data-hacking and digital temporalities
abstract: This article maps the experiences of victims of the Vastaamo psychotherapy centre data hack by analysing their stories through a lens provided by the digital hauntology framework. The article views the data-hacking incident as a form of terror that continues to weigh on the victims in several ways, including by giving birth to new forms of harm and injury. The data consist of anonymous written narratives collected via the digital tool Penna (N = 100). I discuss and analyse the leaked data, in all their liveliness and with their own multitemporal (after)lives, as both haunted and haunting. While disparate sites of trauma can haunt each other, datafication also carries with it distinct particularities, which stresses the transformations in the practices of memory and forgetting in the digital age. Such practices carry the potential for digital archives to revitalise data: in the case of a data breach, personal data generated in the past may continue to haunt the victims in future, in various ways. The article provides insights into the ways in which digital temporalities entangle with the affective experiences of mental (ill-)health. It argues that the digital age provides entangled and networked sites for recurrent wounding, thus ultimately generating a form of affective inequality. Many victims register the Vastaamo data breach and its aftermath as a loss of the ontological and epistemological certainty and security that previously provided an experience of being psychically held.

title: Notting Hill Carnival as a ‘place’ of struggle in 1970s Britain
abstract: The ‘riots’ at the Notting Hill Carnival on 30 August 1976 are recognised as a pivotal moment for post-war race relations in Britain, taking place at what Hall et al. identified as a critical conjuncture in the mid-1970s. Nevertheless, the broader contribution of the carnival towards the fight against racism during this period remains overlooked within academia. This article reframes Notting Hill Carnival as a ‘place’ of struggle. Drawing on Massey’s notions of ‘a global sense of place’, the carnival is re-examined as a site where local, national and global processes intersected in the 1970s, shaping the wider struggle against racism. The article is underpinned by in-depth qualitative interviews with participants and organisers of the Notting Hill Carnival, alongside archival research. The analysis highlights how the carnival operated not merely as a cultural event, but as a microcosm of broader conflicts unfolding during a crisis of hegemony for the establishment.

title: When the guess becomes a default: Imagined audiences as production constraints
abstract: Taking up a question opened by Siao Yuong Fong’s recent Cultural Commons essay, ‘Imagining audiences in the age of generative AI’, this essay asks how audience imaginaries acquire operational force inside production and take aesthetic form. Fong’s palimpsest foregrounds how heterogeneous audience assumptions accumulate; the default names which of them returns with the least resistance and which becomes costly to refuse. Drawing on an AI-enhanced virtual-production archive in South Korea, and on a history running from radio’s absent listener to the mechanical storage of audience response in 1950s television, the essay argues that generative AI does not make actual audiences more knowable. It makes the audience position sedimented in the apparatus partially reconstructible – through recurrent outputs and the labour required to undo them. Model defaults meet budgets, workflows and cultural expertise, leaving formal traces in framing, movement, atmosphere and signage. Following those traces shows who pays when cultural specificity does not arrive by default.

title: Between concrete and current: Econostalgia and the reimagining of urban-nature relations along Tbilisi’s Mtkvari river
abstract: This article examines how the Mtkvari river in Tbilisi is remembered, narrated and politically reimagined after decades of infrastructural enclosure. Based on multi-method anthropological research, including participant observation, interviews, digital materials and archival sources, it traces the river’s transformation from a sacred, social and ecological presence into an increasingly marginalized urban watercourse shaped by embankments, highways, pollution and concrete. The article conceptualises these damaged relations through ecological nostalgia, understood not as passive longing for a lost past but as a situated civic repertoire through which memories of riverine life become claims for repair, access and responsibility. The analysis focuses especially on Dighomi Meadows, one of Tbilisi’s last semi-wild riverside ecosystems, where activists mobilise memories and imaginaries of floodplain forest, riverine sacredness and more-than-human life against extractive development and new cycles of concrete urbanisation. By linking ecological nostalgia to riverine citizenship, the article shows how care for a damaged river can expand urban belonging beyond property, residence or administrative citizenship towards responsibility for shared human and more-than-human worlds. Finally, it situates the Mtkvari/Kura as a transboundary river, inviting comparative attention to river memory, attachment and ecological vulnerability across the wider Kura-Aras basin.

title: Artificial intelligence as a ‘dictionary of accepted ideas’
abstract: Contemporary large language models function as word-pattern-recognition systems crunching Big Data to identify the most commonly associated interdiscursive patterns in contemporary language and thought. Similarly, in the late 19th century, Gustave Flaubert, using rather simpler, artisanal techniques, produced a set of condensations of the linguistic patterns and received wisdoms of his own age in his ‘Dictionary of Accepted Ideas’. This article examines some of the analogies between artificial intelligence’s methodologies and Flaubert’s literary approach. By linking these issues to Stuart Hall’s arguments about the constitutive role of common sense in providing the horizons of thought, we can then clarify artificial intelligence’s (inevitably ideological) role in policing those horizons in our own time.
