From margins to mainstream: a critical network analysis of the #MosqueMeToo hashtag
abstract: This study critically examines the discourse around sexual assault in religious places within the Muslim community, as facilitated by the #MosqueMeToo hashtag on Twitter. Initiated as part of the broader #MeToo movement, #MosqueMeToo offers Muslim women a platform to share their experiences and raise awareness of the problem. The researcher used critical methods combining computational analysis and qualitative analysis to examine 6,790 tweets shared on the hashtag at its peak. The findings highlight the narratives of the compelling need to expose sexual assault in religious places, debunking modesty myth, and the dynamics of suppression and voice. This study challenges the idea that social media has a transformative potential in amplifying marginalized voices. The findings suggest that certain topics, taboos, and cultures might find it more challenging than others to address deep-rooted issues within their communities. This research contributes to the broader conversation around the #MeToo movement and its impact on raising awareness and empowering women to seek justice.

title: From secularism to freedom: The hijab debate in the 2024 Olympics and its reflections in Türkiye
abstract: In recent years, the issue of Muslim women wearing hijabs has become a controversial topic in Western societies, particularly within the realm of sports. This study examines the reactions to France’s ban on Muslim athletes wearing hijabs during the 2024 Paris Olympic Games, with a focus on Türkiye’s discussions on the X platform (formerly Twitter) between July 26 and August 11 2024. The study analyzes the themes and trends in public discourse, exploring how the ban was perceived in terms of gender, religious freedom, and cultural differences. Two main categories emerged in the analysis: “Supporters” and “Opponents” of the ban, with subthemes including “Secularism,” “Gender Discrimination,” “Islamophobia,” and “Freedom.” The findings reveal a polarized debate, with supporters emphasizing secularism and gender norms, while opponents highlight concerns about religious freedom and Islamophobia. This research offers insights into how social media shapes public opinion on contentious issues.

title: Complicating the Sk8rgrl: asymmetrical visibility of feminisms in Olympic skateboarding
abstract: This study analyzes the mediated narratives of three skateboarders—Rayssa Leal, Alana Smith, and Leo Baker—and their experiences of the Tokyo 2020 Olympic skateboarding competition. Through a critical discourse analysis of media coverage as well as the athletes’ social media posts, the analysis explored how the athletes’ mediated narratives upheld and deconstructed articulations of popular feminism. The findings show that each skateboarder’s narrative varied in its relationship to popular feminism, due in part to the athletes’ diverse gender identities. Therefore, the study contends that the popular feminist narratives common within sporting contexts uphold a binary notion of gendered competition, showcasing the need for a further incorporation of queer and intersectional feminisms into sport media and the sporting industry broadly.

title: Defining premium advocacy documentary TV: analyzing the coexistence of popular feminism and care-based feminist advocacy in Hulu’s Untouchable: The Rise and Fall of Harvey Weinstein (2019)
abstract: This article identifies an emergent television genre that has developed with the dissolution of traditional genre distinctions at a time of amplified cultural, industrial, and technological media convergence. I call this genre premium advocacy documentary TV. Through a close analysis of Hulu’s Untouchable: The Rise and Fall of Harvey Weinstein (2019), I explore how the streaming industry’s acceleration of media convergence across digital platforms permits competing and coexisting discursive attitudes toward feminist advocacy. I argue that changes in the configuration of genre have enabled the production of post-#MeToo television documentaries that claim to uphold care-based feminist ethics and advocacy practices, even as they are mutually underpinned by the values of popular and neoliberal feminism. I demonstrate how such programming illustrates the cultural and economic valuation of “prestige” media production through its narrative alignment with “quality” television programs responding to the dissolution of hegemonic masculinity at the turn of the twenty-first century. By exploring how Untouchable pursues industrial legitimacy and advocacy-based cultural status simultaneously, I demonstrate how women’s testimony in such docuseries is filtered through the formal and narrative affordances of multimedia convergence and its facilitation of multiple iterations of genre in an era of digital television streaming.

title: Rhetorical strategies in the speeches of Mrs America
abstract: Mrs America, a 2020 TV miniseries created by Dahvi Waller, examined the history of the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in the USA, highlighting the struggles between feminist and anti-feminist groups that affected the amendment’s failure to gain ratification in the 1970s. The protagonist, portrayed by Cate Blanchett, was Phyllis Schlafly, a conservative political activist who worked tirelessly to prevent the ratification of the amendment by means of an active discreditation campaign. Historically, Schlafly utilised dissociation of certain aspects of the amendment text to favour her anti-ERA interests and employed a variety of rhetorical strategies to persuade her listeners of the correctness of her ideas. This article analyses how Schlafly’s rhetorical strategies, particularly her use of dissociation, are dramatized to shape the portrayal within the miniseries, with a focus on three key rhetorical figures. These figures, choice, presence, and communion are presented as devices used to enhance dramatic tension while nevertheless remaining rooted in Schlafly’s real-life writing and public statements. While the series dramatized many aspects of Schlafly’s personal life, it can thus be seen to provide a relatively nuanced representation of her role in shaping conservative activism, offering an invitation to viewers to critically assess the cultural tensions of the period.

title: Have a cup of coffee: the techno-spatial tactics of female urbanites and the production of “mobile publicness” in digital urban China
abstract: Female urbanites play a particularly visible role in the burgeoning coffee culture of megacities like Shanghai. The remarkable visibility of female coffee house consumers contrasts with the dominance of the male bourgeoisie in Jürgen Habermas’ public sphere, making it a phenomenon worth investigation. Meanwhile, female participation in coffee houses is inseparable from digital culture. However, existing research has not connected women’s digital technology use to urban space production. To bridge this gap, this paper adopts an approach derived from “everyday life” to conceptualize how women use social media to produce urban space in Shanghai. Building upon Michel de Certeau’s conceptual framework, we propose to understand female urbanites’ techno-spatial tactics as an extension of his concept of tactics. In the case of Shanghai’s coffee houses, we argue that the techno-spatial tactics of female urbanites include hybrid appropriation, participatory storytelling, shared coding, and place collage. With these tactics, female urbanites have reconstructed the “publicness” of unconventional public spaces, which we term “mobile publicness.” The mobile publicness of coffee houses can translate into a rejuvenated public life in twenty-first-century Shanghai, shaped and embraced by women’s assertive digital power.

title: Vertical representation of gender in the Ghanaian broadcast media
authors: Samuel Danso; Gifty Appiah-Adjei; Theodora Dame Adjin-Tettey
abstract: The gender gap in media organizations has drawn research attention in recent years. This study, through the lens of the glass ceiling concept, draws on interview data to explore how gender is represented in managerial positions within Ghanaian broadcast media. The study’s findings indicate that, despite progress towards gender equality, men continue to dominate top managerial positions in Ghana’s broadcast media. The absence of institutional policies specifically targeting gender representation perpetuates these inequalities. Further, informal efforts by some media firms to ensure fair representation lack the effectiveness of formal guidelines and accountability mechanisms. Thus, women in the Ghanaian broadcast media experience the “glass ceiling” effect and are excluded from managerial decision-making processes. The study highlights the importance of promoting gender equity and diversity in leadership within the Ghanaian broadcast media.

title: Postfeminist branding: masculinity and nationalist sentiment in Li Jiaqi’s beauty livestreaming
abstract: This study examines the phenomenon of Li Jiaqi, China’s top beauty KOL, conceptualizing his success as a form of “nationalizing postfeminist branding.” This term refers to a symbolic strategy that intertwines postfeminist discourse, hybrid masculinity, and patriotic sentiment to reconfigure gendered authority within the commercial logics of China’s platform economy. Drawing on a critical discourse analysis of 28 livestreams, the paper reveals a central paradox in this branding: male influencers seemingly empower female consumers while reinforcing traditional notions of male privilege. The analysis identifies the underlying logic of this paradox as a “patriarchal meritocracy,” a discourse that justifies patriarchal authority through merit-based rhetoric, which becomes fully visible during moments of public controversy. By theorizing this dynamic, this study contributes to feminist media and platform studies by revealing how patriarchal power is reconfigured through the unique entanglement of commerce, gender performance, and state-aligned nationalism in China’s digital economy.

title: Women don’t look up? Female roles in climate change cartoons
authors: Sara Moreno-Tarín; Tatiana Pina; Martí Domínguez
abstract: In this article, we analyze the representation of women in cartoons related to climate change published over the last 40 years. A sample of 3,770 cartoons, drawn by professional cartoonists, was obtained from the CartoonStock database. Our results show that only 25% (N = 973) of the cartoons studied include at least one female figure. Moreover, when women do appear, they are often depicted in secondary and stereotyped roles, with minimal representation in leadership positions, particularly in scientific and technical fields. Beyond their underrepresentation, the study identifies four biases in climate change communication through editorial cartoons: omission, trivialization, credibility, and androcentrism. These biases not only undermine the legitimacy of women’s contributions to climate discourse but also shape public perceptions of the environmental crisis, diminishing its urgency when framed through feminized narratives. These findings highlight the need to redefine the representation of women in editorial cartoons, especially in the climate movement, where their role is more active and significant than depicted by cartoonists.

title: Gold diggers in the digital age: unraveling the “Lao Nü” stereotype in contemporary Chinese social media
authors: Weiqi Tian; Jingshen Ge; Haotian Guan
abstract: This study investigates the construction and perpetuation of the “lao nü” (gold digger) stereotype within Chinese digital culture, focusing on the “Fat Cat” incident that garnered significant social media attention. Utilizing Feminist Critical Discourse Analysis (FCDA) within the broader framework of Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA), the research critically examines how gender ideologies and power dynamics are articulated and reinforced in digital discourses. Data were systematically collected by analyzing popular WeChat posts related to the “lao nü” stereotype across multiple dates, capturing a wide array of public opinions and sentiments. The findings reveal that social media platforms, emphasizing specific beauty standards and materialistic values, normalize and perpetuate the “lao nü” stereotype. Linguistic and rhetorical strategies in the online portrayal of women like Tan, involved in the “Fat Cat” incident, reinforce traditional gender roles and societal power imbalances. Moreover, the persistence of the “lao nü” discourse, despite contradictory evidence, underscores deep-seated socio-economic anxieties and entrenched gender ideologies within contemporary Chinese society. The analysis identifies the coexistence of feminist and anti-feminist discourses surrounding the “lao nü” stereotype. This duality underscores the complex, contested nature of gendered narratives in digital spaces and their implications for understanding gender dynamics in contemporary China.

title: Can action heroines age? The return of Sarah Connor in Terminator: Dark Fate (2019)
abstract: This article examines the return of Sarah Connor in Terminator: Dark Fate as an aged action heroine played by the 63-year-old Linda Hamilton. Her return is a very rare example of an older action heroine coming back to be the main protagonist of a sci-fi/action franchise, in contrast with older male action heroes, whose return to the screens has led to a whole subgenre of “geri-action” films. Furthermore, contrary to Victoria (Helen Mirren) in the RED movies and Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher) in the latest Star Wars trilogy, Sarah Connor challenges conventional femininity and occupies a central place in the marketing and narrative of the film. She is a source of regeneration rather than degeneration, leading a team of younger women for whom she becomes a mentor. However, a comparison with the older Terminator played by Arnold Schwarzenegger reveals that ageing comes at a greater cost for women than for men. While the Terminator is fully integrated into society and continues to benefit from spectacular action scenes and witty dialogue, Sarah Connor appears as a much more tragic figure of ageing, marred by loss, loneliness and bitterness.

title: The interface gaze: on the (sexual) objectification of domestic workers in the gig economy
abstract: In contemporary capitalist societies, domestic work is increasingly externalised and marketized, allowing profit-oriented gig-economy platforms to emerge as new actors in this field. Considering that such digital marketplaces shape the interactions and relationships between clients and workers, it is crucial to examine the experiences of household workers in relation to the norms, beliefs and ideas embedded in the functionalities and design of the platform. This is particularly relevant concerning the historically prevalent (sexual) objectification of domestic cleaners. Therefore, the present paper presents 15 problem-centred interviews with female domestic cleaners working in the gig-economy in Vienna. The results are complemented by applying the walkthrough method and discursive interface analysis on the website of Betreut.at, one of Austria’s largest platforms for domestic services. Our study shows that the interviewees’ experiences reflect the culturally embedded objectification of domestic workers. Recurrent themes identified include clients’ practices related to lookism and the prioritization of attractiveness, unwanted dating requests, and sexual harassment, all of which are, to some degree, shaped by the platform’s technological design. Additionally, the platform’s website interface lacks essential safety features, exacerbating the vulnerability of household cleaners, who are at high risk of sexual abuse.

title: From collective struggle to individual hustle: gig work and neoliberal feminism in Working Mother magazine
abstract: This article traces coverage of gig work in the U.S. magazine Working Mother from the 1970s to the 2020s. The study uses critical discourse analysis to conduct a comparative historical examination of 289 articles, focusing on how coverage of gig work and feminist themes evolves. Whereas early issues of the magazine align closely with second-wave feminist principles, such as encouraging women to pursue collective solutions for social change and compete with men for jobs, later issues embrace neoliberal themes of self-reliance, hustle, and gendered entrepreneurialism. In addition to encouraging risky and exploitative working arrangements, such as in multilevel marketing, Working Mother reinforces traditional gender roles and forecloses discussion of the structural inequalities that push mothers into the gig economy in the first place.

title: The endless project of the feminine self: ‘locked-down femininity’ and becoming #ThatGirl on TikTok
abstract: Encouraged by the solitude of COVID-19 lockdowns, the social media platform TikTok gained prominent cultural attention. This study capitalises on the increased visibility of people online and focuses on how women utilise the platform as a space for self-transformation during crisis. From a critical post-feminist and neoliberal perspective, this study undertakes a combined content analysis and digital ethnography of “ideal” femininity as articulated on the #ThatGirl hashtag on TikTok. Three patterns are revealed in the data. Firstly, isolation appears as not only a by-product of lockdown but a space where the full potential of ideal femininity is realised. Following this, wellness and consumption materialise as the broad aim of #ThatGirl, where the body emerges as a site of protection against disease and place to exert control against an uncontrollable cultural landscape. Ultimately, lockdowns facilitated a certain femininity where women negotiated protection, health, and survival in times of crisis by a return to the body as armour and individualisation as a moral ethic of safety. These ideals are entrenched within both hegemonic and critical expressions on TikTok, as feminist resistance in the form of feedback occurs in tandem with the discourse it attempts to challenge.

title: (Un)Girly girls: reimagining femininity on Japanese TikTok
abstract: The development of digital media forms allows young women to reclaim spaces to build communities, showcase different aspects of their identities, and critique societal expectations and norms. A short-video app TikTok has become an important site among young Japanese women for identity work and self-expression while extending on earlier aspects of Japanese techno- and visual culture—a self-portraiture via purikura photography, keitai digital camera, and girly (shōjo) culture. The study employs participant observation and content analysis to understand how TikTok can accommodate expressions of femininity through public self-staging while producing novel forms of feminised labour and algorithmic resistance. On TikTok, young Japanese women create a site for rejecting normative scripts of femininity, through creative agency, reclaiming gender performance, and sexuality, while navigating commodified and commercialised images of girlhood. Young women’s practices are studied outside of pastime, frivolous consumption patterns, and essentialist frames to examine their continued cultural significance and responses to oppressing social issues.

title: “Sisters, are you running out of menstrual supplies??”:exploring #SistersFightPandemicWithEase and tactical hashtag feminism in the COVID-19 crisis
Negotiating visibility: Women in comedy and polymediated politics in Turkey
authors: Ipek A. Celik Rappas; Suncem Kocer
abstract: This article examines the polymediated performances and political humor of women comedians in Turkey’s emerging comedy landscape. Based on a long-term ethnographic study conducted between January 2024 and June 2025, we explore how the comedy scene operates as a male-dominated field that simultaneously includes and excludes women, revealing the constraints women comedians face, including patriarchal norms, censorship, and the precarities of neoliberal creative labor. Through participant observation and interviews, the study highlights how women comedians utilize polymedia—the selective and multidimensional use of media platforms—to overcome these constraints, cultivate audiences, and craft feminist and political critiques. Women comedians build networks of solidarity while competing for limited resources, using polymedia as a means of empowerment and survival. Their efforts reveal both the potential and the limits of polymediation, as they contend with unequal access to audiences, line-ups, and institutional support. Their strategies illuminate the entangled dynamics of gender, digital media, and power within Turkey’s contemporary comedy landscape.

title: Trapped in the simulation: Tradwife culture, fake allyship, and the exhaustion of the domestic dystopia in Don’t Worry Darling (2022)
abstract: This article examines Olivia Wilde’s Don’t Worry Darling (2022) as a critical impasse in popular feminist cinema’s deployment of the domestic dystopia. Rather than offering another comparative reading with Bryan Forbes’s The Stepford Wives (1975) or its 2004 remake (dir. Frank Oz), the article situates Wilde’s film within three interconnected contemporary contexts: the tradwife movement’s appropriation of Stepford aesthetics; post-#MeToo discourse around fake male allyship; and the exhaustion of the ‘fiftiesness’ that the nostalgia film recycles as a substitute for historical engagement with the postwar period. Drawing on scholarship on postfeminist domesticity, popular feminism and the female fantastic, I argue that Don’t Worry Darling inadvertently reveals the limits of recycling the Stepford trope at a moment when tradwife creators already deploy identical aesthetics to resell domesticity as aspirational choice. Distinguishing period drama, pastiche and simulation as different modes of ‘fiftiesness,’ the article shows that the film’s simulated suburb converts critique into seduction. It further examines how the film’s troubled production and reception, including Florence Pugh’s public distancing and the casting of Harry Styles, symptomatically reproduce the contradictions the film ostensibly critiques. The article concludes by asking whether popular feminist cinema can move beyond these structural limitations.

title: “ This data is really sensitive ” – the making of non-commercial menstruapps as productive resistance within Femtech
abstract: Digital menstrual cycle tracking is a booming business and a burgeoning field of study. Although often framed as empowering, researchers have recognized serious problems in menstrual cycle tracking apps, or “menstruapps.” These include the lack of accuracy in predictions, the enforcement of harmful stereotypes, and above all, the ways in which sensitive user data is collected and used for profit-making. However, in recent years, a number of non-commercial apps have become available. In this study, nine makers of non-commercial menstruapps were interviewed. Through analyzing their goals and motivations, making non-commercial menstruapps is shown to function as a form of productive resistance within the female technology or “Femtech” sector. Setting themselves in opposition to commercialized Femtech, the makers aim for solutions that enhance self-understanding through the use of data technologies while ensuring privacy, considering human individuality, and enhancing transparency and inclusion. The article discusses the potential and limits of challenging Femtech from within.

title: Unleashing menstrual blood: a qualitative study of free-bleeding activism on Instagram
abstract: Free-bleeding practices gained visibility on Instagram during the 2010s, when a series of posts became emblematic moments of digital menstrual activism. Yet little scholarship has examined how menstrual blood operates as a site of power and resistance in everyday digital contexts. Through a critical discourse and semiotic analysis of six high-profile Instagram posts published between March 2015 and September 2019, this study explores how menstrual blood is visually and discursively represented on the platform and how these representations challenge and reconfigure dominant discourses of menstruation among audiences. The findings demonstrate that free-bleeding mobilizes menstrual blood as both a symbolic and political resource to contest menstrual taboos, disrupt normative representations of menstruation, and foster more inclusive understandings of menstruating bodies. More broadly, the study advances scholarship on how social media mediatizes embodied resistance and facilitates feminist counter-narratives that challenge the gendered norms and structural inequalities surrounding menstruation. In doing so, it contributes to broader debates on gender, embodiment, and feminist activisms while preserving a digital “archive of resistance.”

title: Lover’s (Dis)comfort: considering the feminist potentials of romance in the digital game
abstract: Romance in mainstream gaming has rapidly increased in visibility over the last decade. Recent titles like Baldur’s Gate 3, Starfield and Dragon Age: The Veilguard have included optional romance features as selling points in promotional campaigns. Despite this rise in popularity, discursively romance is still a confused and contested term amongst scholars, players, developers, and games journalists. It is used as a catch-all term to refer to a diverse range of social interactions and gameplay mechanics. Some scholars have argued that romance has been a gateway for transgressive, feminine, and pro-social play. As Anastasia Salter states, the decision to feature romance in play can be viewed as an act of “feminist game design”. However, without a discerning understanding of the different presentations of romance within gaming it is challenging to recognise where feminisms are happening and where they are distinctly not. Through an exploration of how romance mechanics navigate issues of consent, objectification, and “pick-up” ideologies, I argue romance in the digital game is not inherently feminist, though still maintains transgressive potentials. Recognising where feminism is potentially happening is especially important as “romance” is becoming increasingly visible as a feature of the AAA game. Without recognising the potentially harmful and troubling mechanics baked into prominent examples (some of which are considered templates for their development teams) there is a risk that damaging presentations will continue to be normalised and expected within these styles of romantic representation.

title: Level up, ladies: Femininity as a total project and the rise of Queen feminism
abstract: Critiques of liberal feminisms are increasingly emerging from the women-led “femosphere,” calling for a revised understanding of feminism through a revaluation of femininity. This article examines one such voice: a group of social media influencers who cultivate and commercialize “queen” femininity as a lifestyle, advising women on how to “level up” their lives and attract provider-minded men. We follow 14 Finnish “queen” influencer–entrepreneurs and ask how they define and practice femininity. Drawing on digital fieldwork and content analysis of 303 Instagram captions, we show how femininity is constructed as a total and infinite project—one that extends across all fronts of life. The study further demonstrates that the cultivation of a “feminine lifestyle” is not merely a set of personal preferences but also implies a broader vision of social order. We term this ideological project “Queen feminism”: an essentialized, spiritualized, and platformed articulation of neoliberal feminism, in which the entrepreneurial ethos is (re)located in the total, perpetual, and crucially impossible project of the feminine self. Beyond analyzing a (counter)movement within feminism, this paper contributes to discussions on influencer politics by showing how the entanglement of ideological work and influencer economics may hamper collective feminist projects yet contribute to wider ideological shifts.

title: Mobilising motherhood: feminist tactical media and platform struggles against environmental injustice in Central Java
abstract: This article examines how rural women in Nguter, Central Java, mobilise environmental resistance through WhatsApp in response to toxic emissions from a rayon factory, PT. Rayon Utama Makmur (PT. RUM). Drawing on feminist political ecology, ecofeminism, and feminist media studies, the study conceptualises digital activism as a situated gendered practice embedded in everyday life. Based on seven years of participatory ethnography (2017–2024), the analysis shows how WhatsApp operates not simply as a communication tool but as a feminist tactical medium through which care, environmental witnessing, and collective action are organised, sustaining a class-action lawsuit that in 2024 won a binding Supreme Court ruling. Mobilisation emerged through domestic and informal networks before extending into digital spaces, where video sharing, voice messaging, and real-time coordination formed counter-publics challenging corporate narratives and institutional inaction. Participation was shaped by intersecting inequalities, limited digital literacy, infrastructural constraints, and exposure to surveillance and gendered risk, so digital activism was both enabling and precarious, relying on affective and communicative labour disproportionately borne by women. The article advances “WhatsApp ecofeminism” to describe a low-tech, high-impact activism grounded in care, relationality, and tactical improvisation, arguing for a rethinking of digital inclusion beyond access toward relational participation and situated counter-power.

title: A Space for Women: Gender, Class, and Women's Lounges in 1930s Chinese Movie Palaces
abstract: This paper analyzes the design and spatial planning of women's lounges in three Chinese movie palaces in the 1930s: Shanghai's Nanking Theater, Nanjing's Xindu Theater, and Nanjing's Dahua Theater. I demonstrate how the appearance of the gendered leisure amenity revealed active efforts by US-trained Chinese and Chinese American architects to transplant a feminized, middle-class, and cross-class American movie palace culture into Chinese theaters, and how the space and its cultural connotations entered into conflict with existing conceptions around gender, class, and leisure in Republican Chinese society (1912–1949).

title: On Aesthetic Re-education: Newsreels in the Aftermath of World War II
abstract: This essay argues that re-education films made in the wake of World War II reorient the historical and political stakes of education filmmaking, thereby contributing to broader film-historical debates about visual propaganda and the ideology of nonfic tion cinema. The essay concentrates on the newsreel series Welt im Film [World in Film], which became a key instrument for re-educating the German public after twelve years of nationalist indoctrination. As fixtures of the postwar screen in Allied zones of occupation, these films reveal how the theatrical distribution of nonfiction films was instrumentalized for an anti-nationalist and globalist agenda.

title: The Sun Tribe films: Moral panic over the taiyōzoku during Japan's long and hot summer of 1956
abstract: During the summer of 1956, a series of films based on novels by Ishihara Shintarō sparked a nationwide sensation in Japan. Their portrayal of a decadent, hedonistic lifestyle sent shockwaves through society and provoked widespread concern. Critics quickly called for the films to be banned, fearing that the antisocial behavior of their affluent protagonists might corrupt unblemished youth across Japan. Drawing on con temporary Japanese sources, this article examines the ensuing moral panic, focusing on the films' reception and the public debate that followed. It further reveals how close Japan came to reinstating film censorship—despite lingering memories of the notorious wartime Film Law of 1939.

title: A Cinema of Paper: Relocating the place of the written word in early British educational film
abstract: From the film medium's earliest years, the written word has been integral in establishing cinema's educational role. Yet historians have largely studied the writings by film companies as "paratexts" to their films. Text was used to integrate panoramas/magic lanterns into knowledge-making, and film was no different. The prose in catalogues, pamphlets, and journalism produced by British filmmakers, served to highlight cinema's pedagogical utility. This article foregrounds the forgotten figure of Thomas Clegg, arguing that Clegg's innovative writings positioned the film producer, Charles Urban Trading Com pany, as an educator. Through Clegg's example, I reveal that, more than image, text was integral to selling the promise of the moving image's unique contribution to instruction, knowledge, and media history.

title: What is an American ?: Tracking the Paths of Immigrants in Early Cinema
abstract: This essay investigates the portrayal of immigrants and immigration in short American films, both nonfiction and fiction, in the decade before the Great War. That portrayal is based on surviving film prints as well as synopses and articles in the trade press. Several questions guide this investigation. Where did immigrants tend to come from, particularly if their ethnicity, as Italians and Jews, could make them "alien" and not always accepted as white ? In the nonfiction films, how were immigrants helped or hindered by government agencies, businesses, and other organizations? In the fiction films, how often do their narrative arcs allow immigrants to confront and overcome all kinds of difficulties, ending in success? In either kind of film, how were immigrants prepared, or not prepared, to become new Americans and even poised to rise socially and economically, as my own ancestors slowly did? The following pages take up these questions in several stages, with emphasis on changes in American society that occurred in the early 1910s. How does this analysis reveal what it meant more than one hundred years ago, in comparison to the fraught experience of current immigrants, to be or become an American ?

title: Editor’s Notebook
“It Is in Our House Now”
abstract: This essay describes the 2.3-acre Hollywood Hills estate of the late director David Lynch—known as “the Compound” to his collaborators and fans—as a unique film studio that played a crucial role in Lynch’s creative practice. Assembled over the course of the 1990s as Lynch purchased and remodeled a series of contiguous properties, the Compound was the decisive environment of Lynch’s multimedia experimentation over nearly three decades of work in Los Angeles. Nieland explores the Compound as a material space and an assemblage of technologies and personnel that shaped key feature films like Lost Highway (1997), Mulholland Drive (2001) and Inland Empire (2006). The Compound became increasingly visible in documentaries about Lynch’s “art life,” in later media experiments like his YouTube channel “David Lynch Theater,” and in its 2026 sale after Lynch’s death. In but not of Hollywood, the Compound served as both home base for the construction of Lynch’s auteur brand and the studio infrastructure of his late modernism.

title: The Birth of the Electrical Boy
abstract: This article maps the connections between David Lynch’s unproduced script, Ronnie Rocket, and his 2017 series, Twin Peaks: The Return (aka Twin Peaks season 3). Focusing on the “Dougie Jones” sequences set in Las Vegas, Nevada, this short article draws parallels between Lynch and Jacques Tati, particularly in their use of slapstick and modern built environments to create physical humor.

title: Uncanny Intimacies, Abject Desires
abstract: This article introduces the dossier “Mulholland Drive at 25.” What did Mulholland Drive (2001) say about female fantasy, suffering, and desire at the turn of the twenty-first century, and how might that matter today? Rather than debate Mulholland Drive’s degree of feminism or the extent to which David Lynch himself proved able to create feminist cinema, the authors of this dossier approach the film as an intricate text that frustrates traditional interpretive approaches based on the specter of the “male gaze” and the assumption of coherent, consistent character subjectivities. Consulting canonical feminist and philosophical texts as well as contemporary queer theory, sound studies, and star studies, the dossier authors write from the perspective of differing generations and disciplines, offering a lively array of critical reads.

title: The Radical Intimacy of Rot
abstract: This article by Laura Westengard, part of the dossier “Mulholland Drive at 25,” uses the lens of decomposition to show how Mulholland Drive (2001) demonstrates the multiplicity of life that always already exists within individuals that are falsely perceived to be singular. Turning toward rot as a model for queering an understanding of life, death, and self, this article provides a framework for analyzing the film's overlap and divergence of characters, the jumble of temporality that challenges a linear narrative, and the recursive merging, gaps, and doubles, offering us a vision of a kind of reproduction that occurs within, outside, and beyond normative understandings of self/other, life/death, gay/straight. Positing the film itself as decomposing corpse, Westengard suggests that the queer proliferations of rot open up not only a new reading but a queer way of engaging life, death, and the messy entanglements of existence.

title: Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)
abstract: This article, part of the dossier “Mulholland Drive at 25,” argues that the “sweet dreams” of the women characters in David Lynch’s Mulholland Drive (2001) invite viewers to “feel like feminists.” Engaging the writings of Simone de Beauvoir in The Second Sex alongside Beauvoir’s 1959 essay on the myths of Brigitte Bardot, Marso finds subversive feminist dreamscapes in Lynch’s film. Feminist sweet dreams exist within the onscreen interactions of Betty/Diane with Rita/Camilla as the two women characters simultaneously navigate the demands of patriarchy and the mythic expectations for “becoming woman.” Lynch’s film demonstrates both gaps and overlap between gendered fantasies and ugly realities, inviting disorienting and uncomfortable feelings for viewers. These feelings, Marso suggests, can be interpreted and mobilized towards “feeling like feminists” such that viewers seek and find a feminist future within current conditions.

title: “That’s Not My Voice”
abstract: This article, part of the dossier “Mulholland Drive at 25,” argues that the telephone plays a critical role in David Lynch’s Mulholland Drive (2001) by disturbing concepts of identity and placing telephonic technology near the heart of the film’s meaning. Drawing on the theories in Avital Ronell’s The Telephone Book: Technology, Schizophrenia, Electric Speech, and other sources, Aghamohammadi limns how the images of telephones in the film disrupt communication and pluralize identities rather than securing them.

title: “This Is the Girl”
abstract: Adopting film critic Melissa Anderson’s “acteurist” approach to Laura Dern in Lynch’s Inland Empire (2009), this essay explores Naomi Watts’s role in Mulholland Drive (2001), putting media scholar Mary R. Desjardins’s ideas around the “recyclable” nature of the female film star in dialogue with Naomi Klein’s theory of the “digital double.” If the Hollywood dream factory recycles, and alienates, female stars whose visage appear onscreen, what to make of the selves curated today for social media—especially among young women? Providing a close analysis of the prophetic declarative “This is the girl,” a revealing motif throughout the film linking Betty’s imagined Hollywood “dream place” to the film’s lackluster LA backdrop, this essay unpacks how Watts’s dual roles as Betty Elms and Diane Selwyn reflect the ways in which the abjection of the would-be Hollywood ingenue, either endured or witnessed from behind a screen, can warp a woman’s sense of self.

title: How George A. Romero Inspired the Horror Studies Center
abstract: This article recounts the genesis of the Horror Studies Center at the University of Pittsburgh. Relationships with the independent horror filmmaker Romero, the non-profit foundation and archival collection created in his name, and the city of Pittsburgh that Romero called home for most of his career are all explored. Romero’s landmark feature Night of the Living Dead (1968) plays an important role in Lowenstein’s personal as well as professional life: he screens it at his bar mitzvah party, and he relies on its lessons to give him hope in the wake of the anti-Semitic killings at Pittsburgh’s Tree of Life synagogue in 2018. Lowenstein’s experience hosting a screening of Romero’s Bruiser (2000) in Pittsburgh with the director in attendance is juxtaposed with a screening of Queens of the Dead (2025) in Pittsburgh with its own director: Tina Romero, George’s daughter.

title: “To Film a Society Is Very Difficult”
abstract: This article pertains to the new film, Miroirs No. 3, by the Berlin School stalwart, Christian Petzold, one of today’s most celebrated German-language filmmakers. It comprises a lengthy interview with Petzold about Miroirs, with discussion of its location in former East Germany, its re-shot ending, and its numerous influences, along with memories of his erstwhile teacher and collaborator, Harun Farocki. Petzold recounts how the new film returns to a family milieu some 26 years after his breakthrough The State I am In (Die innere Sicherheit, 2000) as well as to the Grimm’s fairy tale “The Burial Shroud,” the basis for Ghosts (Gespenster, 2005). The interview includes a discussion of Petzold’s own refugee family and its relationship to Nazism. The piece also comprises an introduction about the titles of Petzold’s films, especially his interest in double figures under the influence of Hitchcock’s Vertigo (1958) and Rebecca (1940).

title: The Call Is Coming from Inside the Cottage
abstract: This essay offers a bold counter-reading to the charmed popular reception of Heated Rivalry, a 2025 HBO television series whose passionate depiction of explicit gay male sex and long-term romantic longing has been hailed as a revolutionary installment in the history of queer media representation. Fawaz identifies how the show’s central formal conceits—including its association of gay sex with competitive sports, the plot’s rapid-fire leaps across time that heighten sexual longing, the eroticization of romantic miscommunication, and the depiction of gay sex in the absence of gay cultural contexts—actually work to transform queer eroticism into a mirror image of heterosexual desire in its most dysfunctional expressions. Fawaz argues that audiences’ fanatical obsession with the show’s central romantic relationship between two closeted professional hockey rivals might demand a collective reckoning with the romance genre as a popular formation that can no longer adequately compensate for the real failures of the contemporary sex and dating scene, gay and straight alike, to provide meaningful or sustainable intimacy.

Introduction: Existentialist Film-Philosophy
Whit Stillman's Cinema and the Existentialist Freedom of Bourgeois Nothingness
abstract: In this article I consider the films of Whit Stillman through the lens of existentialism to highlight ideas around freedom in contemporary society. I concentrate on the films of the Doomed Bourgeois in Love trilogy, Metropolitan (1990), Barcelona (1994) and The Last Days of Disco (1998) to show that these films offer us sympathetic understanding of a privileged class who struggle with questions of purpose, identity and absurdity in a world that seems to have no meaning. Jean-Paul Sartre's conception of nothingness underwrites the possibility of radical freedom and Stillman's films show how such freedom might look in the real world. I also offer a novel way of considering the difference between Sartre and Albert Camus's conceptions of the absurd.

title: L’Avenir and Simone de Beauvoir on Independence, Freedom and Happiness
abstract: Mia Hansen-Løve's film L’Avenir depicts a philosophy teacher, Nathalie Chazeaux, undergoing a serious existential crisis. Her husband Heinz ends their long marriage, her mother dies, and her book series is cancelled. Rather than despairing, Nathalie continues to pursue her projects and claims to be experiencing total freedom for the first time. Simone de Beauvoir contends in The Second Sex that in considering women's emancipation, we should not take happiness to be the aim, as it is a confining emotion. Instead, using the perspective of existentialist ethics, we should aspire to freedom. I examine how Beauvoir's distinctions between happiness, independence and freedom illuminate L’Avenir and how L’Avenir's portrayal of Nathalie's life crisis enhances understanding of their potential. We might see Nathalie as an example of what Beauvoir calls the independent woman and possibly even a free woman able to live without her ex-husband. I argue that closer analysis of the film does not support the view of Nathalie as completely free and happy. She herself says that older women are not valued, and she is harassed. Furthermore, the songs of lost love in the final scenes and the last shot of her living room with no-one in sight suggest her situation is ambiguous and that her Stoicism belies a loneliness and dread of the future.

title: Éric Rohmer with Kierkegaard and Nietzsche: Desire, Chance and Freedom
abstract: This article examines Éric Rohmer's cinema through the perspective of existential reflection, showing how his films engage with morality, faith and chance in everyday life. With particular attention to Søren Kierkegaard and Friedrich Nietzsche, I trace how these perspectives unfold across his major cycles. In the series of films known as the “Six Moral Tales” (1962–1972), Rohmer's protagonists embody a Kantian concern with self-imposed moral law, testing principles against desire and circumstance. In the later “Comedies and Proverbs” (1981–1987) and “Tales of the Four Seasons” (1990–1998), this framework widens: characters confront contingency and coincidence, evoking Kierkegaard's notion of faith as a leap beyond rational proof and Nietzsche's affirmation of chance as necessity. Through chance encounters and games of probability, Rohmer transforms ordinary experiences into existential moments, showing freedom not as certainty but as a negotiation between desire, chance and belief.

title: Existentialism and Freedom in WWI Films: The Soldier as Being-for-Itself
abstract: Drawing on Jean-Paul Sartre's concepts of being-in-itself and being-for-itself, this article examines how war reduces soldiers to cogs in a war machine and transforms individuals into soldiers whose sole function is to fight, thereby reducing them from what Sartre terms free beings- for-themselves to limited beings- in-themselves. However, despite such attempts to impose constraints on human freedom, individuals can still exercise their freedom through acts of choice. I will examine two films set during World War I, Wooden Crosses (Raymond Bernard, 1932) and Paths of Glory (Stanley Kubrick, 1957), to explore the problem of radical freedom in existentialism. This article ultimately suggests that Sartre's existentialism enables a reading of war films that recognises that individuals assert their freedom and shape themselves even under the most constraining circumstances.

title: Djibril Diop Mambéty's Decolonial Existentialism: Sartrean Praxis and the Critique of Bad Faith Humanism
abstract: This article argues that Jean-Paul Sartre's writings on existentialism and political praxis illuminate the critical decolonial work of Djibril Diop Mambéty's cinema. The article analyses Touki Bouki (1973), Hyenas (1992), Le Franc (1994) and The Little Girl Who Sold the Sun (1999) in terms of Sartre's notions of bad faith, praxis and his critique of bourgeois humanism. This Sartrean reading of Mambéty's cinema foregrounds the relevance of the philosopher's thinking for decolonial film analysis. In drawing out the existentialist dimensions of Mambéty's film-philosophy, the article links the filmmaker's critiques of neocoloniality and universal humanism to adjacent conversations in Africana existentialism and Black studies.

title: Bad Faith, Death and Neoliberal Funny Business in Weekend at Bernie's : The Working Dead
abstract: This article reads Weekend at Bernie's (Ted Kotcheff, 1989) as not merely a throwaway farce, but an elucidation of the ways in which the logic of late capitalism both cultivates and relies on what Jean-Paul Sartre terms bad faith. Situated within this context, the film crystalises neoliberal logic through a highly specific rendering of 1980s corporate culture, from which the central conceit of the plot emerges: the absurd spectacle of a dead man dragged around, his corpse manipulated and posed to sustain the illusion of life. I triangulate the concepts of bad faith, death and neoliberalism by reading Weekend at Bernie's as a commentary on the cultural logic of late capitalism.

title: Freedom, Anguish and Bad Faith in Mr. Nobody : Sartrean Existentialism in Cinema
abstract: This article explores how the film Mr. Nobody (2009), directed by Jaco Van Dormael, illustrates key concepts of Sartrean existentialism. The film exemplifies an existential condition through the character of Nemo Nobody (Jared Leto), whose life unfolds across multiple possible futures. His indecision and avoidance of choice reveal existential anguish and bad faith. The film's structure, which fragments time and narrative, mirrors the weight of responsibility inherent in every decision. Through detailed examination of key scenes and choices, I argue that the film not only illustrates Sartrean thought but also deepens it by dramatizing philosophical dilemmas in a concrete, affective form. Ultimately, Mr. Nobody affirms that freedom, though distressing, is inescapable and constitutive of human existence.

title: Kore-eda with and against Sartre: Existential Education in Nobody Knows
abstract: This article makes a case for Hirokazu Kore-eda as an existential director. By reading his film Nobody Knows (2004) against Sartre's anti-essentialist existentialism, I will show that the film disabuses us of several Sartrean doctrines and reorients us towards an existential education in Kore-eda's cinema. Contrasting the despair and disappearance of Keiko, a Sartrean existentialist heroine par excellence, with the development of Akira, Nobody Knows moves us away from the freedom and transcendence in Sartrean existentialism and emphasises the formation of the self and the growth in self-knowledge through navigating the division between existence and essence. Portrayed by suggestive dialogue, tactile close-ups, and spontaneous performances, this existential education is advanced through a series of mirror images that invite comparison and reflection. The film peaks in a tragic wisdom before death and opens the transformed self to community.

title: Iris Murdoch's Existentialism in French Exit : The Difficulty of Thinking Perpetually of Oneself
abstract: This article argues that the popular perception of Sartrean existential bleakness permeates French Exit (Azazel Jacobs, 2020), and its publicity, and yet Iris Murdoch's take on Sartre emerges as the film's overriding perspective. I propose that the film stages an encounter between Sartrean and Murdochian understandings of existentialism. The film is about a cold, cynical, widowed woman, who is longing for death to solve all her problems. She is in a state of paralysis, ignoring reality, and emotionally dominating her son, who is similarly inert. Neither of them seem concerned with creating meaningful lives, and – when faced with the shame of their impending penury – they run away to Paris. In the capital city of existential ennui, however, their inertia is invaded by people who represent their pasts, presents and futures, ensuring that they are not able to stay alone wallowing in their familial purposelessness. Protagonist Frances Price learns to see beyond her egocentrism and to release her son to pursue love. Murdoch's vision of our loving interconnectedness trumps Sartre's commitment to our suffering at the judgement of others.

title: Indigenous Existentialism in the Films of Warwick Thornton
abstract: Existentialist philosophy, in particular the work of Franz Fanon and Jean-Paul Sartre, was crucial to early postcolonial theorising and, as demonstrated in the work of Brendan Hokowhitu, continues to be an important perspective for understanding Indigenous postcolonial experience. Existentialism is a valuable tool in the on-going attempt to gain clarity about the nature of racist oppression and ways of overcoming it. We focus on two films by Warwick Thornton: Samson and Delilah (2009) and Sweet Country (2017) that together form a study of an Indigenous existentialism, and in contrasting ways illustrate both the difficulty of, and possibility of, emergent transcendent agency in postcolonial environments.

title: Stan Brakhage, Jean-Paul Sartre and Existentialism: Cinema de trop
abstract: In 1961, Stan Brakhage made Sartre's Nausea for a public television introduction to existentialism hosted by Sartre scholar and translator Hazel Barnes. Brakhage later returned to that work, editing and intervening on a copy of it to make Black Vision (1965). We argue that despite Brakhage's ambivalence towards Sartrean existentialism, these works illuminate Sartre by demonstrating important continuities between hypnagogic consciousness and nausea. We additionally argue that Brakhage was likely the most appropriate filmmaker for adapting Nausea, owing to his careerlong grasp of how the experience of radical contingency could permeate not only individual consciousness, but also the filmmaking medium itself.

title: Existential Failure and Utopian Collapse in Megalopolis : A Philosophy of Imperfection
abstract: This article examines Megalopolis (Francis Ford Coppola, 2024) as a cinematic enactment of existential imperfection – where failure is not merely depicted but structurally embedded through narrative collapse, temporal disjunction and the erosion of authorial coherence. Drawing on the existential philosophies of Albert Camus, Søren Kierkegaard and Samuel Beckett, alongside critical frameworks from Trinh T. Minh-ha, I argue that Coppola does not simply risk failure but that he formalizes it as a philosophical operation. Through close analysis of recursive structures, visual dissonance and mise-en-scène destabilization, the article explores how Megalopolis renders revolt, paradox and collapse as aesthetic logic. Yet the film also interrogates the ethical limits of this wager: when failure is mediated by auteurist discourse, it risks becoming stylized spectacle rather than ontological exposure. Rather than framing Megalopolis as a misunderstood masterpiece or failed epic, I position it as a contested site where cinematic imperfection confronts the limits of sincerity and philosophical legibility in contemporary screen-philosophy.

title: What Can Cinema Do? Saint Omer and French Existentialist Disclosure as Film Theory
abstract: France's leading existential phenomenologists Simone de Beauvoir and Jean-Paul Sartre both wrote extensively about literature and rather less about film. Concentrating on Beauvoir and especially on a lecture she gave at a televised event in Paris in December 1964, I ask whether the lecture, “What Can Literature Do?”, can also apply to the medium of film, answering this question in the affirmative. It then considers the resulting Beauvoirean film theory alongside a contemporary French film, Alice Diop's Saint Omer (2022), analysing the film's visual style as is required by reading the theory alongside its fictional presentation of real events. Diop is one of France's few successful black female directors and since the two protagonists of Saint Omer are also black women, the article concludes by asking what the writings of Frantz Fanon have to offer to an existentialist screen theory seeking to build the racialisation of looking into the spectatorial dynamics of film.

title: The Existential Ambiguity of Authentic Love in Alice Diop's Saint Omer
abstract: Using Simone de Beauvoir's and Frantz Fanon's existentialist phenomenology, this article examines an existentialist ethics of recognition as an act of authentic love in Alice Diop's Saint Omer (2022). Loosely based on a true story, Saint Omer tells a story of filicide: Laurence Coly leaves her baby on a beach to die and we follow the subsequent courtroom drama as it unfolds. The film also follows Rama, a literature professor intending to write up the case as a contemporary version of the Medea myth. I suggest Saint Omer presents an ethics of recognition in its avoidance of the superficial question of what is ethical (the act of filicide); instead it shows how cinema might express an ethics that is central to reciprocal recognition, an expression of authentic love for the other. It asks whether such an ethics of recognition is even possible if it cannot be authentic, that is, if it cannot escape the prescription of recognition already embedded in gendered and colonial relations. Through Beauvoir's philosophy of love and Fanon's notion of ankylosis, I consider how an ethics of recognition can serve as an actional aspect of ambiguity, valorizing the unrealizable of the Other helping to determine the possibility of authentic love.

title: Magical Emotions: Jean-Paul Sartre and The Headless Woman
abstract: This article reexamines Jean-Paul Sartre's early theory of emotion in light of his reflections on ego, consciousness, language and narrative, clarifying his often-overlooked but critical conception of magic. I first show how magical emotional consciousness transforms the instrumental world by disrupting deterministic logic and then trace a parallel reversal in The Transcendence of the Ego, where spontaneity is displaced onto the ego and its states. I argue that these forms of magic converge with Sartre's concern about narration and expression – how meaning is retroactively conferred on events and how representation both reveals and degrades lived experience – thereby sharpening Sartre's enigmatic suggestion that the social world itself has a magical structure. To assess and concretize these claims, I turn to Lucrecia Martel's The Headless Woman (2008), whose protagonist's headlessness uncannily illustrates, yet also puts pressure on, a Sartrean account of emotional transformation as conscious but unreflective, as purposive yet spontaneous. I show that Martel's attention to framing echoes Sartre's suspicion of language's hold on things, exposing the limits of expressive mastery and thereby revealing the stubborn autonomy of objects and others. The film thus illuminates how emotional magic implicates freedom, bad faith and social complicity.

title: Screening Existentialist Narcissism in Todd Field's Tár
abstract: Inspired by the writings of Jean-Paul Sartre, this article approaches Todd Field's Tár (2022) as an existentialist satire, in which humour is borne out by a conflict between bad faith and the way in which people can miss the truth about themselves by self-delusion. Commonly classified as a psychological backstage drama, many of the scenes in Tár rely on darkly humorous delight, deliberatively indulging in vindictive attitude that clashes with our basic moral feelings. This article analyses the aesthetic-affective conflicts in Tár manifesting themselves along the axis of seeing and being seen, as much of its protagonist's efforts are defined by how she wants to appear in the eyes of others and her sense of self based on narcissistic delusions. But she cannot control the field of vision organized by the others’ perceptions, and as soon as Tár starts recognizing herself in these various perceptions, her mental stability dissolves while her disavowed guilt takes the upper hand. The final part of the article discusses the ethical implications that result from the film positioning the spectators within the very experience of a morally inscrutable character.

title: Existential Feelings in the Cinema of Ingmar Bergman
abstract: In this article I propose that films typically described as existential are not only concerned with classical existential themes – alienation or anxiety, solitude and despair – but with affective states that Matthew Ratcliffe calls “existential feelings” or “feelings of being.” These terms designate various bodily feelings – the bodily feeling of being, of existence, of belonging - that express a relationship towards the world understood as a space of possibilities. To explore this idea, I turn to a discussion of Ingmar Bergman's Silence of God trilogy, comprising Through a Glass Darkly (1961), Winter Light (1963) and The Silence (1963), and explore negative existential feelings that underlie more familiar existential moods or emotions such as anxiety or dread. This consideration of the important role of existential feelings in the work of a canonical existentialist auteur opens new ways of understanding existential moods in contemporary cinema.

Beyond Game Blocks: Adolescent Girl Players' Perspectives During COVID-19
authors: Katherine J. E. Hewett; Bethanie C. Pletcher
abstract: The Entertainment Software Association (ESA) found that women accounted for 46% of U.S. gamers in 2024. However, women players (especially girl players) remain an under-researched demographic in game studies. The aim of this qualitative case study was to expand upon previous research discoveries and explore the 21st-century skills, design processes, perspectives, and behaviors of adolescent girl players as they played, created, and survived in a video game ( Minecraft ). The data analysis involved triangulating eleven qualitative case study interviews with visual artifacts and observations from twenty-one girl players. A hundred and fifty students collaborated with the participants throughout various stages of the study's three phases. The qualitative coding process generated five themes: (1) Father Figures , (2) Community House , (3) Gamer Girl , (4) Lockdown , and (5) Trial and Error . Each theme organizes and shares how girls viewed, theorized, and interpreted their video game experiences during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Minecraft as a Pedagogical Tool: A Systematic Literature Review (2014–2024)
abstract: On the 15th anniversary of Minecraft's release (2009), this systematic review of 106 articles has been conducted to outline the scientific production of the past decade regarding the use of Minecraft in education. Among the most notable findings is the relationship between the most frequently employed game mechanics and the most recurrent educational objectives, determining that construction and programming/problem-solving are the primary mechanics utilized in educational interventions, while the analysis of Minecraft as a tool and its influence on cognitive development constitute the most extensively studied research objectives. Some of the main identified limitations highlight the need to analyse in-game activities through standardized methodological frameworks to enhance comparability with other studies, thereby facilitating the association between game mechanics and learning processes. Finally, further exploration of underdeveloped research areas is encouraged to expand the understanding of Minecraft's impact across diverse educational settings.

title: ‘Born of the Blood, Made Men by the Blood, Undone by the Blood’: Bloodborne as a Critical Reflection of Ghosts of the Anthropocene
authors: Sara Skott; Karl-Fredrik Skott Bengtson; Michael Fiddler
abstract: Drawing on critical frameworks in criminology, including Popular Criminology and Ghost Criminology, this paper aims to explore how Bloodborne offers a critical reflection of the haunting nature of the harms inflicted by humans in the age of the Anthropocene. More specifically, we aim to examine how the cultural text of Bloodborne illustrates humanity's corruption of the natural and the harms this inflicts, arguing that this can be understood as a reflection of ghosts of the Anthropocene. Using ethnographic content analysis, three main themes were uncovered in Bloodborne that related to humanity's corruption of the natural, the harms this inflict, as well as how this can be understood as a reflection of ghosts of the Anthropocene: Sanguine Exploitation, Horrific Creation , and Monstrous Extinction . We conclude by arguing that Bloodborne , in evoking the horrors of climate catastrophe, is an important cultural script that responds to McBrien’s necrocene and Haraway’s Chthulucene.

title: The Business of Play: Financialization and Optimization in World of Warcraft
abstract: In World of Warcraft (WOW) , thousands of players work together to analyze the game's rules and maximize their rewards. Organized boosting—a paid player service—is widely seen as undermining the meritocratic ideal that ties rewards to effort and skill. Drawing on semistructured interviews with six former providers of boosting services, this study argues that optimization in digital games is not solely a strategic choice, but often a necessity shaped by financial pressures. The introduction of token-based economic elements, such as the WoW token, nudges players into financial speculation and wealth accumulation, transforming optimization into a form of labor. This study considers boosting within the framework of financialization, highlighting how optimization mirrors broader tensions in a game culture shaped by corporate commodification practices.

title: Do Video Games Matter? Examining Video Games’ Pathways to Legitimacy and Cultural Value Through Cultural Intermediaries
authors: Charlotte Gislam; Garry Crawford; Gaynor Bagnall; Victoria Gosling; Neta Yodovich
abstract: After years on the fringe of our cultural and social life, video games are becoming more recognized as legitimate and culturally valuable. This paper examines the process of their legitimation through the role of ‘cultural intermediaries’, who frame video games as meaningful cultural artifacts. Drawing on Bourdieu's theories, this paper explores how external cultural institutions legitimize video games and how cross-media pollination further reinforces their cultural status. By analysing how broader industries have integrated and contextualized video games within their own domains, this paper highlights how video games contribute to cultural production and are gradually being positioned within established cultural hierarchies.

title: Queer(ed) Avatars: Exploring Visual Identity Construction in Final Fantasy XIV Online Gaymers
abstract: I explore gaymers’ use of virtual photography to construct their avatar persona in Final Fantasy XIV Online . The study of game photography is a field that has seen relatively sparse engagement from scholars in the past decade. In this article, I discuss virtual photography's potential in gaymers’ visual construction of avatar personas in massively multiplayer online role-playing games. I focus on “gaymers” as they seek alternative identity affordances, expressing dissatisfaction with the narrow range of possibilities in games. In contextualizing the phenomenon, I engage with theories on virtual photography, persona studies, and social networking. I apply this theoretical framework to a series of Instagram accounts dedicated to FFXIV Online avatars. I incorporate a queer methodology in my research to expose how gaymers resist heteronormativity in games. My findings indicate that gaymers queer FFXIV Online 's mechanics and visuals through modding and shaders to visually co-construct a digital self.

title: Emotions in Game Data Work
authors: Taina Myöhänen; Heikki Tyni; Olli Sotamaa
abstract: This study explores the emotional dimensions of data work within the game industry. Through interviews with Finnish game industry professionals, the research reveals that data-driven work practices evoke a wide range of emotions, ranging from pleasure and satisfaction to insecurity and frustration. Data can act both as a helpful workmate and as a source of professional conflict and frustration, impacting the worker's sense of professionalism. Data-driven work also compels workers to individually confront ethical questions. Our findings highlight the interplay between creative work processes and data analytics, emphasizing the emotional labor that game industry professionals need to handle in a data-driven work culture. Additionally, the research addresses ethical considerations and the emotional work required to reconcile public perceptions of data usage. The study contributes to the broader understanding of emotional work in new data-intensive professions and advocates for more emotionally sustainable practices in data-driven game development.

title: Understanding How Marginal National Video Game Industries Differ
authors: Jacqueline Burgess; Elina Roinoti; Alexander Muscat; Anthony Grace; Christian Jones
abstract: This article compares small (19 employees or fewer) video game developers’ commercial and creative mindsets in three marginal video game industries, Australia, New Zealand, and Greece, to understand how these industries differ. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 62 participants across the three countries and analysed using thematic analysis. Despite all three national industries’ marginal status, there were similarities and clear differences in how the participant developers approached video game production. In particular, the lack of institutional support available for the Greek industry resulted in developers utilising networks and reputation. The research highlights how marginal, national video game industries cannot be simply grouped together because the developers within them display differences, as a result of their industry contexts, which influence and impact their video game development. These findings have implications for support from governments and education.

title: Trains, Stations, and Railways as Harbingers of Biopolitics in Digital Games: From Governance to Hauntology
abstract: This article presents research on the digital game representations of trains, stations, and railways from the perspective of the biopolitical theory. We aimed to analyze and depict different elements of life governance mediated by games that use rail infrastructure in their main narrative arcs, mechanics, and esthetics. We chose rail because of its well-documented role in colonial and imperial projects of modernity which have become the objects of game representations. Analyzing how games mediate rail infrastructure is therefore important for understanding how they mediate biopolitical projects, which elements can be traced as manifestations of biopolitics in these games, and what role they play in representations of ideas such as nationality, progress, history, and modernity.

title: Datafication of Digital Intimacy: The Dual Logic of Empowerment and Commodification
abstract: This study explores the datafication of digital intimacy in female-oriented otome games, analyzing how these games construct databases of idealized masculinities and romantic narratives, balancing empowerment and commodification. Through digital ethnography, walkthrough, and interviews with Chinese women players between 2023 and 2024, we reveal how otome games mediate intimacies between women players and virtual male characters, reflecting sociocultural values and shaping affective experiences. These women-oriented games collect intimate data to optimize design and profitability, offering immersive, customizable romantic experiences while commodifying emotional investments. This dual dynamic underscores a tension in emotional capitalism, where intimacy is both enriched and exploited. By examining the interplay between digital intimacy, datafication, and emotional capitalism, our study further contributes to the critical discourse on how role-playing games monetize personal and emotional experiences, emphasizing the need to safeguard user sovereignty as digital platforms capitalize on affective labor.

title: Rhyming Rudely: From Medieval Flyting to Invective Poetry in Video Games
abstract: This article examines how games continue and represent the historical rituals of invective poetry exchanges. The article juxtaposes the analog, multiplayer card game Cards Against Humanity , known for its transgressive, profanity-based humor, with two single-player video games that present the invective poetry competition as (more or less) historically accurate activity. The former is argued to be a continuation of the same tradition that encompasses various historical practices such as Germanic flyting or African sounding, while the latter is an attempt at representation, without inviting the players to participate in the same practices. The difference between the card game, which makes a freer use of profanities, and the video game representation, which is devoid of it, are used to discuss to investigate the importance of the rituals involving invective poetry in the contemporary culture, as well as theorize about the differences seen in the analog and video games.

title: The Dullahan, From Fairy to Undead Tracing the Cultural Hybridization of Irish Folklore in Japanese Games and Their Paratexts
abstract: This study investigates how the Irish Dullahan—a headless fairy death messenger—came to be recast as an undead monster in Japanese popular culture. Contrary to the trend of Western tabletop role-playing games playing a central role in similar Japanese reinventions, our analysis reveals that the undead Dullahan was an exception. Instead, we demonstrate how it was shaped by the convergence of foreign influences during the 1980s and 1990s, with a central role played by the Japanese Celtic boom in that period. By examining early video games, fantasy dictionaries, and other paratexts, we highlight how cultural brokers (e.g., game artists and editors) actively reshaped imported folklore. Our findings contribute to broader discussions on cultural hybridization and underscore how games and related media powerfully influence the global perception of folkloric motifs across the broader mediascape.

title: Exploring Online Gaming Communities Through Documentary Filmmaking
abstract: This paper explores video game documentaries as a method for researching online gaming communities. We begin by framing documentary filmmaking as a practice-based approach, a creative form of video ethnography, with the film serving as the focal output. Our analysis draws on a close reading of four recent video game documentaries that highlight European voices, alongside insights from our own fieldwork. We focus on the affordances of this approach in capturing embodied, affective, and performative aspects of play that text-based ethnography may struggle to convey. The selected films also offer different stances on the agency of both participant-protagonists and researcher-director. In light of these observations, we propose a multimodal research output in which the documentary film takes center stage.

title: Tomes and Tombs: Toward a Phenomenology of Interiors in Dungeons & Dragons
abstract: This article examines the evolution of immersive spatial design in Dungeons & Dragons through phenomenological analysis of interiors in Tomb of Horrors , the only module recurrent for all the game's major editions. Drawing on game studies, phenomenology, and historiography, I compare the module's textual and visual assets to assess how spatial immersion is constructed, disrupted, and reimagined. The analysis shows that the first edition's visual–textual dissonance produces interpretive ambiguity that might enhance embodied player engagement. Later editions increasingly removed visual assets, but the rise of mixed-media platforming via virtual tabletops (VTTs) brings the visuality of spatial immersion back into focus. By reading the dissonance of visual and textual assets through Heideggerian and Merleau-Pontian models of space, I argue that VTT designers can benefit from intentional ambiguities to enrich experiential depth. Tomb of Horrors thus becomes a key site for understanding how tabletop and digital design practices shape ludic interiority.

title: Geopolitical Implications of E-Sports
abstract: The meteoric rise of electronic sports (e-sports) has transformed competitive gaming into a platform for geopolitical influence, cultural diplomacy, and digital governance. This article explores how e-sports reshape international relations and soft power, using frameworks from international relations, cultural studies, and political economy. It highlights how states like South Korea, China, Russia, and Arabian Peninsula leverage e-sports to project cultural capital, while Western markets promote corporate-led models that extend platform capitalism. It examines tensions between state-driven cyber sovereignty and corporate control over digital infrastructure. Regional dynamics from Southeast Asian cooperation to U.S.–China tech rivalries highlight e-sports’ role in economic positioning and international relations. As AI and blockchain reshape gaming's future, the article calls for deeper inquiry into e-sports’ implications for global governance, digital citizenship, and cultural diplomacy.
