title: ‘Pawing the story forward’: The producer as embedded creative mediator in a Danish writers’ room
abstract: Collaborative screenplay development is frequently associated with distributed creativity and collective authorship within writers’ rooms. At the same time, screenplay development unfolds within institutionally embedded production environments shaped by broadcaster expectations, production realities and organizational accountability. Drawing on an ethnographic case study of the Danish television Christmas calendar , this article examines how a producer participated within a Danish writers’ room as an embedded creative mediator. Based on ethnographic observations and interviews, the article analyses how creative direction was established interactionally through situated practices of mediation, calibration and institutional translation within collaborative screenplay development. The article contributes empirically grounded insights into the comparatively underexplored role of the producer within Scandinavian writers’ room cultures.

title: Céline Sciamma’s writing through desire: A new approach to writing women’s stories
abstract: The hero’s journey and the conflict model of storytelling have had a strong hold on western screenwriting since the mid-twentieth century. Increasingly, this is being questioned, especially by feminist scholars and storytellers, who find the hero’s journey exclusive of women’s stories and narrow in storytelling possibility. Maureen Murdock, Kim Hudson and others have all developed models of the heroine’s journey, but do these go far enough? Are they still too closely related to the conflict-based model entrenched by the hero’s journey and not bold enough in their scope of change? In her 2019 British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA) Screenwriting Guru talk, French writer/director Céline Sciamma proposed a new model of screenwriting emerging from her own practice that might more widely offer new possibilities for telling stories on-screen. Sciamma calls it writing through desire and argues for driving screenplays through desire, not conflict, especially when telling the stories of women and gender-diverse characters. Her three-step approach involves identifying the desires of the writer, working at the scene level and mapping the scenario. Sciamma used this method to develop and write the screenplay of her breakthrough film, Portrait de la jeune fille en feu ( Portrait of a Lady on Fire ) (2019), which won the ‘Best Screenplay’ at Cannes in 2019.

title: Web series written by women and targeting female audiences: An exploratory analysis of narrative practices in a cross-cultural context
abstract: This study presents an exploratory analysis of narrative practices in web series authored by women and targeting female audiences, examined through an intersectional feminist framework. Focusing on creative verbalization (the verbal expression of the narrative within a series, including dialogues, monologues and narrative storytelling devices), narrative expression and audience reception, the research analyses linguistic, literary and sociocultural features of ten widely viewed women-oriented web series produced in the United States and China for target audiences aged 18–45. A multidisciplinary methodology was employed, combining quantitative linguistic analysis (including type-token ratio and metaphor usage), natural language processing techniques for assessing lexical complexity, qualitative literary and thematic analysis and a sociological survey involving 386 female respondents. The findings indicate a high degree of lexical variation and a context-dependent relationship between metaphorical density and reported emotional engagement within the analysed corpus. Series that foreground marginalized identities and complex narrative perspectives earned higher audience ratings (4.3–4.8 on a five-point scale), underscoring the interpretive relevance of culturally situated storytelling. Rather than offering prescriptive models for content creation, the study contributes to feminist media scholarship and screenwriting studies by highlighting how female-authored web series employ narrative structures, character development and dialogue strategies to negotiate identity, representation and narrative agency in digital spaces.

title: Script development and audience influences: Towards a typology of audience-making practices
abstract: In this theoretical article, I offer new insights into script development as a negotiated and sociocultural process. Adapting the cultural studies concept of audience-making to screenwriting research, I argue that audiences are a contextual structure that industry practitioners contend with in various ways during negotiated script development processes. In doing so, the article addresses a research gap in screenwriting studies pertaining to the interplay between industry practitioners and audiences. I argue that audiences are embedded in script development processes, as feedback and suggestions for improvement are often based on notions of audiences and because audience analytics and direct feedback are increasingly employed during development, albeit to varying extents. To theorize this interplay, the article introduces a typology of four audience-making models deployed during script development. These models consist of imagined, measured, competent and creative audiences. Each model affords audiences different levels of agency during script development with implications for the creative process. This framework is especially timely, given the growing reliance on data-driven decision-making in contemporary screen production and the increased potentials for interaction between industry and audiences in the digital realm.

title: ‘Claiming the right to know’: Samia Henni in conversation with Balbir K Singh and Gabrielle Moser
authors: Samia Henni; Gabrielle Moser; Balbir K Singh
abstract: Samia Henni’s practice as a researcher and exhibition maker investigates spaces of destruction, disappearance and colonial resistance, working across publications, exhibitions and public lectures to excavate the history of French colonial nuclear intervention in Algeria and Africa more broadly. On the occasion of the opening of ‘Toxicité Coloniale’ at the Centre de design at the Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM) and the launch of her new book, Toxicité Coloniale: Documenter le paysage radioactif dans le Sahara (Éditions B42, 2026), a French translation of Colonial Toxicity: Rehearsing French Radioactive Architecture and Landscape in the Sahara (If I Can’t Dance, Framer Framed, edition fink, 2024, 2025), Journal of Visual Culture editorial collective members Balbir K Singh and Gabrielle Moser spoke with Henni about the limits of investigative aesthetics, visualizing what cannot be seen and the possibilities for reparation in the still unfolding histories of colonial nuclear intervention in Algeria. ‘Toxicité Coloniale’, was exhibited at the Centre de design de l’UQAM, and ran from 19 February to 12 April 2026, in Tiohtià:ke/Montréal, Canada. The exhibition was coproduced by Framer Framed and If I Can’t Dance, I Don’t Want To Be Part Of Your Revolution and supported by the Swiss Arts Council Pro Helvetia. It was first presented at Framer Framed in Amsterdam in 2023, then it travelled to the gta Exhibitions in Zurich, The Mosaic Rooms in London, DOC! in Paris, Kunstraum Kreuzberg/Bethanian in Berlin, Brown University in Providence and Carlton University in Ottawa.

title: Feeling survival: diasporic visual practices by UK–Hong Kong indie publishers, Deacon Lui and Kayla Lui
abstract: This article examines how diasporic visual practices mediate the emotional aftermath of Hong Kong’s 2019 protests and the ensuing wave of migration to the UK. Focusing on the self-published works of Hong Kong artists Deacon Lui and Kayla Lui, the author explores how zines, comics and experimental photography register not only political rupture but the ambiguous affective states that follow – fear, absurdity, ambivalence, intimacy. Rather than documenting crisis from a distance, these alternative media forms enact the disorientation of diasporic life from within. Deacon’s photographic practice centres on disappearance and quiet endurance, while Kayla’s comics embrace queer visual excess and emotional instability. Together, their work resists linear narrative and stable identity, holding space for forms of feeling that are still in formation. This analysis positions indie publishing as a method of survival – an affective and aesthetic strategy through which diasporic subjects navigate dislocation, remain connected and make sense of life in transit.

title: Edging aesthetics: queer and trans undocumented migrant images and imaginations
abstract: This article attends to erotic imaginations dreamed within the everyday material realities of queer and trans undocumented migrants in the US. Focusing on fictional representations in narrative cinema, the author analyzes depictions of nonnormative noncitizen life in two independent narrative feature films: Aurora Guerrero’s Mosquita y Mari (2012) and Isabel Sandoval’s Lingua Franca (2019). The author argues that, amid feeling out of sync with the normative nation-state’s organizations of space and time, quotidian erotic imaginative acts (like daydreaming, reminiscing and fantasizing) allow these films’ gender- and sexual-nonconforming illegalized main characters momentary access to otherwise arrangements of time–space and bodies. These different arrangements of spatiotemporality and interbodily relation rebut the placelessness that conditions queer and trans migrant life while opening further possibilities for survival and togetherness across time and space. The article proposes ‘edging’ as a framework for studying these imaginative rearrangements of time–space and proximity and the cross-ethnic decolonial coalitions they can activate. The author then reads edging’s filmic representations through what they call ‘edging aesthetics’. In so doing, they suggest these films surface the oft-overlooked significance of ordinary rituals of imagining for staging forms of being-with that exceed the US nation-state’s attempts to manage and control intimacies between people.

title: Identifying for discarding phobias: alterity endorsed
abstract: Based on the third session of her inaugural lecture at the Collège de France in 2023, in this article Mieke Bal focuses on the phobias, the excessive fears, against confrontations with alterity such as, today, refugees and other migrants. The famous masterpiece of cultural heritage, Don Quijote, from the 16th century, is so striking in that its world-wide fame seems challenged by its poetic, chaotic anti-linearity. The author explains that lack of structure due to the experience of slavery that the author, Cervantes, suffered during more than five years, without a sense of an ending. The strange situation in which the author found himself when, after a victory of the Spanish army, he and his brother were captured and sold into slavery, can only have traumatized him. The article examines how such awful socio-cultural situations make reasonable story-telling impossible. Through that narrative incapacitation, the true masterpiece from the past resonates with today once we realize that slavery still exists, but also with the indispensable anachronism that we need to understand how it makes the past an integral element of the present.

title: Solidarity movement photography: visual activism for Palestine in Berlin
abstract: Protest photography is important for articulating and materializing emotions, and for connecting movements across different places. Through conversations with four photographers in the Palestine solidarity movement in Berlin, the article discusses how they not only seek better ways to represent protest but also deploy photography as a practice of solidarity and care for the activists involved. As such, movement photography creates an ‘oppositional gaze’ to domination, based on a ‘civil contract’ between the photographer, the photographed and the viewer, that is upheld not by empathy alone but by relationality and mutual commitment to the cause of Palestinian liberation. Taking these arguments further, the article explores photography as a collective emotional practice that sustains political bonds and imagines alternative futures. Tracing how photographers navigate care, accountability and emotional intensity within protests, it highlights the role of images as both evidence and affective expressions of solidarity amid the growing repression of internationalist movements.

Enacting postcolonial digital citizenship: Malay Muslim women, social media and the politics of (un)belonging to “Thainess”
abstract: Although Malay Muslim women’s increasing role in the peace process in Thailand’s southern border provinces has become a subject of scholarly interest, their use of social media in activism remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, this paper examines how Malay Muslim women activists employ social media to strengthen their human rights advocacy, based on in-depth interviews with 10 women activists. The findings reveal that, given the highly securitized environment and the shortcomings of Thai mainstream media, social media provides an alternative civic space where Muslim women activists form a political subject, namely “pious online rights claimants.” This paper argues that this emerging social media practice contributes to the enactment of “postcolonial digital citizenship” which allows these women to contest the constructed category of Malay Muslims and Muslim women. Such intersectional contestations not only legitimize their political participation in the peace process, but also strategically manage the multifaceted boundaries of belonging as Malay Muslim women in the male-dominant sphere of the peace process and the enduring colonial notion of “Thainess.”

title: Whose voices count? Participation, power, and communication in the Global South
abstract: This paper critically reviews participatory communication in the communication for social change (CFSC) tradition in the Global South, following its development from radical origins—grounded in Freirean pedagogy and grassroots action—to its co-optation within neoliberal development frameworks. Through a comparative analysis of Latin America, Africa, and Asia, the paper questions the enduring gap between rhetoric and practice while observing how participatory action is usually caught between donor agendas, state regulation, and structural social hierarchies. Conceptually, the paper thematizes tensions around power, voice, and epistemic justice, contending that real participation necessitates more than technical participation; it needs the redistribution of communicative agency and a critical attention to the politics of voice, listening, and representation. In conclusion, the article urges a rethinking of participatory communication as a locally specific, contested practice grounded in local epistemologies and collective struggle that can promote social transformation in the face of persistent structural inequalities. The paper also contributes to ongoing efforts to rethink communication theory from Global South perspectives within contemporary media and communication scholarship.

title: “My body has gone out of style”: A critical examination of fashion magazines’ GLP-1 agonist drug discourse
abstract: This paper examines the fashion media discourse on the rise of the “Ozempic Era” in the American editions of Vogue and Elle magazines published in print and online since the announcement by the FDA clearing a GLP-1 agonist to be prescribed as a weight loss aid. Using critical discourse analysis, I explore the coverage of Ozempic and other brand name drugs in the fashion press. I situate the discourse on GLP-1’s ability to reshape the body to fit a long-held esthetic ideal at the intersection of lifestyle/fashion and health/wellness journalism and the intertextual context inherent to each. The voices and perspectives of fat women on this medical development and its relevance to both the fashion industry and their own lived experience are prioritized in the analysis.

title: Building transversal feminist politics online: A digital ethnography of Ni Una Menos (2015–2018)
abstract: Ni Una Menos is one of the most powerful transnational feminist collectives of Latin America, drawing from legacies of feminist organizing in Argentina as well as the media acumen of its founding members. This digital ethnography leverages the online discourses of Ni Una Menos and interviews with activists to examine the early years of the collective. The study helps to understand how NUM embraced transversal politics to construct its objectives and collective identity through online discourses. The ethnography also provides insights into the relevance of media and mediated activism as structuring forces in social movements, highlighting that no study about political activism is ever complete without considering media power.

title: Human directing the Loop? Rethinking automation through Chinese transnational platform expansion in Oceania
abstract: Digital platforms are often portrayed as increasingly dependent on automation to optimise user engagement and streamline governance, a logic commonly captured by the notion of the ‘human-in-the-loop’. Emerging evidence from transnational platforms, however, points to a more hybrid operational model in which algorithmic systems are actively steered through context-sensitive human intervention. This article examines Bigo Live, a Chinese-owned livestreaming platform, as it expands into Oceania, specifically Australia, New Zealand (ANZ), and Papua New Guinea. Drawing on in-depth qualitative research, including interviews and participant observation conducted in Guangzhou and Sydney, the study demonstrates that Bigo’s internationalisation relies heavily on human-led adaptation to negotiate intercultural sensitivities, localise marketing strategies, and comply with highly varied content regulations. Unexpected developments, such as the platform’s unanticipated popularity in Papua New Guinea, reveal the limitations of automation and the continuing centrality of human labour in recalibrating platform operations. The article introduces the concept of ‘human-directing-the-loop’ to describe a mode of platform governance in which human labour does not simply validate algorithmic outputs, but actively shapes how automation is deployed across culturally, legally, and infrastructurally uneven transnational environments.

title: Rohingya participatory media in protracted displacement: Counterpublic formation through calibrated participation
authors: Faheem Hussain; Sara N. Amin; Tanya Trussler
abstract: This article examines Voice of Palong (VoP), a participatory audio-visual media initiative co-produced by Rohingya refugees and the Bangladeshi host community in Cox’s Bazar camps. Based on focus groups and field observations from 2023 to 2025, the study analyzes how VoP operates not simply as a communication project but as a relational media infrastructure through which counterpublic formations are assembled under conditions of displacement, surveillance, and legal precarity. Participation is calibrated and situational, shaped by mobility restrictions, gendered risk, limited access to technological resources, and asymmetries between host and refugee participants. VoP functioned as a situated counterpublic in which members calibrate storytelling, visibility, and circulation in relation to infrastructural and regulatory constraints. Findings also show that relational processes of co-production and circulation enabled incremental social repair across refugee-host divides. By situating participatory refugee media within border and media infrastructures, this article argues that counterpublic formation in protracted displacement is materially contingent, emerging through sustained negotiation with uneven conditions of access and control.

title: Negotiating historical television in an era of political fragmentation and austerity: Tactics of heritage practitioners in Flanders, Belgium
abstract: In Western regions, tensions surrounding mediated nation-building progressively converge with growing commercialization of cultural institutions. The Story of Flanders (2023), a docudrama that narrates the genesis of Belgium’s northernmost region, proves exemplary of how reimaging national identity through public service media heightens fears for instrumentalization. This study investigates how heritage practitioners “make do” with the series and broader restrictions defined by austerity and political fragmentation. Despite ample research on historical television, identity and production, works commonly engage with historians as key expert contributors. Yet, important alternative roles have been neglected as central to the construction of televisual history. Results show austerity-drive imperatives guide practitioners to leverage discreet tactics to navigate this sensitive climate. Three areas of tension manifest, as the burden of history is weighted down by an added ideological layer: anticipating political fragmentation and fostering trust, negotiating authority and authorship, and facilitating dialogue and navigating austerity.

title: Why does distant suffering matter? Discursive domestication in Chinese mainstream media and social media on the Shanghai Jewish Refugees Museum
abstract: This study examines how distant suffering is domesticated across Chinese mainstream media and social media through the case of the Shanghai Jewish Refugees Museum. Existing research has largely focused on media representations and audience responses to mediated suffering events, paying less attention to commemorative spaces and users’ digital participation in non-Western contexts. Drawing on critical discourse analysis of mainstream media texts and Xiaohongshu posts, this study identifies three institutional domestication strategies, namely emotional, familiarizing and moral domestication, and shows how social media users re-domesticate commemorative meaning through affective resonance, geopolitical reframing and everyday spatial practices. The findings reveal that social media participation neither simply accepts nor rejects institutional narratives but produces a negotiated field of meaning shaped by platformed affect, contemporary geopolitical imagination and urban spatial consumption. By conceptualizing this process as participatory re-domestication, the article extends the study of distant suffering from media events to commemorative spaces, showing that spatial encounters with distant suffering do not automatically generate cosmopolitan empathy but are filtered through local platform practices and ideological structures.

title: Contextualising the precarities of social media influencership in Nigeria
abstract: This study draws on and extends Duffy et al.’s framework of nested precarities of visibility by conceptualising platforms, brands and the Nigerian state power geometry through the situatedness of Nigerian X influencers’ digital labour and entrepreneurship experiences. I argue that platform algorithms, markets and ecology operate within contexts that disproportionately affect Nigerian influencers. First, algorithmic suspensions cause influencers to lose their accounts for opaque and discriminatory reasons, particularly along capitalist, cultural and political lines. Second, the X creator revenue-sharing programme does not reward influencers equally because of its geopolitical and discriminatory criteria for earnings. Third, the exploitative, bureaucratic and gendered nature of the Nigerian influencer entrepreneurship industry drives up the cost of campaigns and forces micro-influencers to do more for less. Fourth, the state’s restrictive policies, such as the 2021 Twitter ban, and ambiguous taxation laws, including the 2025 Nigeria Tax Act, significantly affect influencers. These findings, engaging Africa’s scholarship on creative labour and the digital economy, contribute to de-westernising media and communication studies, as Nigerian influencers’ experiences serve as a normative critique of platforms, brands and the state’s hegemonic power. I rely on in-depth interviews of 15 influencers and representatives of corporate organisations and PR agencies.

title: Mapping worker-led AI governance in the global cultural industries
abstract: Between 2022 and early 2026, hundreds of cultural workers’ organizations around the world have mobilized in response to generative AI. From the Hollywood strikes of 2023 to voice actors’ protests in Mexico City, from pan-European game workers’ declarations to the first workers’ appendix to Brazil’s national AI bill, these mobilizations are reshaping how AI is deployed across cultural industries. This article presents a tracker of worker-led AI governance, documenting 142 worker organizations in 34 countries across eight cultural sectors. The tracker’s evidence suggests that collective bargaining is one of eight repertoires documented in the field, and not the most frequent; that most organizations target the state rather than employers or AI companies; that workers’ claims cluster around compensation, consent and copyright, with unauthorized training on creative output as the most cited harm; and that voice acting, the sector with most presence of Majority World, mobilizes a cultural-identity register that tracks the sector’s position in global screen value chains.

title: Connectivity justice: A new concept for the post-digital society
authors: André Jansson; Cornelia Brantner; Karin Fast; Linda Ryan Bengtsson
abstract: This theoretical commentary introduces the concept of connectivity justice and discusses how it can be utilized in research on mobile, digitally reliant lives. Connectivity justice reframes questions of mobility and data justice for a post-digital world in which digital connections have become both indispensable and intrusive. The concept extends recent work on digital disconnection by examining the institutional and sociotechnical drivers of connectivity (in)justice, such as state actors, tech industry, labor conditions, and cultural norms, rather than individual-level correlates alone. By combining the capabilities approach with a feminist ethics of care, connectivity justice highlights that justice today involves not only equitable access to infrastructures but also the relational capacity to connect well, to engage, withdraw, and sustain digital life responsibly. This lens opens new directions for mobilities research, and beyond, inviting analyses of how digital infrastructures, labor platforms, and everyday practices shape people’s freedoms to move, communicate, and care. In doing so, it bridges normative and empirical inquiry, providing a vocabulary for understanding justice as an evolving balance between autonomy and interdependence within networked societies.

title: The nation’s third body: Shein’s paradox between performed nationhood and transnational operations
abstract: The intensifying global tariff tensions are reshaping the operations of cross-border e-commerce platforms. This study examines Shein, a Chinese-origin e-commerce platform with global reach, to explore nationhood and transnational operations amid emerging tensions through a communication lens. Conducting Shein as a case study, this paper draws on the nation’s two bodies to conceptualize the third body as a distinct form of nationhood in the platform age. Findings reveal that Shein enacted a deterritorialized yet embedded nationhood, performing through logistical sovereignty, digital infrastructure, and transnational governance. These dimensions indicate that the third body provides insight into how state power can remain invisible yet operate through platforms. This paper concludes with implications for future research on the infrastructural turn of platforms in today’s global ambivalent moment.

title: Britain’s State-Endorsed ‘Radical Left’: Fireweed , A Magazine of Working-Class and Socialist Arts, 1975–1978
abstract: This article presents the first history of Fireweed, ‘a magazine of working-class and socialist arts’ and in so doing reveals a forgotten contribution to British literary and artistic culture. This article argues that Fireweed—overlooked by existing research—is worthy of rediscovery owing to its improbable Arts Council funding and its unique blend of elements: it was multi-disciplinary, mixed-media and featured the work of amateur and professional contributors. Fireweed is remarkable because of its emergence from a Lancashire writers’ group, its avowed socialist leaning and its endorsement by the British state; its pages offer a vivid insight into the cultural and political life of the 1970s.

title: Selective Racism, the Daily Mail , and the Anglo-Japanese Alliance
abstract: This article examines the role of the popular press, particularly the Daily Mail, in shaping public opinion to facilitate the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902. It focuses on the role and writing of Herbert Wrigley Wilson, long-time contributor and assistant editor of the Mail. It is argued that, especially through Wilson’s writings, the Daily Mail sought to recast Japan’s image in British public opinion from negative to positive, and to create an atmosphere more conducive to alliance. The ‘selective racism’ of the Mail is shown—defending Japan in racial terms while publishing intensely racist statements regarding South African Boers and Eastern European Jewish immigrants. This was not driven by racial hierarchy but by support for the realist imperatives of the British Empire—subordinating racial prejudice to strategic needs. This study presents a significant correction to scholarship on the alliance focused solely upon elite diplomacy and discourse.

title: Capturing the Audience: Advertising’s Role in American Journalism in Historical and Critical Perspective
abstract: The advertising revenue model for supporting journalism has long been an article of faith for scholars and policymakers alike. This paper challenges that assumption by examining advertising revenue as a share of the newspaper industry’s total revenue from 1880 to the present as part of a larger political economic analysis. By historicizing the complicated relationship between journalism and advertising and arraying its critical historiography, we arrive at implications vital to the industry’s foundations and future.

title: Representations of the Peace of MÜNSTER: News Genres and Communication Networks in Early Modern Spain (1647–1648)
abstract: This article examines Spanish representations in printed news pamphlets of the Peace of Münster, a treaty that recognised the independence of the United Provinces of the Netherlands from Spain and concluded the Eighty Years’ War. Often considered part of the broader Peace of Westphalia, the agreement was made possible after years of diplomatic negotiations in Münster. This study analyses two news pamphlets printed in Spain reporting on the agreement signed on 8 January 1647 and the treaty’s ratification on 15 May 1648. It explores news genres, communication networks, discourse and representations, offering insights into the early modern communicative landscape and how power can be exercised through texts.

title: ‘Their problems are in many ways ours too’ – The Tanzanian Ujamaa -philosophy in Swedish foreign aid information and the Karibu Campaign of 1974
abstract: This article examines Karibu, a 1974 nation-wide Swedish governmental information campaign about Tanzania aimed at influencing public opinion in favor of Sweden's aid policies. The campaign praised President Julius Nyerere's Ujamaa-philosophy of communal farming even as it turned into coercive displacement of millions of Tanzanians. Drawing from archival sources and read against research on Swedish foreign aid history and issues of representation in development aid discourses, the study is driven by the assumption that post-colonial aid-relations share with colonialism the perceived necessity for the donor/colonizer to justify its actions by communicating ‘knowledge’ about the aid-receiver/colonized subject back to the home-front. The result shows that such representations do not necessarily uphold the traditional interpretative privilege and agency of the Global North. In Karibu, the Ujamaa-philosophy saturated the campaign to such an extent that it even shaped Swedish agency in blind compliance with Nyerere's development politics.

title: From the Digital City to the Network Society: Tracing Sociotechnical Imaginaries of the Dutch Web (1994-2004)
authors: Nathalie Fridzema; Susan Aasman; Tom Slootweg; Rik Smit
abstract: This article examines how the meanings of ‘the web’ were constructed and contested in the Netherlands between 1994 and 2004. Drawing on a wide range of public sources, the study identifies four overlapping sociotechnical imaginaries. Each framed the web differently, respectively as civic infrastructure, a state-led modernisation project, speculative engine, and everyday network, and each drew on distinct social groups with unequal reach and institutional authority. Treating public discourse as the primary arena in which the web’s meaning, morality, and materiality were negotiated, the article contributes to the historiography of the early Dutch web and to broader debates in media history about how newly emerging technologies acquire social meaning. The early web in the Netherlands offers a valuable case as an infrastructural frontrunner, positioned at the intersection of American techno-entrepreneurial imaginaries and European policy ambitions, yet largely absent from existing web historiography.

title: The 1897 Visit of King Chulalongkorn to Italy: A Media Frame Analysis of Italian Newspaper Articles
abstract: This study examines how the Italian press represented the King of Siam, Chulalongkorn, during his first European tour in 1897, which marked a fundamental step in the rapprochement between the West and the East. On the one hand, Europe gained direct contact with Siamese culture; on the other, the Siamese monarch—through his diplomacy and affable character—managed to avert the threat of colonial invasion and, simultaneously, elevate his country to the status of a European nation. The articles examined are drawn from seven major newspapers and have been analyzed using the media frame analysis method and interpreted through the lens of Van Waarden’s theoretical framework. Through the media coverage of Chulalongkorn’s visit, this study also aims to examine the characteristics of the ‘New Journalism’ style that Italian newspapers adopted.

title: Tracing the Turkish modernization: A content analysis of newspaper ads depicting children in the Early Republican Period (1923–1950)
authors: Uğur Bakır; Murat Çelik; Süleyman Aşık
abstract: Children were positioned as one of the essential symbols in the dissemination of Turkish modernization discourse. This study examines the portrayal of children in advertisements during the early years of the Turkish Republic, aiming to explore how the ‘modern’ Turkish child was conceptualized in mass media. Through a content analysis of 491 advertisements published in national newspapers, the study reveals that children’s representation in advertisements played a significant role in negotiating broader processes of social and cultural transformation. Furthermore, the findings suggest that advertisements served as a cultural mechanism for conveying modernization efforts in Turkish society by aligning children with emerging ideals of modernity. This research underscores the role of advertisements not only as communication tools but also as critical sites where national identity, social values, and ideologies were constructed during a period of profound social and cultural transformation.

title: ‘Covering Our Tracks’: Archival Research on Liberation Movement Communication in South Africa, 1963–1980 | Limits and Possibilities
abstract: Archival research in post-colonial contexts poses challenges to researchers, with archives often telling us more about their creators than their subjects. In the modern South African context, a thirty-year period of censorship led to further silencings in the media and greatly affected the ways in which the liberation movement communicated. In order to avoid capture, activists rejected the practice of collating their communicative processes, covering their tracks, as it were, and leaving distinctly thin, sometimes coded, paper trails. This paper addresses the domino effect of censorship on liberation movement communication practices between 1963 and 1980, examining the ways in which state suppression forced resistance underground, posing various challenges (and opportunities) for historians. The paper argues that decolonial approaches to research—foregrounding resistance, orality and moving beyond conventional understandings of the archive—are best suited to researching dissident communication.

title: Eclipse in the Press. The Circulation of News on the 1919 Total Solar Eclipse
authors: Ana Simões; Luís Miguel Carolino; Samuel Gessner; Hugo Soares; Cristina Luis
abstract: On 29 May 1919, one of the most famous total solar eclipses in history provided a crucial test for Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity. During approximately five minutes of totality, British astronomers photographed the star field behind the eclipsed Sun to try to detect the predicted bending of light. Their successful confirmation transformed Einstein into an international icon, and newspapers worldwide reported the results. This article examines how news of the eclipse and the scientific expeditions spread through the global press. Rather than focussing on the later impact of Einstein’s relativity, it examines coverage of the expeditions themselves. Digital newspaper archives from Portugal, Brazil, Great Britain, Germany and the United States of America were surveyed for all eclipse-related news published between 1 January 1919 and 31 December 1920. This analysis provides the first systematic overview of how information about the eclipse and the expeditions circulated internationally, reflecting its transmission across different audiences in Europe and the Americas.

title: Reading, writing, rumour: press readership and the making of war knowledge in Australia 1914–1918
abstract: Studies of the media during the First World War have highlighted its weaknesses and deficiencies, yet the question of how citizens actually engaged with the press and made sense of the war remains elusive. Based on extensive analysis of Australian civilians’ correspondence, this article argues that citizens were capable of engaged and effective reading of the forms of information available in the press, including reportage, casualty lists and extracts from soldiers’ letters. That sensitive reading of the press, made in conjunction with their own contacts with soldiers on and returned from the front, allowed civilians to achieve a genuine, if necessarily imperfect, understanding of the nature, course and shocking costs of the war. Far from being entirely deceived, Australians’ determination to continue the struggle suggests they fought with their eyes open, even as they longed for the conflict to end.

title: Propaganda in Pre-Soviet Caucasian Press at The Example of Comparative Analysis of Georgian Newspapers: ‘Ertoba’ (1919) and ‘Sakartvelo’ (1919)
abstract: In Georgia, as well as in Transcaucasia in general, from the first appearance of print media until the beginning of the twentieth century, only the interests of Tsarism were pursued in the press. The Tsarist and Communist press used similar propaganda styles while advancing different political interests. The shifting political climate of the transition period fostered media content distinct from Tsarist influence and shaped by relative freedom. Propaganda texts were, of course, still to be found in the pre-Soviet Caucasian press, but pluralism, the striving for independence of the countries conquered by the Russian Empire, and chaos created a different situation. This paper discusses the peculiarities of the propaganda activities of the pre-Soviet Caucasian press of the beginning of the twentieth century using the Georgian newspapers published in 1919: the social-democratic, Ertoba (Unity) and the national-democratic, Sakartvelo (Georgia).

title: Transoceanic News for the Overseas Possessions: The Distribution of Periodical Publications ( Impresos ) in Spanish America, 1764–1781
abstract: This essay examines the dynamics that facilitated the circulation of periodical publications (impresos) produced in Spain across the Spanish Atlantic during the second half of the eighteenth century. The category of impresos includes three periodicals published in Madrid: theGaceta de Madrid (Madrid Gazette), the Mercurio Histórico Político (Historical-Political Mercury), and the Guía de Forasteros (Foreigners’ Guide). These impresos spread news and reflections about Europe, Africa, and Asia. It is argued that the postal administrations created by the Spanish Empire after 1764 were fundamental to the circulation of printed news to Spanish America. The urban post offices established by the Bourbon government not only facilitated distribution but also served as centers for sales. Similarly, price reductions, tax exemptions, and frequent distribution encouraged the purchase of these materials. This study contributes to an understanding of how inhabitants of Spanish American territories accessed news from other parts of the world and the mechanisms that made this possible.

title: Archival Marginalia: Metadata as Discursive Practice and Epistemic Redress in Diasporic Audiovisual Heritages
abstract: Researching the film and media histories of migrant and diasporic communities presents significant archival challenges due to both the complex nature of audiovisual media and the historical neglect by memory institutions. While critical archival scholarship has emphasized proactive acquisition and appraisal to counter archival absences, this article argues that equal attention must be paid to the role of metadata practices. Building the concept of “archival marginalia,” the article proposes a framework for understanding archival metadata as a site of epistemic redress, drawing from decolonial and reparative archival theories. It highlights the under-explored realm of reparative description in audiovisual archives and presents a case study from the DE-BIAS project at the Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision, focusing on the postcolonial Surinamese community in the Netherlands. The article advocates community-led, social-justice-oriented reparative work that reclaims marginalized perspectives and transforms archival knowledge production.

title: The Regency Crisis and the Development of Organised Adversarial Party-Political Press in Britain
abstract: With the incapacity of King George III in 1788 and early 1789, a political crisis developed as the opposition Whigs looked to force a regency for the Prince of Wales, which would potentially see the fall of the Pittite government. The political machinations of this unsuccessful parliamentary campaign are well established; however, the political battle was not only fought in parliament but at length through the press. This article examines the press war that was fought between the opposition and the government. It shows that the developments in opposition party political management in the 1780s meant that the press war during the Regency Crisis represented a further development in the organisation of adversarial party politics. This was established by parliamentary and press arguments which were intrinsically intertwined for both opposition and government across newspapers, pamphlets and graphic satire as well as in Westminster.

title: Airborne Coloniality Aerial Media and the Vertical Politics of Mediation and Violence
abstract: This article explores the colonial foundations of aerial media—those that operate in and as the atmosphere, from drones and satellites to data signals. Rather than simply transmitting through air, these media territorialise it, transforming the sky into a site of surveillance, control, and communicative violence. While some media scholarship has treated air as an elemental medium for sensory connection, its colonial-military histories remain largely overlooked. Drawing on archival research and engaging the anticolonial turn in media studies, this article examines how air was organised as a vertical medium of domination in 1920s Iraq under British mandate rule. Through wireless telegraphy, aerial photography, and bombardment, empire restructured the atmosphere into a communicative field of power. This study reframes air not as a neutral conduit of meaning, but as a historically saturated medium through which empire sees, knows, and breathes force—remaking how life is sensed, valued, governed and amputated from above.

title: The risks of taking journalists for a ride during the Anglo-Irish War
abstract: This article focuses on the aftermath of a skirmish between British forces and the Irish Republican Army [IRA] in November 1920 in a remote village near the town of Tralee in the south-west of Ireland. It examines newspaper reports of the incident and an accompanying photograph that purported to show three dead ambushers. The photograph was, in fact, staged after the event in a different location to provide some positive news during a difficult period for the British administration in Ireland. The discovery of the fraud undermined British efforts to cultivate positive relations with the national and international media. The fraudulent nature of the photograph has long been known to Irish historians, but this article examines its appearance in the context of the broader reporting of the crisis by English daily national and provincial newspapers. Finally, this piece also uses the skirmish to examine the creation of stock film footage of the Irish conflict by Pathé News that could be re-produced as news reporting in different contexts.

title: AANZCA2025: ‘Turning the tides’: communication studies in an age of epistemic flux
authors: Harry Dugmore; Susan Grantham; Phoebe Macrossan
abstract: This introduction situates the nine papers selected for this Media International Australia AANZCA2025 Feature Topic. These papers were originally presented at the 2025 Australian and Aotearoa New Zealand Communication Association (AANZCA) conference hosted by the University of the Sunshine Coast (26–28 November 2025) amid an accelerating crisis of credibility in knowledge production. Social media and generative AI have deepened the destabilisation of various knowledge orders and fields of expertise, i.e., who gets to make knowledge and judge its veracity. This has reshaped public trust in expertise in general and journalistic knowledge production in particular, with profound implications for civic engagement and public deliberation. We argue that communication and media studies must continue recalibrating its theoretical and methodological tools to help turn the ‘tides’ of disengagement and democratic backsliding. Collectively, the nine papers in this Feature Topic demonstrate that the ongoing epistemic flux in our society and in our scholarship is not a uniform phenomenon, but one that plays out unevenly across audiences, industries and platforms, producing both new vulnerabilities and new forms of resistance and resilience.

title: Mis- and distrust cues: investigating how people determine who and what to trust online
authors: Tanya Notley; Aimee Hourigan; Sora Park; TJ Thomson
abstract: The sheer volume of news and information people see online, especially on social media, can be overwhelming and make it difficult – or impossible – for people to fact-check the content they come across on a daily basis. In light of this, our study explored the everyday methods people use to decide who and what to trust online. Using a 1-week digital diary study with 55 adult participants living in Australia, we learnt that mis- and distrust cues provide people with a coping mechanism to deal with information overload. However, when we fact-checked content participants labelled as untrustworthy, 39% of these examples were factually correct. This suggests that people's hypervigilance in using mis- and distrust cues results in them frequently mis-categorising content. We draw on these findings to make recommendations relevant to news publishers and media literacy practitioners.

title: Searching for the truth? search engines and their AI affordances’ responses to conspiratorial search practices
authors: Kateryna Kasianenko; Caroline Gardam; Katherine M. FitzGerald; Ashwin Nagappa; Axel Bruns; Shir Weinbrand; Daniel Angus; Samantha Vilkins; Abdul Karim Obeid
abstract: Search engines are a common pathway to conspiracy theories, and producers of conspiratorial narratives actively encourage users to search for particular terms. Understanding how search engines respond to different information-seeking practices is therefore essential for explaining the dynamics of online conspiracy theories. Existing audits of search engines rarely account for systematic variation in query formulation arising from users’ differing levels of engagement with conspiratorial beliefs, nor do they consider recently introduced AI-powered search features. To address this gap, we developed search query sets informed by conspiratorial and non-conspiratorial information-seeking practices of online forums, using the chemtrails and 15-minute cities conspiracy theories as case studies. We performed algorithmic audits of Google's first-page search results and AI Overview responses. Our findings show substantial differences in the information returned for queries representative of general public information seeking compared with those reflecting conspiratorial perspectives. These differences appear to arise partly from Google's efforts to moderate sensitive topics, but also from the limitations of those interventions in recognising and responding to conspiratorial modes of query formulation. AI Overviews likewise vary according to query framing and generally attempt to debunk conspiratorial claims. However, these responses are often brief, provide limited supporting evidence, and are less effective for the newer 15-minute cities conspiracy theory, suggesting that current AI-mediated search guardrails remain uneven and require further development.

title: Did journalists ‘sanewash’ Donald Trump during the 2024 election campaign? an empirical analysis
authors: Stephen Harrington; Timothy Graham; Ella Chorazy; Kristy Hess
abstract: Donald Trump's political and rhetorical style has presented a challenge to journalists’ modus operandi since he first announced his candidacy for President. During the 2024 election campaign, the practice of ‘sanewashing’ became a talking point among media and political commentators. The term describes the way Donald Trump's rambling, generally unfocussed speech would appear more coherent (and ‘sane’) when it was presented in news reports. In this paper, we empirically test whether ‘sanewashing’ occurred during the 2024 election campaign, focussing on two speeches that drew the most criticism for how they were covered in the media: one delivered to the Economic Club of New York, and the other given at a rally in Latrobe, Pennsylvania. Using topic modelling and semantic similarity analysis, we examine which components were covered and the language used in reporting. We conclude that while ‘sanewashing’ did occur, this may reflect standard journalistic procedures, rather than ideological motivations.

title: From national outlets to transnational audiences: far-right hyperpartisan news sources on YouTube
abstract: In the past two decades, far-right movements have gained significant power in a variety of countries around the world, coinciding with increasing cooperation between far-right actors across borders. While the transnational convergence of these movements has been documented at elite and institutional levels, there has been limited investigation into the transnationalisation of the digital environments through which far-right narratives circulate. This article addresses this gap by examining the transnational far right through the lens of hyperpartisan news sources on YouTube. Through a novel data-gathering method, this study constructs a unique dataset comprising metadata from 114,025 videos and 51,449,494 comments across the entire lifetime of four channels, each based in a different English-speaking country. Using a unique combination of digital methods, including social network analysis and topic modelling, this article documents the content strategies of these hyperpartisan news sources and the resulting audiences across the entire lifespan of the channels. The findings reveal a highly integrated transnational far-right information space on YouTube with significant and sustained audience overlaps between the channels. Furthermore, the analysis identifies several strategies used by hyperpartisan news sources to attract and engage international audiences and raises critical questions about the transnational influence of the far right from the United States.

title: Trending perceptions of loss: influencers and the visual economy of breakup grief on TikTok
abstract: When grief becomes social media content, boundaries between private mourning and public spectacle dissolve. This article examines how romantic relationship dissolution, or breakup, emerges as grief content on TikTok. Using qualitative content analysis of a breakup grief influencer's TikTok account as a case study, it explores how narratives of breakup grief are produced, circulated, and consumed on the platform. The analysis identifies three key dynamics: the mobilisation of positivity as a healing resource, the construction of ideals of the perfect self, and the formation of a niche community centred on breakup grief. The findings demonstrate how experiences of romantic loss are transformed into content capital, positioning grief as both a personal experience and a cultural resource on the platform. The article argues that influencer-mediated breakup grief not only reflects experiences of loss but also shapes the emotional norms and meanings through which grief is understood and communicated within platform cultures.

title: The cosy-turn: theorising cosy community as emergent counter-infrastructure in platform capitalism
abstract: As trust in centralised social media platforms declines amid algorithmic harm, extractive data economies, and the erosion of psychological and epistemic safety, users are migrating toward smaller, semi-private digital spaces – a phenomenon some design and technology practitioners have termed the “cozy web.” While this shift is commonly characterised as retreat from digital publics, this paper offers the first sustained academic theorisation of the cosy web and the communities it gives rise to as a re-decentralisation of online social life and governance. Drawing on media and communication scholarship, feminist care ethics, and infrastructural critique, we conceptualise cosy communities as a distinct sociotechnical formation organised around care-centred governance, deliberate boundary-setting, and relational accountability – rather than visibility, automation, and scale. We build on the concept of cosy agency to describe the active work through which participants reconstruct stable, bounded digital environments in response to platform volatility, and draw on Giddens’ ontological security and Kelty's recursive publics to theorise the conditions under which such communities emerge and govern themselves. Examining three key terrains – decentralised and federated environments, independent hosted platforms, and enclaves within Big Social – we argue that cosy communities are not merely nostalgic retreats, but emergent counter-infrastructures that relocate governance from opaque platform systems to situated human judgement. The ‘cosy-turn’, we contend, represents a politics of maintenance and a reassertion of community as a governable social form within and against platform capitalism.

title: AI-mediated witnessing: refugee testimony and visibility in Australia's Exhibit A-I
abstract: This article examines Exhibit A-I: The Refugee Account as a case of AI-mediated witnessing, exploring how ethical storytelling practices can centre marginalised voices without exposing vulnerable communities to further harm. Situated within Australia's offshore detention regime, which is characterised by restricted access and limited visual documentation, Exhibit A-I uses AI-generated imagery and synthetic audio to translate refugee testimony into publicly circulating artefacts. Drawing on scholarship on mediated suffering and witnessing, the article argues that generative AI introduces a new mediating layer that transforms testimony from direct forms of recorded evidence into AI-mediated reconstruction. This enables forms of visibility that would otherwise remain inaccessible, while raising important questions about authenticity, authorship and the ethical shaping of representation. The concept of AI-mediated witnessing is proposed to capture these dynamics and to show how generative media, alongside more conventional forms of anonymised mediation, can support the communication of sensitive experiences while reconfiguring the conditions under which voice, visibility and public engagement are produced.

title: The limits of disruption: AI and the persistence of VFX labour
authors: AD Narayan; Angelique Nairn; Justin Matthews; Duncan Caillard
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and generative AI are increasingly framed as transformative forces in film production, particularly visual effects (VFX). Yet current debates often overstate their replacement of creative labour or integration into final-pixel production. This article examines how AI is understood, evaluated, and constrained in contemporary VFX practice through qualitative analysis of twelve interviews with VFX practitioners and twenty-six online news articles published between January and June 2025. Using reflexive thematic analysis, it identifies three themes: hype and hyperbole, efficiencies and employment, and actual application. Findings show that AI is valued mainly for ideation, rapid visualisation, prototyping, decision support, and selected technical tasks, while final production use remains limited by control, continuity, fidelity, intellectual property, data provenance, and pipeline compatibility. The article argues that AI adoption in VFX is a negotiated sociotechnical process, not a seamless technological rupture.

title: Human versus AI-generated emergency alerts: a comparative study for AI emergency communication applications
abstract: This study explores the capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) to generate emergency alerts, using Tropical Cyclone Kirrily as a case study, which made landfall in Queensland, Australia, on 25 January 2024. ChatGPT-4 was used to recreate official alerts issued during the event via structured prompts informed by the Internalisation, Distribution, Explanation, Action (IDEA) model and Australian disaster communication guidelines. Findings indicate that AI-generated alerts largely satisfied the core IDEA model components and demonstrated a strong ability to personalise messages for specific needs and audiences with clear safety instructions. However, human oversight remained necessary, particularly as conditions escalated, to ensure alerts reflected the evolving risk context. The comparative analysis undertaken shows that while both human- and AI-generated alerts had limitations, AI has the potential to enhance clarity and personalisation of emergency messages. Overall, the study highlights the value of combining structured risk communication frameworks with human oversight to effectively integrate AI into emergency communications.

title: What factors influence Australian media professionals’ level of agreement with guidelines for reporting suicide?
authors: Jaelea Skehan; Ross Tynan; Renate Thienel; Jane Pirkis; Myfanwy Maple; Brian Kelly
abstract: This study examined whether Australian media professionals agree with guidelines for reporting suicide (Mindframe guidelines) and the factors that may influence their level of agreement. Participants completed an online survey to assess their level of agreement with Mindframe guidelines and to explore factors that might be associated with guideline agreement. These factors included demographic variables, suicide stigma, exposure to suicide, perceived strength of the evidence, personal use of guidelines, organisational compliance with guidelines and prior exposure to Mindframe. In total, 262 Australian media professionals from broadcast, print, digital and other media were recruited. Participants agreed with 15 of the 16 guideline statements, with linear regression showing that prior exposure to Mindframe was a significant predictor of agreement as was the perceived strength of the evidence, personal application of guidelines and stigma. Guidelines for reporting suicide should be enhanced by an active implementation strategy informed by knowledge and views of media professionals.

title: The “renaissance” of auditory medium in China: a study on the motives of Chinese podcasting users and corresponding development strategies of Chinese podcasting
abstract: In 2020, China witnessed its own “Year of the Podcast.” Podcast, an auditory medium that dominates the Western market, is once again enjoying a “renaissance” in China after years of silence. This article begins by tracing the development trajectory of Chinese podcasting and examining the reasons behind its “renaissance.” Then, based on Grounded Theory Methodology, this article utilizes user reviews from Little Universe, the first Chinese RSS podcast application on the App Store, as research samples. Assisted by qualitative research software Nvivo12, it analyzes the motives of Chinese podcasting users and the corresponding development strategies of Chinese podcasting. The research reveals that emotional needs, platform needs, and cognitive needs are the three prominent categories of needs, accounting for 45%, 34%, and 22%, respectively. Chinese podcasting users are particularly concerned about the adaptability of podcasting platforms to various devices in changing usage scenarios, the future direction of commercialization, and the usefulness and diversity of podcast programs. Unlike Western podcasting, social needs play a crucial role in Chinese podcasting, but there are divergent opinions among Chinese users regarding them. Therefore, the development of social functions needs to be carefully controlled within certain limits.

title: Indonesian mum-influencers: motherhood, creative work and the challenges of a precarious workforce
abstract: This study explores how Indonesian ‘Mumpreneur’ Influencers (influencers) navigate neoliberal precarity and patriarchal gender norms through their work as stay-at-home mum influencers on Instagram. This research combines a qualitative analysis of the Instagram accounts of Indonesian mumpreneurs with in-depth interviews with 32 mothers, who identify as mumpreneurs and mumfluencers. The interviews shed light on their motivations, content strategies and the challenges of self-entrepreneurship in an increasingly saturated market. The study argues that influencer Mumpreneurship is a complex and contradictory phenomenon. Although mumprenuerships are often praised as empowered entrepreneurs, this research shows that mumprenuership is not just a strategy for fiscal sustainability but is also a symptom of broader problems. These include precarious childbirth and gender barriers to formal employment, the absence of supportive employment policies for working mothers, and widespread gender bias in the world of work.

title: ‘I don’t want to live their lives’: the dynamics of Vietnamese digital media
abstract: This article examines Vietnam and unpacks how its digital media is operating somewhat successfully. It demonstrates how contemporary online content creators adapt and thrive within a platformed, social media ecology that pushes back against non-authentic media through what locals refer to as ‘online experience intermediators’. Using interviews with Vietnamese creative industry experts, online content creators and younger users, this article articulates how Vietnamese digital media is built on similar practices to its Western counterparts, but has a distinctiveness that provides positive spaces for online communication for particular groups of users. Through a pushback media lens, Vietnamese digital media, specifically social media, is broadly progressive, inclusive, at an arms-length from hate speech, misinformation and vitriol content, and provides a burgeoning digital media market for multiple industries. Vietnam demonstrates a pushback against what has been described as influencers, while at the same time hinting at a desire towards online experience intermediators.

title: White supremacy on Goodreads: intertextuality and community management in reader reviews of The Swan Book
abstract: Online book review platforms, such as Goodreads, are popular sites for readers to connect with other readers, and they enable researchers and professionals working in the publishing industry to gauge how readers respond to specific books. The Swan Book , first published in 2013 and written by Waanyi author Alexis Wright, is strongly influenced by Wright's positionality as a First Nations author. In this article, I study 197 reader reviews that have been posted to the Goodreads page of The Swan Book , and examine how readers enact or reject White supremacist approaches to literature in their reviews of the novel. To conduct this study, I completed close reading analysis of Goodreads reader reviews, drawing upon theoretical approaches from book history and critical Whiteness studies. In this article, I find that the formation of reader review communities, enabled by the deployment of intertextual references within the Goodreads review space, is key to how White supremacist review practices are supported or rejected by readers in their responses to The Swan Book .

title: Exploratory worldbuilding: bottom-up strategy and continuity in Ejen Ali transmedia narrative development
authors: Umar Hakim Mohd Hasri; Md Azalanshah Md Syed
abstract: This study investigates the Ejen Ali franchise, a popular Malaysian animation brand that began with a TV series first broadcast in 2016 and has since garnered a significant following. The franchise expanded into a feature film, which premiered in 2019. In addition to the TV series and film, Ejen Ali exists across various media forms, including comic novels, mobile games, and trading card games. By leveraging transmedia storytelling, Wau Animation (the producer) has built a complex and immersive narrative world for Ejen Ali, attracting diverse audiences and fostering engagement in television, films, comics, and games. Through in-depth interviews with 15 key members of the production team, including directors and writers, this research explores the strategic process behind worldbuilding directly from its primary creators. This research uncovers that Wau Animation approaches worldbuilding through exploratory method, using a bottom-up strategy and ensuring continuity in storytelling across media.

title: Public service sentiment in Australian digital communities on Reddit and Whirlpool during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Verity Trott; Ben Lyall; Callum Jones; Brady Robards; Steven Roberts
abstract: This paper explores the role of digitally networked local communities on the platforms Reddit and Whirlpool in helping citizens navigate and understand Australian public services during the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. The study incorporates an analysis of six location-based Australian subreddits and nine discussion forums on the platform Whirlpool. An inductive content analysis on a dataset of 14,000 posts and comments collected across February to April of 2020 was conducted resulting in a dataset of 2012 posts that mentioned public services. Following this, a bipartite network analysis combined with a sentiment analysis was employed. The findings highlight how localised online spaces work as peer-to-peer information aggregates that curate and make visible citizen understandings of Australian public services. This research contributes an understanding of how online communities intersect with urban and regional localities and the implications of these spaces for civic engagement and access to support during times of crisis.

title: Motherhood among immigrant entrepreneurs in Chile: tensions and coping strategies in digital entrepreneurship
authors: Catalina Ramírez González; Sònia Parella Rubio; Alisa Petroff
abstract: Amidst the digital transformation that has accelerated gig work globally, this article tackles the digital entrepreneurship experiences of immigrant mothers in Chile, a demographical group uniquely impacted by the digitalization trend and the COVID-19 pandemic's shift towards remote work. More specifically, it addresses the underexplored nexus of digital entrepreneurship, migration and gender, and how digital platform-mediated self-employment aids in balancing professional and domestic spheres. Based on the analysis of 41 qualitative interviews, with migrant women participating in the ‘Digital Business Transformation’ program, results show a set of coping mechanisms displayed by immigrant mothers to juggle the pressures of motherhood and digital entrepreneurship. The analysis highlights that digital platforms are strategically used as a response to unemployment, inactivity or labour market segmentation, while mothers develop adaptive strategies that combine parenting, entrepreneurial endeavours and additional income-generating activities. While entrepreneurship theoretically promises time autonomy, its daily interweaving with familial responsibilities leads to significant stress, indicating the need for support systems to recognize the complex roles of motherhood, business ownership and formal work engagement. The findings contribute to the discussion on the gendered nuances of migrant entrepreneurship and require a policy framework supporting the multiplicity of roles assumed by women in digital environments.

title: Foregrounding Hiss: Debord, Adorno, and Akerman in Sonata Form
abstract: Despite its presence as both an embedded element in film optical tracks and as sound in cinema loudspeakers, hiss – present in all films from the earliest talkies to Dolby-encoded titles – has been largely ignored by media scholars. The present study ruptures this silence by acknowledging the sound of hiss as a meaningful component of the cinematic apparatus and experience. To do so, this essay – structured in sonata form – contextualises and juxtaposes Debord’s Howls for Sade, Adorno’s scholarship on radio, and Chantal Akerman’s News for Home, all of which foreground hiss as they engage with or disrupt the notion of ‘spectacle’. An examination of these sources and their historical constellations (elucidated through discussions on CBS, Dolby, and the Vitaphone as well as projection manuals) puts forth three theses: one, that the ‘visibility’ of hiss in cinema undergoes a century-long evolution, first as an engineering concern, later as an artistic device, and finally as a curiosity for digital spectators; two, that historical movements of attenuating or foregrounding hiss, often conceptualised as a visual phenomenon, trace political efforts of concealing and uncovering the cinematic apparatus, specifically the mediations responsible for the illusion of synchronisation; and three, that hiss in cinema ensures a pleasurable spectacular reassurance of formal continuity through sound.

journal: Music, Sound, and the Moving Image
title: Inverting the Acousmêtre
abstract: This article advances a revised conception of Michel Chion’s archetype of the acousmêtre in light of recent scholarship on narrative film and television. It begins by evaluating Chion’s criteria for the acousmêtre, arguing that its attendant traits are either essential or ancillary, contrary to Chion’s general implied necessity in traits he theorises. The article undertakes a set of inversions of ancillary traits to explore limitations and new applications of the trope as an interpretive lens. Through four primary case studies – Moon Knight (Jeremy Slater, 2022), Love Actually (Richard Curtis, 2003), Halloween (John Carpenter, 1978), and Parasite (Bong Joon Ho, 2019) – this expansion addresses a wider range of film and television genres than is typical for applications of the acousmêtre, including romantic comedy and family animation. These permutations bring out the acousmêtre’s ability to highlight structural power dynamics that might otherwise be overlooked, extending the trope’s relevance beyond characterisation and insular narrative concerns to implications of social commentary, an application of the trope that scholars seldom consider. The culminating analysis centres on the acousmêtre’s affordance of socio-economic critique in Bong’s Parasite.

journal: Music, Sound, and the Moving Image
title: The Spectre of Film Music: A Hauntological Study of the Vaporwave Aesthetic in The Neon Demon (2016)
abstract: This article explores the vaporwave aesthetic of The Neon Demon (Nicholas Winding Refn, 2016). Vaporwave is an electronic musical genre that emerged in the early 2010s, reconfiguring electronic music from the 1980s and 1990s. French philosopher Jacques Derrida coined the term ‘hauntology’ in the 1990s to describe a ‘thing’ from the past haunting the present, like a spectre that cannot be seen, through time being out of joint. Vaporwave music haunts The Neon Demon like Derrida’s spectre by harmonising audiovisually with the visual language of the film. I call this audiovisual harmony and haunting the vaporwave aesthetic. Set in Los Angeles in the present day, The Neon Demon follows Jesse, a 16-year-old orphan who moves to the city aspiring to become a fashion model. Jesse is lured by the vaporwave aesthetic’s futuristic, utopic guise which haunts the LA fashion industry, in the hope of achieving immortality in the industry after the decay of her traumatic past. However, Jesse is exposed, consumed, and ultimately killed by the spectral haunt of the fashion industry’s decayed capitalist utopia. The vaporwave aesthetic in The Neon Demon shows film music’s power to manipulate the film image.
