journal: New Review of Film and Television Studies
title: When Billie Holiday went to Hollywood: the biopic as reputation management in Lady Sings the Blues
abstract: When Lady Sings the Blues, the autobiography of jazz vocalist Billie Holiday, was published in 1956, the image that the book presented of Holiday defied midcentury politics of respectability and fashioned a notion of ladyhood borne from the struggles of Black women. While numerous producers showed interest in adapting the source material to the screen, the book’s image of Holiday proved difficult to reconcile with the strictures of Black representation within Hollywood. By analyzing archival materials that give insight into several attempts to adapt this book to film, this article chronicles Holiday’s relationship to Hollywood both via her own brief screen career and through the fifteen-year period in which producers sought to bring Holiday’s life to the screen as Hollywood negotiated the possibilities of Black representation from the Civil Rights years to the Black Power era. In so doing, I argue that biopics constitute a form of reputation management wherein the cultural value of a public figure is negotiated within the industrial priorities of entertainment institutions. The case of Holiday and Lady Sings the Blues illuminates the politics of the possible in adapting a Black woman’s defiant image of selfhood to the screen within the industrial conditions and narrative conventions that defined Hollywood during a crucial period for African American cinema.

journal: New Review of Film and Television Studies
title: “My job is to live my life, not save yours”: queer emotional labor, audiences, and Netflix’s Queer Eye
abstract: In this article, I argue that audience members of Netflix’s Queer Eye expect the Fab Five to perform emotional labor to access a genuine self. Specifically, audiences’ expectations of emotional labor come from their (self-)reflexive understandings of the Fab Five’s role as laborers responsible for helping the people they make over start and finish the process of self-actualization, a core tenet of the reality makeover genre. To accomplish this, I conducted in-depth interviews with 30 adults who had seen at least one episode of Netflix’s Queer Eye. From these interviews, I argue that audiences of Netflix’s Queer Eye engage with the Fab Five, and by extension queer men, as people who are expected to perform emotional labor. These reception practices reveal that queer folks are still burdened with unique pressures and expectations to perform a specific task to bolster a heterosexist culture.

journal: New Review of Film and Television Studies
title: Serializing Islamophobia: anti-Muslim racial paranoia and HBO’s The Night Of
abstract: Analyses of racism and its contradictions in the US in the 2010s must contend with a dialectical tension between public expressions which support tolerance and inclusivity, and the public resurgence of white nationalism. While the global project of US empire in the wake of the War on Terror animates these contradictions, it is sometimes treated as though it were a separate matter. This article analyzes The Night Of (HBO, 2016) to examine how anti-Muslim racism in this period found expression not just in the form of the flat Islamophobic stereotype, but also in the form of complex and sympathetic main characters who nonetheless remain suspicious. It advances a close reading of how the show naturalizes a kind of anti-Muslim racial paranoia that is also gendered. By drawing on critical studies of race and Islamophobia, transnational televisual genre, and surveillance culture, it examines how this racializing frame construes Brown and Muslim people as a potential threat without making direct reference to terrorism. It draws conclusions which problematize the promise of racial inclusion.

journal: New Review of Film and Television Studies
title: Scalar vicissitudes and minute creatures: reexamining insects as cinematic subjects in Microcosmos and Life in the Undergrowth
abstract: This article examines insects as subjects in the documentary moving image and scalar vicissitudes in two different kinds of wildlife documentaries: Life in the Undergrowth (2005) and Microcosmos (1996). Western relationships with insects are intimately tied to technology and visual perception. The mass extinction of insects remains largely overlooked; however, their disappearance poses a significant threat to ecosystems and biodiversity. I argue that insect documentaries have roots in early depictions of microscopic illustrations as well as in the tradition of wildlife documentary. Although the wildlife documentary genre focuses on animals, its narrative tradition lies in representing bigger animals, usually mammals. By contrast, the theorization of cinematic scales lies in relation to the human figure. The convergence of these visual traditions raises considerations regarding documentaries about insects, while it also prompts us to reflect on the ethics of scale in the human – insect relationship. I argue that examining insects as proper cinematic subjects contests anthropocentrism in cinematic scales and rethinks understandings of ecological relations. The article examines the spatial scales and framings of the films, especially close-ups, when the subject of the framing is an insect instead of a human figure. I argue that taking the insect instead of the human body as the reference point shifts the scalar framework through which these films operate, unsettling the human body’s role as the implicit measure of scale. This shift brings questions of image size and scale to the fore and makes visible alternative ecological relations.

journal: New Review of Film and Television Studies
title: National identity and global imaginary in China’s ‘citizen evacuation’ films: from Wolf Warrior 2 (2017) to Home Coming (2022)
abstract: With the expansion of China’s global economic involvement since the 2000s, ensuring the safety of Chinese nationals and assets abroad has become a diplomatic imperative for Beijing. In recent years, the evacuation of overseas Chinese from conflict-stricken countries such as Libya and Yemen have inspired a number of film adaptations, exemplified by Wolf Warrior 2 (2017), Operation Red Sea (2018), and Home Coming (2022). These ‘citizen evacuation’ films adopt Hollywoodized narrative and generic conventions, portraying China’s evacuation efforts as thrilling rescue missions led by a powerful nation-state. Given their subject matter and market positioning, these films are uniquely located at the intersection of Chinese cinematic traditions, Hollywood narrative and generic conventions, and China’s foreign policy. As such, they act as a focal point for the negotiation between local and global (Hollywood) narrative patterns as well as for Chinese cinema’s search for a cultural vision of ‘the global’ that is aligned with Chinese political discourse. This article examines how these forces have shaped the national and global imaginary in ‘citizen evacuation’ films and traces changes across the three films. The article further argues that Home Coming embodies a significant shift in the representation of China’s global activities and national identity, characterized by a return to indigenous narrative tropes and an emphasis on the non-interference principle, the central pillar of China’s foreign policy that has been called into question as China becomes increasingly engaged in the political dynamics of other regions.

journal: New Review of Film and Television Studies
title: ‘ The Invisible Man is in your home’: pandemic-era Watch Parties as ephemeral media events
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has transformed the distribution of many films since 2020, but none more so than films that were in theaters when lockdowns closed multiplexes. To compensate for the collapsed theatrical window, studios quickly shifted films like Emma, The Hunt, and The Invisible Man to premium video-on-demand (or PVOD) rentals and fashioned ad-hoc promotional campaigns accentuating the surprise of their sudden digital availability. The centerpiece of these studio efforts was the ‘Watch Party’, which asked people to rent and watch the films ‘together’ with synchronized start times and real-time Twitter conversations. Studios also enlisted celebrity participants, including filmmakers who shared behind-the-scenes insights and digital influencers who delivered reactionary riffs on the films. Close analysis of promotional materials (e.g. social media posts, videos, key art) reveals that rather than replicating the theatrical viewing environment, Watch Parties instead imitated Social TV initiatives of the 2010s, including live-tweeted chatter, targeted hashtags, celebrity contributions, and canned production anecdotes. Although Watch Parties waned as the pandemic brought new distribution challenges, their emergence demonstrates Hollywood’s continued interest in constructing shared, limited-time, and now multi-screen experiences. This article identifies Watch Parties as ephemeral media events that are part of the lineage of ritualistic media events and nine-figure marketing plans but that also leverage the surprise of unique distribution circumstances to create short-lived bursts of virality and immediacy. The framework provides a new perspective on digital distribution and media events amid the increased industry and consumer preoccupation with on-demand streaming portals.

journal: New Review of Film and Television Studies
title: From the figure of the obscene rich to the fantasy of its destruction: on Succession , schadenfreude and the godlike power of the super-rich on screen
abstract: A significant part of contemporary popular culture portrays the rich as obscene, self-destructive, addicted and deranged. This article analyses the affective intensities circulating around this trope by close reading the award-winning television series Succession and its media reception. Drawing from cultural analyses of the entrepreneurial myth and of the tensions between patrimonial capitalism and the ideals of meritocracy, the article analyses the figure of the obscene rich, the ambiguities such portrayals seem to carry and the experiences of schadenfreude they generate. The article asks what is at stake in the tendency to represent the rich as obscene and analyses the subjectivities and affects this trope creates or postulates both for the rich characters and the audience. Looking beyond the critical concepts of ambiguity and ambivalence, the article asks to what extent the affects around the obscene rich are linked to the contemporary economic formation, characterised by a strong belief in meritocracy but growing dynastic tendencies. It argues that Succession creates a fatalistic sense of no escape, leaving its audiences with ambiguous affects, mixing disgust with envy and moral superiority. Ultimately, the article analyses Succession as a series that fosters a fantasy in which rich dynasties will eventually destroy themselves, or at least suffer, while the rest of us are left entertained.

title: Our Own Garden of American Heroes: 27 Responses
abstract: In the wake of the Trump Administration's call to create a “national garden of American heroes,” October decided to invite submissions for our own Garden of American Heroes, to exist only in the conceptual realm. Contributors were asked to submit some or all of the following items: reflections on the administration's initiative as defined in Executive Order 13978 and its monumental strategy; illustrated proposals for their own vision of a garden of American heroes or alternate forms of homage and monument-making in any format; and nominations for the inclusion of “American heroes” not listed in the executive order who should be considered integral to our national heritage. We also welcomed written reflections on the current condition of monuments and monumentalization in the United States. We hereby publish the proposals submitted by the following people: Firelei Baez, Julia Bryan-Wilson, Tom Burr, Dana Claxton, Michael Mark Cohen, Paul Farber, Victoria Fu, Nicholas Galanin, David J. Getsy, Alicia Harris, Sky Hopinka, Sherrilyn Iffil, Marci Kwon, Zoe Leonard, Sarah Lewis, Cannupa Hanska Luger, Ken Lum, Susette Min, Karthik Pandian, Kelvin Parnell, Joseph M. Pierce, Leigh Raiford, Charles Ray, Kirk Savage, Amy Sillman, Kenneth Tam, Salamishah Tillet, Hank Willis Thomas, Kara Walker, Carrie Mae Weems.

title: The Practice of Everyday War
abstract: This essay examines how art and visual culture participate in what it terms “the practice of everyday war”—the routinization of political violence across ordinary spaces and times, rather than its confinement to discrete battles or events. Taking Barton Gellman's 2022 Atlantic essay “January 6 Was Practice” as a point of departure, the author argues that the Capitol riot functioned less as an isolated event than as rehearsal for an ongoing authoritarian project, one whose consequences have deepened by 2026. Drawing on Michel de Certeau's distinction between strategy (spatial, top-down) and tactics (temporal, opportunistic) and Carl von Clausewitz's writings on “small war,” the essay traces how paramilitary violence—historically associated with irregulars and the “weak”—has been appropriated as a tool of state and reactionary power. The argument moves through three case studies. First, it analyzes photographs from January 6 taken inside the Capitol rotunda, where rioters clash beneath John Trumbull's monumental Revolutionary War paintings, arguing that the juxtaposition collapses supposedly discrete historical registers into a single continuum of “everyday war.” Second, it turns to Trumbull himself, reading his decades-long practice of picturing “1776”—and his fraught encounter with the French Revolution of 1789—as an early instance of art mobilizing history as ideological material. Third, the essay examines photographer An-My Lê's work, particularly Small Wars and 29 Palms, as counter-practices that expose the recursive, non-linear temporality binding past wars (Vietnam, the Civil War) to present and future militarism, without recourse to conventional antiwar rhetoric. Ultimately, the essay contends that art's engagement with war's imagery—whether complicit, critical, or ambiguous—reveals history itself as a kind of ideological arsenal, one weaponized anew amid the contemporary erosion of democratic norms.

title: Crimson Soil
abstract: On July 4, 2020, Donald Trump's proposal for a “National Garden of American Heroes” at Mount Rushmore framed national memory as something that can be fixed in soil. Against this, the article reads W.E.B. Du Bois's account of Georgia's “crimson soil” as a counter-archive in which land serves as a record of imperial conquest, slavery, and racial violence rather than stable national foundations. Soil is a witness to history. Beginning with Mount Rushmore and the Black Hills, we examine the logics of subtraction that produced the monument and trace this settler-colonial system of extraction, displacement, and substitution to the nineteenth-century agricultural crisis, when soil exhaustion in plantation economies drove the rise of industrial fertilizers. Guano, ground bison bones, and phosphate rock became central to regenerating depleted land, converting ecological and human violence into agricultural possibility. Fertilizer thus emerges as a key infrastructure of settler expansion. Visual culture is central to this process, rendering these transformations legible and naturalizing them as the nation's destiny. The article concludes with George Washington Carver's soil experiments, and Amanda Williams’ contemporary paintings, which are indebted to his research, as a counterpoint that reopens questions about environmental knowledge, labor, and land rights.

title: Memory Practices: Murray Sinclair, the Medicine Box, and His Portrait by Kent Monkman
abstract: The Carlisle Indian Industrial School was the subject of one of the most arresting images in American history: hundreds of Indigenous children from across the country arranged in neat rows before a school building, not a parent in sight. A record of the assimilative project and nation-building ambitions of the federal Indian boarding school system, the photograph also serves as a prompt to remember. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission stands as a blueprint for a process that many hope might take place in America. A bentwood medicine box by sculptor Luke Marston and a portrait by Kent Monkman of the late Murray Sinclair—both tied to Canada's history of Indian residential schools—embody the mnemonic practices essential to truth-telling.

title: Soft Censorship
abstract: This essay examines the phenomenon of “soft censorship” in American museums during the second Trump administration, drawing on the author's firsthand experience as dean of the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts at the National Gallery of Art. Nelson defines soft censorship—a concept long familiar to librarians—as indirect suppression through relocation, reduced visibility, relabeling, or “contextualization” of controversial content, rather than outright removal or cancellation. The essay centers on the case of “Color Lines Across the United States and Mexico,” a Wyeth Foundation symposium on race in American and Mexican art, scheduled at the National Gallery for May 2025. Following a visit from DOGE representatives and mounting institutional anxiety, National Gallery leadership ordered the symposium moved off-site rather than canceled outright, resulting in its removal from the museum's website, relocation to a smaller venue, and loss of virtual access—despite ultimately taking place as planned via an emergency partnership with Dumbarton Oaks. Nelson situates this episode alongside other instances of institutional response to political pressure, including Amy Sherald's withdrawal of her exhibition American Sublime from the National Portrait Gallery, the Smithsonian's handling of The Shape of Power, and Philadelphia's successful legal fight to reinstate a slavery exhibit at the President's House Site. He argues that unlike outright refusal or legal resistance, the National Gallery's and the Smithsonian's strategies of anticipatory compliance—reducing access while claiming to preserve content—constitute a distinct and insidious form of censorship enabled by executive orders targeting DEI initiatives and reframing American history. Nelson concludes that such preemptive self-restriction, rather than protecting institutions, normalizes self-censorship and transforms museums into complicit agents of authoritarian control, undermining their stated commitments to diversity, academic freedom, and the free exchange of ideas.

title: The Arts at Risk USA: An Incomplete Chronology (Part 2)
abstract: From this second, radically incomplete chronology of the Trump administration's assaults on American culture,1 it is clear that the concerted, multipronged effort to control the American cultural landscape, one unprecedented since the McCarthy era, continues unabated. It is still a battle over narrative: what is to be remembered, what is to be forgotten, what it means to be American. And it still has, as scholar Sarah Lewis puts it, a “hue,” with many of the attempts to fundamentally transform the culture targeting people of color. The 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence is now upon us, and we must once again recognize that the administration's tactics are not only illegal and immoral but also fundamentally anti-American. What kind of culture is necessary for democracy? How can we defend it? How can we reimagine it? The time for answers is upon us as well. —The Editors

title: On MONUMENTS : A Conversation with Hamza Walker and Bennett Simpson
authors: George Baker; Leah Dickerman; David Joselit; Pamela M. Lee; Steven Nelson
abstract: This article documents a roundtable conversation held on December 12, 2025, in which October editors George Baker, Leah Dickerman, David Joselit, Pamela M. Lee, and art historian Steven Nelson met with curators Hamza Walker and Bennett Simpson to discuss MONUMENTS, a two-part exhibition co-presented at the Brick and MoCA's Geffen Contemporary in Los Angeles. The show paired ten decommissioned Confederate monuments and related statuary (including works depicting Robert E. Lee, Stonewall Jackson, and Jefferson Davis) with contemporary art by figures such as Andres Serrano, Stan Douglas, Hank Willis Thomas, and Leonardo Drew, as well as a new work by Kara Walker composed of the fragments of a decommissioned monument, all addressing the afterlives of the antebellum period and Jim Crow. The conversation traces the exhibition's eight-year gestation, situating it against the 2017 wave of monument removals following Charlottesville, the 2015 Charleston church shooting, and the current administration's efforts—via executive orders such as the proposed “National Garden of American Heroes”—to reinstate celebratory national narratives ahead of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Walker and Simpson describe their curatorial strategy as nuanced: Rather than staging a debate over whether monuments should stand or fall, they treat the decommissioned objects as aesthetic and material artifacts—removed from outdoor “unidirectional” public speech and recontextualized indoors, on the floor, in dialogue with contemporary work. This reframing, they argue, exposes monuments’ mythic (rather than strictly historical) function and their entanglement with surveillance, racial capitalism, and militarized control. Participants discuss the exhibition's reception, including right-wing accusations comparing it to the Nazi Degenerate Art exhibition. The dialogue extends to the Los Angeles context—LA's own submerged Confederate and Southern migrant history—and closes with broader reflections on the distinction between monuments, memorials, and sculpture, and on art's comparatively “slow” but reflexive power to counter the accelerated, euphemistic rhetoric of contemporary political discourse.

title: Mainstreaming the Extreme: An Introduction to the Special Issue
authors: Mikkel Bækby Johansen; Jullietta Stoencheva; Tina Askanius; Line Nybro Petersen

title: The Exchange Model of Mainstreaming
abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual model of online mainstreaming. The model emphasizes communication flows and actor trajectories back and forth between center (the mainstream) and periphery (the extreme), identifying a logic of exchange as a key driver of contemporary mainstreaming processes. The model illustrates a perpetual exchange of content, actors, and practices between mainstream and off-mainstream domains. The paper focuses on three under-theorized aspects of mainstreaming in the digital age: (1) the linguistic configuration of the concepts of extremism and mainstreaming, including their inherent spatiality; (2) the possible significance of mundane and arbitrary media practices rather than intentional and strategic engagement of extremists; and (3) the enabling and constraining conditions of online platforms and internet culture. Understanding the exchange logic of mainstreaming can help scholars, media professionals, and security practitioners to better distinguish between controversial and harmful phenomena in a hybrid and fragmented media environment.

title: Everyday extremism: memes and the mainstreaming of extremist narratives around the 2024 European Parliament election
authors: Jullietta Stoencheva; Miriam Haselbacher; Tina Askanius; Ursula Reeger
abstract: This paper takes the 2024 European Parliament election as an empirical starting point to examine the circulation of extremist narratives on social media in three European countries: Sweden, Austria, and Bulgaria. Drawing on a visual content analysis of memes, the study focuses on visual articulations of violence and hostility directed towards perceived enemies and out-groups. The study asks: How did extremist narratives emerge around key contentious political issues? What forms of violence are articulated through these narratives? What shared visual grammars and coded symbols underpin the translocal entanglement of extremist narratives enabling them to travel across national boundaries and fuel everyday extremism in the digital mainstream? The findings highlight how memes contribute to what we term everyday extremism to describe a context in which dehumanising and violent narratives have been normalised to the point that they increasingly saturate everyday political discussions between ordinary citizens across Europe.

title: Ideological entrepreneurship, memetic participation, and the co-production of misogynistic ideology on X
abstract: This study examines how misogynistic ideology is co-produced on X through the interplay between ideological entrepreneurship, participatory audiences, and algorithmic infrastructures. Using Andrew Tate as a case study, the analysis draws on a dataset of 500 of his most liked posts and 500 highly visible user posts to investigate the circulation of hierarchical gender narratives in high-engagement environments. Building on research on ideological entrepreneurship, understood as actors who mobilize algorithmically favored and emotionally resonant content, the article foregrounds the memetic dimension of ideological reproduction. Drawing on the concept of deep memetic frames, it shows how hierarchical gender narratives are negotiated and amplified within algorithmically structured visibility environments. In doing so, the article contributes to research on influencers and the manosphere by demonstrating how ideological entrepreneurship operates within a broader ecology of memetic circulation, where meaning emerges through participatory repetition and infrastructural amplification, rather than solely as strategic persuasion.

title: Cultural transgressions and media contestation: a qualitative study of the tradwife trend in Dutch media
abstract: This article explores how the tradwife (short for traditional wife) movement, an internet trend where women embrace traditional gender roles and decry feminism, is contested by mainstream media in the Netherlands. Analyzing 44 articles published by diverse outlets between January 2023 and December 2024, this study identifies three key themes of contestation: “Return to the past,” “Fantasy and amusement,” and “Female unawareness.” These discourses frame the movement as regressive, escapist, or misguided. Considering tradwife to be a highly aestheticized form of cultural transgression, it is proposed that these arguments not only reflect a broader cultural pushback against perceived rejections of feminist values but that by framing the movement as relatable or unserious, these contestations inadvertently contribute to the normalization and hybridization of fringe ideologies. This contribution expands previous research on the mainstreaming of extremism, demonstrating how media contestation relates to the diffusion of transgressive ideologies in the digital age.

title: Invisible string(s): Exploring conspiratorial participatory practices among Swifties
abstract: This study explores how Taylor Swift fans, so-called “Swifties,” engage in playful, conspiratorial participation by interpreting hidden messages and developing fan theories, especially around Swift’s queer identity (the “Gaylor” discourse). Drawing on interviews with 18 fans, this article presents an in-depth perspective, demonstrating how speculative fandom blurs the line between interpretive play and conspiracist logic. This helps reveal how participatory practices mirror the structures of (political) conspiracies. Fans organize around theory-building, decipher cryptic clues, and negotiate interpretive boundaries, which echoes behaviors found in extremist communities. These findings suggest that conspiratorial thinking and practices are no longer confined to fringe groups but are embedded in everyday cultural participation, including mainstream pop-culture fandoms. By tracing these participatory practices among Swifties, this research contributes to a broader understanding of how conspiratorial play becomes normalized, offering a cultural lens into the mainstreaming of extremism in today’s societies.

title: Mainstreaming violent extremism through language play in the Halle manifesto
authors: Line Nybro Petersen; Marie Bojsen-Møller; Tanya Karoli Christensen
abstract: In 2019, a perpetrator opened fire outside the local synagogue in Halle, Germany. Prior to the terrorist attack, he had posted several documents and links on social media, including a manifesto. These documents draw on participatory practices familiar to mainstream participatory communities, while deemphasizing the ideological motivation of the attack. Through an interdisciplinary approach combining media studies with linguistics, this article analyses the multi-document manifesto posted by the perpetrator ahead of the attack and considers how these documents engage with mainstream participatory culture through language play. Most significantly, the three documents engage in language play addressing its intended audience through fan practices, humor, and memetic gamification of his terrorist plans. The analysis demonstrates how far-right terrorists are not just “lone-actors” motivated by extremist ideologies, they are also eclectically intertwined with different mainstream practices, thus underlining the importance of ingroup interaction and incitement in cases of far-right terrorism.

title: Politicization of lies about the indigenous peoples in Brazil: frequency and thematic of information in Lupa digital fact-checking agency
abstract: The insertion and daily use of social media, from the 2010s onward, provided a wide circulation of content. This information is sometimes false and affects vulnerable groups, such as indigenous peoples. To understand this fake and false information about Brazilian indigenous peoples, we evaluate the fake news checked by the Lupa agency since its creation. From 2018 to 2023, there were 36 items focusing on the indigenous peoples, including only three without the “False” label, but still contributing to information disorder. Although speech by far-right politicians and supporters has brought lies about the indigenous peoples to the attention of Lupa, this movement by the agency is strengthened by the current government, since it created the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples and increased attention around this population. The politicization was observed indirectly in two lies and directly in 28 fake news items, with 24 benefiting the far-right and four the left part of the political spectrum.

title: Drenched in blue: Black audiences’ TV viewing and perceptions of the police
abstract: Amid conversation about police conduct, understanding the mechanisms that may be related to Black audiences’ police procedural consumption and attitudes toward the police is noteworthy. Accordingly, we adopted social identity gratifications theory to analyze survey data from US Black adults (N = 434) regarding consumption of Black police procedurals, scripted shows focused on police investigations with Black actors, and attitudes toward the police. Results suggest a significant relationship between increased consumption and favorable attitudes toward the police. However, data indicated that adherence to racial identity moderated the relationship, acting as a safeguard against heavy media exposure and viewer attitudes.

title: Reconfiguring affective structures: main melody films, youth subcultures, and platformed nationalism in contemporary China
abstract: This article examines how Chinese main melody films construct structures of feeling that resonate with youth subcultures in the digital era. Drawing on Raymond Williams’s concept of structure of feeling, the study theorizes a new affective structure shaped by the entanglement of state narratives, youth participation, and platform infrastructures. Through analyses of Wolf Warrior 2 (2017), The Battle at Lake Changjin (2021), and the web animation That Rabbit (2015–present), it explores how nationalist discourses are emotionally reinterpreted through genre hybridity, algorithmic visibility, and participatory practices. It foregrounds how fandom-based nationalism and affective labor enable youth to emotionally negotiate identification with state ideology, a process termed affective negotiation. Main melody films are reframed not as static ideological vehicles but as affective infrastructures shaped by platform capitalism and youth-mediated recoding. This study contributes to debates on soft power, emotional governance, and the mediated politics of belonging in contemporary China.

title: “But this is just feminist man hating propaganda:” popular feminism, postfeminist masculinity and popular misogyny in Barbie and She-Hulk ’s reviews
abstract: This paper analyzes the reviews received by the movie Barbie (2023) and the TV show She-Hulk: Attorney at Law (S1, 2022). After framing them as popular feminist texts that are arguably socio-politically involved, we discursively analyze online reviews on IMDb and Metacritic to observe how viewers articulate thoughts and critiques of feminist issues. We found nuanced and contrasting discourses. On one hand, some reviewers focus on the popular feminist message disclosing more constructive expectations for popular feminist culture. On the other, we found a popular misogynist review-bombing that operates in reaction to the feminist texts by instrumentalizing postfeminist masculinity as a misandrist and oppressive form of representation. We conclude by advancing the construct of postfeminist masculinity as a potential tool that complicates the antagonistic relationship between popular feminism and popular misogyny, and by suggesting implications this can have on the popular feminist media landscape.

title: Editorial
authors: Feona Attwood; John Mercer; Clarissa Smith
abstract: This general issue of Porn Studies brings together research articles ranging across eighteenth-century erotic literature, 1970s sexual manuals and queer art, post-socialist gay pornography, Hong Ko...

title: Reading sociopornographic books: genre and dirty work
abstract: During the 1970s, before the rise of freely accessible hardcore pornographies, there was a brief moment of a few years where books and magazines ostensibly sought to ‘teach’ about sex, while providing pornographic imagery to curious readers. These books were often marketed as ‘educational’ and often marketed towards ‘married couples’, or at the very least, committed couples. In this article, I seek to study these books by framing them as ‘sociopornographic’, defining what is meant by that term and outlining key elements of the genre. To these ends, I study books that attended to analism, anality, and anal sex.

title: ‘You can’t do that’? The ambiguities of Wet and Messy fetish videos
abstract: Although the study of transformative works and the study of pornography are both decades old, there has been little analysis of any pornographic text as a transformative work. This article aims to address this through analyzing the Wet and Messy (WAM) fetish video series You Can’t Do That On Set (YCDTOS), a fan-created iteration of the transnationally successful Canadian series You Can’t Do That On Television (YCDTOTV; CTV/Nickelodeon 1979–1990). The article also addresses issues of genre and format with regard to pornography, in that YCDTOS is both a fan-created iteration of an episodic television series and features no explicit sex or nudity but is still positioned as pornography by its producers. The article also addresses the false binary of mimetic/affirmational versus transformative works, and the unclear boundaries between amateur and professional in fetish/WAM production, to illustrate just how messy a concept WAM fetish media can be.

title: I know it when I see it: art, pornography, and Andy Warhol’s Sex Parts
abstract: The article analyses Andy Warhol’s Sex Parts print series through a connoisseurship methodology to argue that the work is a culmination of subject matter and formal aesthetics the artist developed throughout his career. Of particular importance to the argument is the work’s relationship to the history of the male body in pornographic magazines and films of the 1970s. The Sex Parts prints imitate a porn media culture that contributed significantly to establishing gay culture at the end of the decade. By connecting elements of Warhol’s pop art of the 1960s to the burgeoning porn industry of the 1970s, the Sex Parts prints document and legitimize the post-Stonewall sexual revolution in the USA.

title: Male rape, female dominance and new sexual economics in Gereon
abstract: The first Russian erotic novel The Story of the English Lord Gereon and the Brandenburg Margravine Friederike Luise (c. 1747) remained in manuscript form and was never published in full. In the world of Gereon, it is not men who pursue women, but women who actively seek sexual encounters with men, and when the latter resist, they are raped. Lustful women are portrayed as a deadly threat to the protagonist. Gereon is forced to suppress his sexual desires and defend himself against the often aggressive and intrusive advances of women. Behind this is the humoral theory of sexual physiology, which posits that male libido is finite and must be preserved, unlike female libido, which is seen as inexhaustible. The erotic and pornographic episodes contribute to an erotic narrative about the value of male sex, modulated by a traditional medieval plot about marital fidelity.

title: Julie Lee and Trilogy of Lust (1995): pornography, moral panic and the politics of belonging in pre-handover Hong Kong
abstract: In 1995 Julie Lee co-wrote, co-directed, co-produced and starred in Hong Kong’s only commercial pornographic film, Trilogy of Lust. Since then, Julie Lee has been vilified in the popular media, leaving her contribution to Hong Kong film culture and beyond either marginalized or obscured within the scholarship on Hong Kong film history. This article provides a needed corrective to Julie Lee’s erasure by examining how the reception of Julie Lee and her film exposed widespread moral panic in Hong Kong around pornography’s impact on youth, along with allied issues of obscenity, morality and freedom of expression in advance of the 1997 handover of the former colony to China. We argue that despite being culturally denigrated, Julie Lee’s hardcore performance in Trilogy of Lust forged an alternative vision of Hong Kong identity to challenge the former colony’s cosmopolitan middle-class version of Hong Kong citizenry, thereby exposing an uneasy tension between the sense of belonging and unbelonging in pre-handover Hong Kong.

title: From exotic ‘other’ to violent sex: positionalities and perspectives of (East) Germany and Eastern Europe in gay porn after 1990
abstract: Within the gay pornographic videos produced by the Berlin studio Cazzo, images of East German skinheads fighting in streets, chasing down punks, and engaging in hardcore, violent gay sex can be found. Since German Reunification, there has been a host of scholarly literature which attempts to comprehend the legacy of the German Democratic Republic. Indeed, following the collapse of the entire Eastern Bloc, a more distinctive and racialized ‘Eastern European’ identity seemingly emerged, bolstered by neoliberal policies and economic exploitation which promotes an ethnic ‘othering’. What is more interesting, however, is that these trends and hierarchies of power are made highly visible in the world of gay pornography, occupying the liminal spaces between fantasy and reality. This article turns to gay porn to examine and interrogate constructions of post-socialist identities as racialized ‘other’ as reflections of the desires of Western consumers and their conceptualizations of the East as fantasy.

title: Becoming pornographic, being ethnographic: exploring the heteroerotic, hierarchies of desire and affective atmospheres in swinger clubs
abstract: The relationship between pornography and ethnography has a long history. It is a history that has often been characterized by ethnographers treating their research participants as sexual objects, to be pornographically used and consumed by ethnographers and their audiences. Drawing upon 18 ethnographies of swinger clubs in the UK, this article, in contrast, explores how the ethnographer, through their experience of pornographic affects, is productive in capturing the erotic dynamics of swinger communities. The article does this by exploring the voyeuristic nature of ethnography and how such voyeurism enables a better understanding of the hetero-erotic in swinger club spaces. It then develops this fusion of ethnography and pornography further by discussing how the ethnographer, in many ways, experiences their research practice as a pornographic practice. Finally, the article then suggests that the ethnographic writing up process can in many ways be pornographic writing. Importantly, the article concludes that rather than viewing the relationship between pornography and ethnography as problematic, the relationship has a queering potential that can provide insights and understandings that ‘straight’ ethnographies may overlook.

title: Sexual media practices in private homemade amateur porn
abstract: Practices of private amateur mainstream pornography are often neglected in porn and sexuality studies. Using a multi-method design triangulating video analysis, video interaction analysis, and narrative interviews with the actors, the qualitative research project Die Praxen der Amateurpornographie [The Practices of Amateur Pornography] investigated sexual interactions shown in amateur pornographic videos, the social contexts they are embedded in, and how these videos are created and used. This article presents reflections on the chosen research methods as well as selected research results, focusing on four aspects of amateur pornographic practice: avenues leading to filming sex, what is (not) being filmed, what people do with their videos, and practices of self-observation.

title: ‘Sex influencers’: a survey of porn workers in the USA
abstract: There are relatively few survey data on the lives of porn workers. This article presents and analyzes broad-based data from a survey of 531 porn industry workers in the USA. The article provides key demographic, economic, and social insights into the lives of porn workers. According to the data, porn workers are not all young, can have long careers in the industry, have high levels of education, do not all come from poverty, are not exclusively cisgender women, and are disproportionately white. Analysis of the data also dispels binary notions of porn workers as either exploited or uniquely empowered – as sex workers have argued repeatedly. Instead, the data show that many porn workers are satisfied with their work yet economically precarious, and that there are notable inequalities within the industry. Crucially, the data add to current conversations in porn studies about porn work as either gig work or influencer work. The article concludes that the data from this survey support the latter framing and that porn workers are best thought of as ‘sex influencers’. By providing a data-driven, broad picture on porn workers, the author hopes that future reporting and research will be more empirically grounded and nuanced.

title: Navigating the edge: liminal intimacies and monetisation of male eroticism on Douyin
abstract: This study examines how ‘male edge-ball wanghong’ on Douyin negotiate masculinity through platform-mediated erotic labour. Using immersive cohabitation-oriented digital ethnography and multimodal critical discourse analysis, the research explores how intersecting gazes, particularly the female gaze, appear to empower women while simultaneously reinforcing existing power structures. The findings reveal a ‘liminal intimacy’ where male edge-ball wanghong perform a vulnerable masculinity through a tiered membership system that commodifies emotional connection. By analysing visual styles, communication strategies, and monetisation practices, the study uncovers how the female gaze creates an illusion of autonomy but ultimately sustains patriarchal and economic hierarchies. The research illuminates emerging sexual subjectivities and the intricate relationships between platform economics, gender representation, and audience interaction in contemporary Chinese digital culture.

title: Sex and play in game and porn studies: an interdisciplinary roundtable discussion
authors: Harrison Charles; Charlotte Courtois; Ummni Khan; Maggie MacDonald; Matthew Wysocki; Jean Ketterling
abstract: Building on a panel discussion which took place at the 2025 Canadian Game Studies Association conference, this roundtable (re)convened a group of game, sexuality, and porn studies scholars digitally in February 2026 to discuss the relationship between pornography and game studies and consider how deeper engagement between these fields might be reciprocally beneficial. Participants include Charlotte Courtois, Harrison Charles, Maggie MacDonald, Ummni Khan, and Matthew Wysocki. Jean Ketterling chaired the panel. This discussion provides the opportunity for participants to discuss play in games and sex, research creation, how definitional challenges can artificially narrow the scope of porn studies, and how shared concerns around platformization and deplatforming might produce the conditions for a broad coalition of ‘sexy media’ scholars and makers.

title: Rethinking Fast Feminism slowly
abstract: As the editor of Shannon Bell’s Fast Feminism, I worked closely with Bell from 2007 to 2010, observing (with delight) her high-velocity encounters with the speed theories of Paul Virilio – including the ‘staircase’ method introduced in Pure War: ‘once an idea is introduced and deployed, jump to linkages with another idea and always, always do violence to the original context’ so that distinctions among points of departure collapse or blur. Fast feminism is an accident of speed theory, a method for writing as morphing, performative action, and situated embodiment. When theory is embodied it is always inflecting, reflecting, disturbing, and relational. In this article, I rethink, engage longitudinally, and do a performative intervention into fast feminism, focusing on how and when this philo-porno-political practice’s affective, high-velocity interventions are deployed with slowness and fast feminism becomes a medium and method for deceleration.

title: Cybersexual moral panics: governing desire in the age of digital censorship
abstract: Drawing on the intellectual legacy of Shannon Bell, I argue that pornography has been politically retooled as a capacious moral category through which non-normative gender and sexuality are rendered threats to social order. Focusing on ‘Project 2025’ as a central case study, I demonstrate how anti-porn discourse functions as an infrastructural mechanism for governing trans life in the digital age. Situating recent policies within a longer genealogy of obscenity regulation, the article traces how appeals to child protection mobilize affective economies of fear to justify expanded censorship, surveillance, and platform liability. I show how these dynamics operate across legal frameworks, platform moderation, and public discourse, producing a regulatory formation in which anti-trans, anti-porn, and anti-sex work logics converge. In doing so, this article contributes to porn studies and trans studies by offering a framework for understanding how sexual stigma structures the conditions of digital visibility, precarity, and survival.

title: Introduction: porn studies and the popular romance genre
authors: Jonathan A. Allan; Catherine M. Roach
abstract: In the 1979 article ‘Mass Market Romance: Pornography for Women is Different’, American feminist scholar Ann Barr Snitow laid the groundwork for what became something of a perpetual debate: is the ...

title: Performing visibility under algorithmic inconvenience: queer digital labour, platform capitalism, and Indian porn on X
abstract: This article examines the precarious digital labour of Indian queer porn performers on X (formerly Twitter), analysing how the platform's algorithm simultaneously enables the visibility of queer sexuality and monetizes performers' free labour. Drawing on content and thematic analysis of 10 performer accounts belonging to gay men and trans women of Indian origin, we analyse 100 posts, 100 captions and 200 audience comments. The comments fall into three categories: requests for sexual contact or specific acts, expressions of appreciation and derogatory remarks. Together they reveal how X extracts affective labour from performers while failing to protect marginalized creators. Using Berlant's concept of in/convenience, Preciado's pharmacopornographic capitalism and Shannon Bell's framework of gender terrorism and anti-pornographic labour, we argue that this content meets Bell's first two conditions for anti-pornographic practice, resisting hegemonic gender scripts and foregrounding heterogeneous erotic grammars, but consistently fails her third: that pornographic labour be non-alienated and self-directed. The article situates this analysis within emerging scholarship on South Asian porn cultures and platform capitalism in the Global South.

title: Navigating racial erotics in adult content creation: comparing black Brazilian and US queer men creator experiences
authors: Dominik Jackson-Cole; J. G. Smith; M. Quiason; L. C. Ng; S. R. Reffuge; S. Y. Dhunna
abstract: This study investigates the racialized experiences of Black LGBTQ+ men adult content creators in the USA and Brazil, an understudied area. Drawing on 22 semi-structured interviews, the study innovatively combines Han’s concept of racial erotics and Yosso’s framework of Community Cultural Wealth to analyse the interactions between and strategic deployment of various capitals by creators. By applying the joint frameworks to porn studies, the article contributes theoretically and empirically to an improved understanding of how erotic capital can be a site of both oppression and resistance. Analysis reveals four key findings: the similarities in racial hierarchies of desire, which privilege whiteness in both countries; the differences in the deployment of erotic capital, mandated by different (inter)national contexts; complex strategies for navigating the adult content field; and acts of resistance against racialized norms. Despite the perceived democratization of pornography through platforms like OnlyFans, structural inequalities persist, with Black creators often earning less, especially in Brazil. The insights add nuanced understanding of experiences of Black queer men navigating online adult content creation across different geopolitical contexts. The article underscores the need for more inclusive frameworks that recognize the agency, resilience, and strategic labour of Black queer creators in globalized sexual marketplaces.

title: Porn slop: conceptualizing synthetic excess in platformized sexual media
abstract: The rapid spread of ‘slop’ as a cultural keyword reflects growing concern about automated overproduction in digital media. This article introduces porn slop as a conceptual lens for examining synthetic excess, platform-facing circulation, and weakened provenance within artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated adult media. Rather than treating porn slop as equivalent to all AI pornography or as a demonstrated condition of dominant porn consumption, the article frames it as an emerging and uneven formation. Drawing on recent developments in generative pornography, deepfake ecosystems, subscription-based automation, and synthetic performers, the article situates porn slop within debates on platformization, algorithmic amplification, and digital culture. A typology distinguishes public-facing synthetic excess from private or semi-private AI sexual automation. The article concludes by outlining implications for porn studies, platform studies, and future research on labour, desire, governance, and authenticity.

title: The copulative hermeneutics of the veil: pornographizing the truth
abstract: This article explores Shannon Bell’s project of deploying the obscene, grotesque, and pornographic to dismantle totalitarian philosophical thought. Bell challenges the notion of ‘truth’ as a pure, noetic concept, reframing it as an authoritarian mechanism that suppresses bodily contingency and ambiguity. By reinserting corporeal excess – scatology, filth, and staged exposure – into intellectual discourse, Bell seeks to democratize philosophy and expose systematic exclusions sustaining its claims to sovereign reason. I foreground Bell’s key methodologies: parrhesia, a risky, dissenting form of truth-telling, and the ‘copulative both/and’ logic that upholds contradiction rather than resolving it. These methodologies are interrogated through the case study of ‘tent theatre’ striptease, where endless tease of exposure and prolonged veiling precludes interpretive mastery and hegemonic spectatorship, securing indeterminacy as an ethical and hermeneutic boon. Ultimately, I argue that, for Bell, the excessive, abject, pornographic body functions as a deconstructive and emancipatory force against fascistic interpretive and political imperatives.

title: Owning the narrative: a roundtable discussion on sex work, stigma, and resilience in the Baltics
authors: Carmela Morgillo; The Latvian Sex Workers Alliance; The Sex Workers’ Rights Lietuva; Aya; Emi; Laine; Marija
abstract: Because of the pervasiveness of anti-sex work stigma in the region, Baltic sex workers' experiences are still underrepresented in both scholarly and activist literature. Produced in collaboration with two sex workers' rights organisations - the Sex Workers Alliance, based in Latvia, and Sex Workers Rights Lietuva, based in Lithuania - this paper focuses on Baltic sex workers' everyday realities, the issues they face, and their collective struggle for safer working conditions and for the destigmatisation of their work. Our work uses a roundtable methodology to explore the complexity of sex workers' experiences within the unique intersection of stigma, flawed legal frameworks, and economic precarity in the Baltics. By situating sex workers' experiences within the broader historical, geopolitical and socio-economic context of the region, the paper contributes to wider debates on gender, sexuality, labour and justice, and highlights the importance of knowledge co-creation.

title: Of mothers and monsters: Shannon Bell’s fast feminism and the radical pedagogy of sexual alterity
abstract: This article engages the work of Shannon Bell through a series of conceptual, aesthetic, and autobiographical encounters unfolding across dreams, archives, literature, cinema, and conversation. Drawing on Bell’s fast feminism and staircase method, the authors bring into relation ethnographic fragments from their research with John Robin Sharpe (1933–2015), Catherine Breillat’s film Last Summer (2023), writings of Tony Duvert, and Ordóñez’ formulation of becoming-maternal. Approaching these materials as affective and sensorial scenes rather than stable objects of interpretation, the article traces unexpected connections among youth, sexuality, maternity, kinship, and embodiment. Through Bell’s commitment to conceptual movement, the authors explore minor archives of queer intergenerationality, the cultural production of childhood innocence, and the interpretive habits through which figures such as the child, the mother, and the paedophile acquire regulatory force. In doing so, the article highlights Bell’s importance for critical inquiry into affect, pleasure, and heterodox forms of truth-telling.

title: Perceptions of pornography among UK sex education practitioners: a qualitative study
abstract: This research explores the perceptions of UK sex education practitioners around pornography within sex education for young people between 11 and 18 years. The article offers crucial recommendations on urgent improvements needed within schools and wider society. This qualitative study is based on semi-structured interviews with 14 sex education practitioners. The findings show they were concerned with inadequate governmental support for pornography education, advocating for increased provision of specialist educators, and highlighting the importance of pornography literacy to navigate key discussions around consent and sex that is depicted in pornography. Based on these findings, the implications of the study are enhanced governmental sex education policy, shame-free sex education that should include pornography literacy, and that which forms a spiral education curriculum which is age appropriate and supports young people’s assets and desires. Further, the article seeks to highlight that removing the discussion of pornography from sex education will only increase the risk of misinformation and perpetuate vulnerabilities within sex education and beyond.

title: Closed without warning: material marginalization of people in the sex trades
authors: Desiree Collins; Danielle Blunt; Lorelei Lee; Ariel Wolf; Janell (Jay/Jae) Johnson-Dash; Gabriella Garcia
abstract: The exclusion of sex workers from financial services raises critical concerns about justice, autonomy, and economic rights. Sex workers report increased vulnerability and violence due to difficulties accessing banking and financial technologies. This paper examines how algorithms used by financial institutions de-platform individuals engaged in sex work under the pretense of risk management, regardless of the legal status of their labor. Using mixed-methods analysis, this study demonstrates that financial discrimination experienced by sex workers leads to housing instability, food insecurity, and broader health and safety challenges. This study employs community-led participatory action research to gather data from individuals involved in the sex trades, documenting their experiences of financial discrimination and the resulting impacts on their lives; 32% of respondents have been banned from a bank account, payment app, or payment processor, 23% reported having funds seized, and financial discrimination increased the longer respondents engaged in sex work.

title: Very large, largely silent: how three pornography-hosting platforms assess their governance of sexual content under the Digital Services Act
authors: Carlotta Rigotti; Nicola Döring; Isotta Rossoni
abstract: In 2023, the European Commission designated Aylo (Pornhub.com), Stripchat, and XVideos as very large online platforms under the Digital Services Act, subjecting them to binding obligations to identify, assess, and mitigate systemic risks. In 2025, these platforms submitted their first risk assessment reports to the European Commission. This article offers a systematic and critical analysis of these reports from a sex-positive, rights-based perspective – treating both non-consensual sexual content and the suppression of consensual sexual content as systemic risks. The analysis reveals four recurring limitations: methodological opacity; a narrow conceptualization of risk that underestimates technology-facilitated violence against women; structural marginalization of performers and content creators from governance processes; and minimal civil society engagement. All three assessments approach sexual content governance almost exclusively through a harm-prevention lens, remaining silent on the freedoms at stake. The article concludes with recommendations arguing that effective governance must hold protection and freedom in productive tension.

title: My year as a Dominatrix: non-recuperable pornography, labour, and the work of Shannon Bell
abstract: In this article, I analyse my experiences working as a Dominatrix in a small Ontario dungeon through Shannon Bell’s writings on the politics of gender, sexuality, and the body. Bell’s philosophic criteria for non-recuperable pornography, outlined in her chapter ‘Post-Porn/Post-Anti-Porn’, provide the structure for my argument. These philosophical criteria include ‘the saying of the work is not lost in the said; the work is produced from a new post-porn/post-anti-porn positionality; [and] the work is an act of labor as self-activity and not labor alienated as labor-power’. Because non-recuperable pornography works to recodify gendered bodies and bodies engaged in sexual action, assessing where it is, and is not, operative is important. I argue that my work in the dungeon (what I call durational pornographic scenes) adheres to Bell’s first two criteria for non-recuperable pornography but not the third (and that this third failure undermines the first and second criteria as well). I conclude that, ultimately, the project of recodifying bodies and bodies engaged in sexual action needs to be tied to the larger project of transforming economic social relations more generally.

title: ‘¡Vive LALExpo!’: power mapping discourses of unity in the webcam studio industry in Colombia
abstract: This article examines the Latin American Livecam Expo (LALExpo) as a key site for understanding power in Colombia’s webcam studio industry. The article argues that industry executives mobilize discourses of ‘unity’ to present a cohesive and legitimate front to the state, while obscuring deeply stratified labour conditions. Drawing on feminist ethnography and discourse analysis, the study introduces the ‘webcam studio industry’ as a distinct formation that complicates dominant frameworks centred on independent cam models or traditional porn labour. In Colombia, webcam work is embedded in studio-based infrastructures and transnational economies, limiting workers’ control over their digital identities and earnings. At LALExpo, narratives of professionalization and survival reframe structural inequalities as individual responsibilities, muting critique and aligning workers with industry interests. The article ultimately shows how unity operates as both a strategy for legitimacy and a mechanism of labour discipline within global digital sexual economies.

title: Eroticized evaluation: casting and labour incorporation in early postsocialist gay pornography
abstract: This article examines Young Russian Innocents and Young Soldiers Disclosed, two 1994 transnational gay pornographic films featuring Russian performers. The article argues that their casting scenes constitute a distinct pornographic form in which recruitment, inspection, and conditional approval become the primary site of erotic investment. Performers are interviewed, translated, examined, undressed, and sexually tested on camera, transforming audition into a sustained structure of labour evaluation. The camera assumes an employer’s perspective, while the translator mediates linguistic and bodily legibility. Produced amid postsocialist economic instability, the films render market incorporation visible within the sexual encounter itself. Rather than treating pornography as merely representing precarious labour, the article shows how these films eroticize the evaluative procedures through which bodies become employable and incorporable within transnational markets.

title: Naked indifferences: the ethics of (a)sexual representation
abstract: Where does the nude as a cyber-body-in-representation situate itself within the contemporary sexual oversaturation alongside the crisis of unfeeling and anxiety surrounding obscenity? Through an auto-theoretical approach, this article examines the circulation of my queer body as it negotiates with its ‘asexual resonances’. I locate my sexuality by looking at adolescence, with attention to the heteropatriarchal Indian discourse and the digital proliferation of pornography and sex as central to the establishment of ‘positive’ identity. I read this private visual modality alongside Shannon Bell’s conception of ‘pornosophy’, a concept that in my analysis allows for the reinstating of a critical distance between sexual representation and sexual acts. How does an alternate (a)sexual image expand this ethical distance and its relation to explicitness and obscurity? How do asexual aesthetics and sexual unfeeling recalibrate the sensational/unsensational dichotomy? I analyse this asexual impasse beyond the economy of sexual optimism and the historically negative construction of sexual coldness within the simultaneous emergence of sexology and popular pornography.

title: Migrant men on OnlyFans: masculinity, precarity, and erotic entrepreneurship in the digital gig economy
authors: Yang Zhao; Garth Stahl; Rohann Irving
abstract: Recent research on OnlyFans creators has focused largely on women, leaving men’s participation comparatively underexamined. This conceptual article adopts an interdisciplinary lens to explore what migrant men’s engagement with OnlyFans may mean for them. We consider how the platform opens spaces for migrant men to commodify their bodies and generate income, often by mobilizing racialized and gendered stereotypes whereby such eroticized performances contribute to the reproduction of gender and sexuality norms. Empowerment framings of digitized sex work may risk obscuring the structural inequalities, emotional labour, and/or exploitation that shape platform labour. Rather than adopting empowerment versus exploitation dichotomies, we conceptualize OnlyFans as a site of contested autonomy for migrant men where their masculinities are refashioned through a mix of entrepreneurship, erotic self-branding, and the logics of platform capitalism. We call for deeper engagement with the gendered dimensions of migrancy – particularly migrant masculinities – in research on digitized sex work.

title: Motivations and outcomes of women’s pornography use
authors: Katerina Litsou; Cynthia Graham; Nicholas Kelley; Roger Ingham
abstract: There is relatively limited information on why women use pornography, what they expect from it, and the emotions they experience after use. Conflicting findings have been reported about the association between pornography use and women’s sexual satisfaction. This study assessed motivations, outcomes, sexual satisfaction, and emotions associated with women’s pornography use. Women (N = 3330, mean age 27.5 years) reporting either solo or partnered pornography use at least once in the past six months completed an online survey. Single women reported more frequent pornography use than those in relationships. More frequent solo and partnered pornography use were both associated with higher sexual satisfaction. Women reported experiencing more positive emotions and fewer negative emotions after solo use. Partnered use was associated with lower levels of negative emotions and higher levels of positive emotions. A principal component analysis identified three main motivations: escape from boredom and entertainment; sexuality exploration and learning; and physical and psychological arousal. Another principal component analysis identified two outcome factors: negative and positive. These findings highlight the complex role of pornography in women’s sexual lives and may help to normalize pornography use and reduce stigma. Clinicians might suggest pornography as a tool to improve arousal, pleasure, and couple communication.

title: Beyond harm narratives: reimagining porn education through ‘safe uncertainty’
abstract: Contemporary UK policy and educational responses to pornography are largely organized around risk, harm, and prevention. Drawing on the UK Independent Pornography Review, this article examines how pornography is constructed as an object of governance and how this framing shapes pedagogy. While harm-prevention approaches prioritize certainty about meaning and effect, interdisciplinary research highlights young people’s interpretive diversity, ambivalence, and contextual negotiation. Pornography education is thus structured by a tension between institutional demands for clarity and the lived reality of uncertainty. To address this tension, the article develops ‘safe uncertainty’ as a pedagogical orientation that combines interpretive openness with relational and institutional safety. The article outlines how this approach can be operationalized in educational settings and considers its feasibility within current policy contexts. By reframing pornography education as engagement with uncertainty, the article contributes to debates on porn literacy, youth sexuality, and educational governance.

In this issue, you will find contributions that reflect that goal.

title: Difficult Relations between the Rescuers and the Rescued: (In)Hospitality and (In)Gratitude in Contemporary Cinematic Superhero Genre
abstract: This article analyzes the emotional attitudes of hospitality, trust, and gratitude in the context of the rescuer(s)-rescued relations found in contemporary superhero films of the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and DC Universe (DCU). The analysis is based on Robert Jewett and John Shelton Lawrence's concept of the American monomyth. It would seem that the key factor for the monomythic adventures to even begin is the hospitality displayed by the threatened community toward the rescuer(s), and the trust laid upon them. And, at the end of a monomythic story, there ought to be expressions of gratitude on the part of the rescued toward their rescuer(s). However, the relations between the oppressed and their redeemers in the twenty-first-century monomythic stories are far more complex. In this article, I analyze factors and variables contributing to the complexity relations between the oppressed, the institutions representing the oppressed, and the (super)heroes.

title: Quantitative Studies on Color and Film Genres: A Systematic Review
authors: Jaime López-Díez; Shu Hu; Lingfei Luan; Thomas Ackerman; Joseph P. Magliano
abstract: This study conducts a systematic review of quantitative research examining the relationship between color and film genres, specifically focusing on the attributes of hue, saturation, and brightness. An extensive search of Web of Science and Scopus identified eight important articles on US film productions published in English. Given that most prior studies in this domain have been qualitative, the advent of quantitative studies offers novel insights. The results suggest that the correlation between color and genre is predominantly modest; still, distinct patterns were seen, including low saturation in action and adventure films, high saturation in animated films, and low brightness in horror films. Proportional weights of the provided findings were computed to assess consistency across research, emphasizing limited still important genre-specific color traits.

title: How Does Television Seriality Reshape Spectator Hypothesis Formation?: The Primacy of the Mesoscopic Level in Serial Engagement
abstract: Television seriality demands sustained cognitive engagement, as viewers form hypotheses to navigate complex narratives. This article argues that beyond moment-to-moment (micro) and ultimate outcome (macro) predictions, medium-term “mesoscopic hypotheses” dominate spectator activity. These concern the unfolding, intersection, and temporary resolution of plotlines and character arcs. We propose a three-level (micro–meso–macro) model of engagement, showing through series like Grey's Anatomy , Breaking Bad , and Game of Thrones how viewers focus on the “middle game.” Genres shape distinct hypothesis patterns, while fan speculation amplifies mesoscopic focus. This framework clarifies how serial narratives sustain pleasure and interest without definitive closure.

title: Understanding Dementia: Puzzle Film Techniques and Affective Experience in The Father (2020)
abstract: With a focus on cinematic subjectivity, this article examines how The Father (2020) uses its formal elements to create spatial, temporal, and narrative disruptions that replicate the effects of the cognitive deterioration experienced by people living with dementia. In doing so, it differs from most screen representations of mental disorders that show symptoms from the perspective of an observer rather than the person experiencing them, consequently objectifying them as “other.” By constructing a subjective portrayal of dementia, The Father —a puzzle film with a few pieces missing—crafts an immersive experience aligning the audience's perceptions with those of its protagonist, offering insight into the lived experience of dementia symptoms and thus the possibility of an affective, experiential understanding of this disease.

title: Handheld in Enaction: First-Person Perspective of Professional Cinematographers
authors: Mehmet Burak Yilmaz; Willeke Rietdijk; William Ruddock Primett; Ksenia Mukhina; Elen Lotman; Pia Tikka
abstract: Empirical studies on cinematographers’ creative processes remain limited, likely due to theoretical gaps. Drawing from the embodied mind theory, we hypothesize that cinematographers in action holistically simulate the characters’ situatedness in the diegetic world and, in doing so, translate it into the future viewers’ experience. We report initial findings from semi-structured interviews with cinematographers after shooting a dramatic scene with a handheld camera. Two main approaches were identified in the interview data related to participating cinematographers’ embodied decision-making processes. We describe detailed themes identified within each of these two approaches and adopt image schematic structures as a provisional explanation of how the cinematographers’ consideration of the actors and viewers’ experience is reflected in their creative decision-making processes. We envision future research building on these findings.

title: Color, Culture, and Filmmaking: A Comparative Analysis of “The Body” and Its Cross-Cultural Remakes
authors: Jaime López-Díez; Víctor Suárez-Paniagua; Beatriz González; Pedro Antonio García López; Manuel Melgosa
abstract: This study examines the cross-cultural use of color in cinema by analyzing El cuerpo (2012) and three remakes from India (Bollywood and South Indian) and South Korea. Using quantitative methods, it compares Hue, Saturation, and Value to explore how filmmakers adapt color to local aesthetics while preserving the narrative. Results show that Hue—especially red tones—varies most, with the South Indian version differing most from the original. Saturation and Value show fewer differences. These findings support theories of cultural proximity and hybridization, suggesting that color is a key stylistic element in cultural adaptation. This study offers a novel approach to analyzing remakes as culturally mediated texts and highlights the value of visual style as an area of divergence in global cinema.

title: Social Interaction and Embarrassment in the Films by Ruben Östlund
abstract: A characteristic of Ruben Östlund’s films is their focus on social behavior and interaction at moments when social scripts are disrupted by instinctual behavior or conflicting concerns. Such disruptions create dilemmas within a given social situation, most often leading to embarrassment. The article examines the nature of (comic) embarrassment as the dominant social emotion in Östlund’s films, typically arising from a contrast between a desired projection of the self and one’s actual behavior within a social setting. Often, though, the durative observational style provides secondary characters and the audience with forms of vicarious embarrassment not necessarily shared by the main characters. It is argued that Östlund utilizes embarrassment in both playful and transgressive ways, which prompts ambiguity about how viewers may react to and interpret his films, but also has the potential to be a cinema of engagement.

title: Theatres of feminism and cinema’s vanished ladies: Dame May Whitty and Margaret Lockwood beyond the narrow gaze of Hitchcock Studies
abstract: In designating the male director-auteur the key to determining a film’s meaning and cultural value, film history and criticism have systematically devalued the impact of women working in the industry in other roles. Since the 1960s and the rise of academic film studies, Alfred Hitchcock has become emblematic of the field’s creative and gendered hierarchy, but among all the films he worked on, The Lady Vanishes (1938) is the one that he and many critics struggled to brand as the unquestionable property of the ‘Master of Suspense’. Claire Warden and Diana Taylor have argued that performance studies can successfully challenge 'the disciplinary compartmentalisation of the arts'; in this essay, focusing on actresses Dame May Whitty and Margaret Lockwood rather than on director Alfred Hitchcock is intended to revive conversations between women in theatre and film history, histories of feminist advocacy and the erasure of women on and off screen. The Lady Vanishes is a site of feminist history, renewal and possibility; in this essay it acts a two-way mirror, reflecting back upon Whitty’s legendary theatrical career and gazing forward to Lockwood’s rejection from the post-war British film industry and return to a life in the theatre. Ultimately, retracing the careers of The Lady Vanishes’ two female stars offers something beyond a feminist reconsideration of one of British cinema’s most beloved films. Whitty’s and Lockwood’s working experiences, spanning British entertainment history from the late 19th century through to the 1970s, offer a sobering comparison between women’s work in theatre and film under the growing shadow of male executives, critics and ‘star’ directors.
